7. The Committee in its meeting held on 13th August, 1998, sought certain clarifications from 
the Secretary, Legislative Department. Under Section 29 of the Administrators-General Act, 1963, 
the Administrator-General is empowered to issue a certificate to a claimant claiming assets of a 
deceased otherwise than as a creditor . The assets left by the deceased person for the purposes of the 
said Section does not include any sum of money in a Government Savings Bank or any provident 
fund account to which the Provident Fund Act, 1925 applies. The Committe wanted to lcnow the 
exact definition of the term 'Government Savings Bank' and the various types of Savings Sanies 
covered by the said term. The Commi11ee further enquired •as to which were the various provident 
funds coming under the purview of the Provident Fund Act, 1925 and whether the General Provident 
Fund and the Public Provident Fund were covered by the said Act. The Committee went on to 
enquire the names of the States/Union Territory Administrations, other than the 23 States/UTs which 
~upported the Bill. and what were their views in that regard. 
8. The Secretary replied that as far as the Bill was concerned, about all the savings schemes of the 
Post Offices like NSS. NSC etc., floated either through subordinate legislation or through notiftcations 
were covered . He clarified that it did not inlcude the savings accounts of the commercial banks and 
nationalised banks. The Secretary stated that in the area of provident funds there were three enactments 
of Parliament. Ona was the Provident Fund Act, 1925; the second one was the Employees' Provident 
Fund, 1952, and the third one was the Public Provident Fund Act, 1968. These three Acts differed in their 
nature. The Provident Fund Act of 1925, was enacted with a view to giving recognition to oertain provident 
funds which were already in existence . It may be a provident fund created under the proviso to Article 
309 of the Consiitution relating to the Government employees or any provident fund created by the 
railways . The Employees' Provident Fund Act covered the industrial employees. The Public Provident 
Fund Act, 1968 was a broad-based legislation. It was applicable to everybody. It was open 10 anybody to 
open an account either in one of the designated nationalised banll:s or in the post offices.

protect the assets. The Administration of the property was always done by the Civil Courts. Even the 
Administrator-General derived power from the High Court. The High Court was the overall authority in

decide the matter. The Administrator-General did not enter into the arena of disputes. He was only the 
custodian of the property. for its safe keeping. The principle underlying this legislation was that the 
property should not be misappropriated or disposed of. It was 81\ interim sort of arrangement. If there was

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Home Affairs, having been authorised by the 
Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Forty-ninth Report of the 
Committee on the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Bill, 1997*. 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Presiding Officer, Rajya Sabha referred**. The Code of Civil Procedure 
(Amendment) Bill, 1997 as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 14th August, 1997 and 
pending therein, to the earlier Committee (1997-98) for examination and report . 
3. The Committee (1997-98) considered the Bill in its meeting held on 30th September, 
1997 and heard the Secretary of the Legislative Department, Ministry of Law, Justice and 
Company Affairs on the provisions contained in the Bill. 
4. In the said meeting of the Committee, having regard to the special importance of the 
Bill which sought to streamline the procedural delays in the judicial process a~d amend 
certain Sections and Orders of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, decided to invite 
memoranda from individuals/organisations/ins titutions etc. interested in the subject matter 
of Bill. The Committee directed that a Press Communique may be issued in this behalf 
fixing November 10, 1997 as the last date for the receipt of memoranda. An advertisement 
was, accordingly, published in all the leading English and Vernacular dailies on 11th 
October, 1997. The matter was also broadcast/telecast repeatedly on All India Radio and 
Doordarshan to give it wide publicity. 
S. Since the intended amendments were of far-reaching importance to the .community of 
lawyers and litigants and would have a significant impact on the administration of justice, it 
was also decided to .invite views/suggestions from the Bar Council of India, State Bar 
Councils and Bar Associations of Allahabad, Bombay, Calcutta , Delhi, Guwahati, Kerala, 
Madras and two District Bar Associations from each S tate. Accordingly, !hey were 
requested to send their views/suggestions on the Bill. 
6. Before the Committee (1997-98) could proceed further with the consideration of the 
Bill, it got dissolved consequent upon the dissolution of the Eleventh Lok Sabha on 
4.12.1997. 
6.1 While the ~arlier Committee started receiving a large number of memoranda from 
different quarters, it also received requests for extension of time from the Bar Council of 
India and some Bar Councils! Associations of a few States seeking extension of time for 
submission of their views on the Bill. Before those requests for extension could be 
considered, the Committee got dissolved as mentioned earlier and the same continued to 
remain pending. 
7. The present Committee (1998-99) was constituted on 5th June, 1998. Due to change 
in Government ' at the Centre, it was decided that a reference may be made to the 
Legislative Deparnnent to let the Secretariat know the views of the present Government

11. The Bill contains 36 Clauses and seeks further to amend the Code of Civil 
Procedure, 1908, the Limitation Act, 1963 and the Court Fees Act, 1870. The Bill has been 
prepared by the Legislative Department in the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company 
Affairs with a view {o implementing the recommendations of Justice Malimath Committee

Report, 77th and 129th Reports of Law Commission of India and the 1st Report of the 
Committee on Subordinate Legislation (Eleventh Lok Sabha). 
11.1 The Statement of Objects and Reasons appended to the Bill says that the law 
relating to the procedure in suts and civil proceedings in India (except those in the State of 
Jammu & Kashmir and Nagaland and tribal areas of Assam and certain other areas) is 
contained in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Code has been amended from time to 
time by various act of Central and State Legislatures. The Code is mainly divided into two 
parts, namely, Sections and Orders. While the main principles are contained in the Sections, 
the detailed procedures with regard to the matters dealt with by the Sections are specified in 
the Orders. under Section 122, the High Courts have powers to amend, by rules, the 
procedure laid down in the Orders. In exercise of these powers, various amendments have 
beep made in the Orders by the different High Courts. 
12. The Secretary, Legislative Department, Ministry of Law, Justice and Company 
Affairs in his deposition on 30th September, 1997 apprised the Committee of the basic thrust 
of the Bill and its salient features. He explained the manner in which the amendments would 
help in the expenditious disposal of the pending cases in the various Courts and informed 
the Committee that the Bill was the first of its kind in the series to achieve the objective of 
ensuring the speedy trial of cases. The Secretary further stated that the Bill sought to 
implement the recommendations of the Report of the Arrears Committee (1989-90) 
constituted by the Government of India on the recommendations of the Chief Justices' 
Conference held at New Delhi on 11-13 December, 1987 (popularly known as the Justice 
Malimath Committee) and the 129th Report of the Law Commission on "Urban Litigants, 
Mediation as Alternative to Adjudication" which inter alia had suggested amendments to the 
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 with a view to making the consiliation scheme effective and to 
allow recording of the evidence by Commission. The Secretary went on to state that the Bill 
also incorporated the recommendations contained in the resolution adopted by the Law 
Ministers' Conference held in July, 1997 and the 1st Report of the Committee on 
subordinate Legislation (Eleventh Lok Sabha) which inter alia had observed that granting of 
unnecessary adjournment had become a regular feature. 
13. The background paper sent by the Ministry state$ that the problem of delay in 
disposal of cases has shaken the confidence of the people in the capacity of the courts to 
redress their grievances and to grant adequate and timely relief. Over the years the issue has 
been the subject matter of study and examination by the various Committees and 
Commissions. Notable among them are Rankin Committee (1925); High Court Arrears 
Committee (1949), High Court Arrears Committee (1969) and a number of reports of the 
Law Commission of India. The Law Commission's Report went into all aspects relating to 
reform of judicial administration (14th Report) and some of the Reports dealt with the 
measures for reducing delay at various stages of trial, both in civil and criminal cases. 
Reference may be made in particular to the 27th, 54th, 70th and 129th Reports. 
13.1 On the lines of the recommendations of the 27th, 54th and 55th Reports of the 
Law Commission, the Code of Civil Procedure was comprehensively amended by enacting 
the Code of Civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1976. 
13.2 Pendency of cases in various courts of the country was also discussed in the Annual 
Chief Justices' Conferences and in one of such Conference held in 1983 a Committee under 
the Chairmanship of Justice Satish Chandra was constituted. Certain recommendations of 
the said Committee have been implemented through various legislative and administrative 
measures. On the recommendation of the Chief Justices' . Conference held in 1987, the 
Government of India constituted a Committee in the year 1989 known as Justice Malimath 

4 
Committee, headed by Justice V.S. Malimath, the then Chief Justice of Kerala High Courts, 
to make indepth study of the problem of arreas in Courts and to suggest remedial measures. 
It is undisputed that for efficient discharge of the responsibility of the court, it is essential 
that the broad confidence which the people nave in them and the high prestige and great 
respect they have enjoyed should be maintained and not be subject to any eclipse. For this it 
is essential that the long delays in the disposal of cases at the stage of trial as well as at the 
appellate stage are to be curtailed. 
14. With a view to implementing the recommendations of the various committees , 
commissions and conferences as mentioned in the preceding paragraphs, Government 
thought that it is necessary to obtain the views of the State Governments on the subject also. 
In the Law Ministers' Conference held in New Delhi on 30th June and 1st July, 1997, the 
Working Paper on the proposed amendments to the Code of Civil Procedure was discussed. 
On the basis of the resolution adopted in the said Conference and with a view to­
implementing the recommendations supra, the Government introduced, the Bill in the Rajya 
Sabha on 14th August, 1997 to amend the Code of 1908, keeping in view, among others, 
that every effort should be made to expedite the disposal of civil suits and proceedings so 
that justice may not be delayed. 
15. Some of the more important changes proposed to be made in the Bill are as 
follows:-
( a) any plaint to be filed shall be in duplicate and shall be accompanied by all the 
documents on which the plainti(f relies upon in support of his claim. It is also to be 
supported by an affidavit stating the genuineness of the claim of the plaintiff and of 
the documents on which he relies upon; 
(b) the written statement in duplicate shall be accompanied by all the documents and 
shall be filed within a period of thirty days from the date of service of summons. 
Written-statement is also to be supported by an affidavit; 
(c) in order to obviate delay in service of summons, it is proposed that plaintiff shall 
take the summons from the court and send it to the parties, within two days of the 
receipt thereof, by post, fax, e-mail, speed post, courier service or by such other 
means as may be directed by the court; 
(d) with a view to implement the !29th Report of the Law Commission of India and to 
make conciliation scheme effective, it is proposed to make it obligatory for the 
court to refer the dispute after the issues are framed for settlement either by way of 
arbitration, conciliation, mediation, judicial settlement or through Lok Adalat. It is 
only after the parties fail to get their disputes settled through any one of the 
alternate dispute resolution methods that the suit shall proceed further in the court 
in which it was filed; 
(e) as the maximum time is consumed in recording oral evidence by the courts which 
causes delay in disposal of cases, it is proposed to reduce such delay by making 
provisions for filing of examination-in-chief of every witness in the form of an 
affidavit. For the cross-examination and re-examination of witnesses it is proposed 
that it shall be recorded by a Commissioner to be appointed by the court and the 
evidence recorded by a commissioner shall become part of the record of the suit; 

5 
(f) with a view to implement the recommendations of the Committee on Subordinate 
Legislation (Eleventh Lok Sabha) relating to steps to reduce unnecessary adjoum­
ments, it is proposed to make it obligatory for a judge to record reasons for 
adjournment of a case as well as award of actual or higher cost and not merely 
notional cost against the parties seeking adjournment in favour of opposite party. 
Further, it is proposed to limit the number of adjournments to three only during the 
hearing of a case; · 
(g) as the party in whose favour an injuction has been granted usually causes delay on 
filmsy and unreasonable grounds, it is proposed that the party who applies for 
injunction shall also furnish security so that that party may not adopt delaying 
tactics during the trial of the case; 
(h) in matters relating to property disputes, particularly in matter of unauthorised 
construction on the land of others, it has been found that, under the existing 
provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure, no application for injunction can be 
moved unless the suit is filed first in the court having competent jurisdiction . With a 
view to obviate this hardship, it is proposed that a person may make an application 
to the court of competent jurisdiction for appointment of a commission to ascertain 
the factual status of the property so that at the time of the filing of the regul~r suit 
the report is available to the Commissioner relating to the factual status. of the 
property in dispute; 
(i) with a view to implement the recommendations of Justice V.S. Malimath Commit­
tee, it is proposed that no further appeal against the judgement of a single judge 
shall lie even in -a petition under article 226 or 227 of the Constitution; and 
(j) with a view to reduce delay, it is proposed that the court shall on the date of 
pronouncement of judgement simultaneously provide authenticated copies of the 
judgement to the parties. Appeal shall be filed in the court which passes the decree 
and no notice shall be served on the advocates of the parties in the court of first 
instance.

18. The observations/recommendations and changes suggested by the Committee in the 
Bill and the reasons therefor are set out hereinafter. 
Clause 9 
18.1 Section 96 of the Code provides for an appeal from original decree. Since the time 
provisions were made, the value of money had considerably decreased and the pecuniary 
limits of three thousand rupees' required to be revised. Clause 9, therefore, sought to 
substitute twenty five thousand rupees in place of three thousand rupees' in Section 96. The 
Committee, however, felt that the enhancement of pecuniary limit suggested was on the high 
side and, therefore, recommended that the monetary limit may be kept at ten thousand 
rupees. 
18.2 The Committee adopted the clause, as amended.

Clause 26 
18.3 Order XVII Jays down the procedure for granting adjournments. The Committee 
on Subordinate Legislation (Eleventh Lok Sabha) recommended that it should be made 
obligatory in the judgement to record reasons for adjournment of cases as well as award of 
actual and not merely notional cost against the party seeking adjournment in favour of the 
opposite party. It is proposed to make it obligatory by amendment of proposed Order. It is 
proposed to make it obligatory for the judges to record the reasons in writing where the 
court grants adjournment and to award the actual cost to the opposite party. Further limit 
upto three adjournm~nts has also been fixed in a case. 
18.4 However. the Committee felt that the cost for granting adjournment should not be 
awarded to any of the parties. Instead that should either be deposited in the Government 
Treasury or should go to legal Aid Services Head of Account so that it would act as 
disincentive to the litigant parties wanting adjournment. 
18.5. As the idea mooted by the Committee was a new concept, the Committee desired 
that the same may be examined by the Ministry with regard to feasibility of depositing the 
cost in the Treasury;State Fund instead of paying it to the party concerned in the court. 
18.6 The matter has been examined by the Legislative Department and vide their 
communication dated 12th December, 1998 has stated as under:-
The hon'ble members of the Committee observed that generally the cost is not being 
paid to the parties concerned and in most of the cases the counsels of such parties 
receive the cost for their own. In this regard, it may be stated that sub-section (1) of 
section 35 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that "Subject to such conditions and 
limitations as may be prescribed, and to the provisions of any law for the time being in 
force, the cost of and incident to all suits shall be in the discretion of the Court, and the 
Court sh~ll have full power to determine by whom or out of what property and to what 
extent such costs are to be paid, and to give all necessary directions for the purposes 
aforesaid." Further, section 35B of the Code provides that costs for causing delay would 
be paid by such party to other party as may be ordered by the court. 
The aforesaid sections read with section 151 of the CPC, confer inherent power on -the 
court which is wide enough to include to give direction to deposit the cost in treasur)Vcourt 
instead of its payment in the court to the_concerned party. 
However, as per the terms and conditions of "V AKALATNAMAS" which are normally 
being filed in the courts in suits, the advocate of the concerned party is authorised to receive· 
or deposit money, etc. in the court on behalf of his client. 
In case, it is provided in law that the co~t imposed will firstly be deposited in the court! 
treasury and thereafter, the same may be paid to the entitled party in accordance with the 
procedure for taking out the money from the couftttreasury, the procedure may again be a 
complicated procedure and may further increase the burden of the concerned party for 
which he has again to depend upon advocates and to pay additional fee. Alternatively, if it is 
provided that cost imposed will be deposited in the State Fund, same shall be unreasonable 
and disadvantageous to the party entitled for such cost as the purpose of such cost is to meet 
the reasonable expenses of the ready party. Adjournment cost are intended to compensate 
the other party for the expenses it has incurred for the date fixed for hearing of the suit. 
18.7 In view of the position explained by the Legislative Department, the Committee 
adopted the clause without any change.

resides outside the local limits of the jurisdiction of the court. It is proposed to amend Order

REPORT OF THE COl\1MITTEE 
L the Chairmar1 of the Dcparlmcnt.- Rc:lated Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Home Affairs , having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its 
behalf, present this Fifth Repor. of the Committ~e. 
2. In pursuanr.:e of the rules relating to the Department-Related Parliamentary 
Standing Committees , the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Speaker , 
Lok Sabha, referred '" The Census (Amendment) Bill, 1992**, as introduced in the Lok 
Sabha on the 18th December, 1992 and pending in that House , to the Committee for 
examination and report. 
3. The Committee in its meeti ngs held on the 18th, 19th and 25th August, 1993 
discussed the provisions of the Bill and also heard the views of the represe:ntative s of 
the Ministries of Home Affairs and Law , Justice & Company Affairs. In its meeting 
held on the 25th August , 1993, the Committee took up clause-by-clause consideration 
of the Bill. 
In the said meeting the Committee considered and adopted the drafl Report. 
4. ln their background note supplied to the Committee, the Ministry of Home Affair~ 
explained the need for amending the Census At"t, 1948 as follows:-
'The Census is normally taken after every 10 years. The last Census being held in 
1991, the next decennial census would lake place in the year 2001 only. However . 
the Census Organisation is required to undertake surveys or census in parts of the 
country from time to time meet the exigencies of the situation. for example, an 
ethographic survey was done in Jammu & Kashmir in the year 1986-87 to identify 
the communities which should be declared as Scheduled Tribe s. Similarly, in 
Punjab, a survey was done in Kandu Khera village in the year 1986. That is, under 
the Census Act, 1948, census can be taken in any part of the country at any 
particular point of time. Accordingly , it is necessary to get the Census (Amend­
ment) Bill passed as quickly as possible to meet such emergent situations. 
Under the Census (Amendment) Bill, powers are being vested with the Central 
Government to determine the question .naire s for the Census. This power was 
earlier vested with the State Governments ... Different State Governments followed 
different approaches. This not only created administrative difficulties but also, due 
to lack of uniformity, led to uneven quality of data. However , the situation has 
changed drastically in the country during the last three or four decades and it is 
essentia l that there should be uniformity of norms and standards, etc. in the 
censuses and surveys throughout the country. It is towards this end that the powers 
to determine the census questionnaires are being vested with the Central 
Government under the Census (Amendment) Bill ... 
The Amendment Bill provides for requisitioning of vehicles and buildings under 
Section 7(A) to (H) so as to tackle difficulties faced in acquiring of buildings and 
the vehicles at the time of the Census. The requisitioning of buildings an.-1 vehicles 
under the Amendment Bill would be for a very short period ... 
The Census (Amendment) Bill also provides for prosecution and penalties for 
certain offences. Increasingly , it has been found that the Census enumerators and 
supervisors who are usually school teachers or other government functionaries are 
•Rajya Sabha Parliamentary B11llctin Part IJ dated the 6th August, 1993. 
••Published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary , Part II, Section 2, dated the 18th December , 1992. 

2 
un-willing to perform the census duty. Many census officials are also found to be 
negligent in discharge of their census duty. Some times there have been cases 
where the local authorities or other government departments refuse to give their 
personnel for census duties. There have been organised movement s hy the unions 
and staff associations against the performance of the census duti es. There have 
been organised movements in many parts of the country making it difficult to take 
the census. Organised movements also put pressure against census officials to 
record the particular responses to the census questions. In the past, the census 
organisations had to contend with organised movements whose aim was to secure 
inflated census returns in regard to certain religions or mother tongues. It is with 
this view that the Census (Amendment) Bill provides for various penalties. 
Creation of hindrance or obstruction by any person in performance of any duty 
under the Census Act is being made cognizable under the Amendment Bill. This 
Bill is primarily directed against the delinquent census officials and it does not tend 
to abridge the fundamental rights of citizens. In fact, the citizens' rights will not be 
abddged in any way by the Census (Amendment) Bill. Rather, it makes it 
mandatory on the part of _the Census enumerators to record an individual's 
response to census questions in truthful manner, and as such, protects the rights of 
an individual's response to census questions in truthful manner, and as such, 
protects the rights of an individual. Towards this end, putting of any offensive or 
improper questions or knowingly making any false return by a census official is 
being made cognizable offence under the Amendment Bill. Some of the other 
offences provided under the Census Act are also being made cognizable so as to 
act as a deterrent to those who refuse to perform census duties.' 
5. As a sequel to the submissions made by the representatives of the Ministry of 
Home Affairs before the Committee with regard to the justification for the Amending 
Bill, that Ministry in their supplementary note supplied to the Committee, stated as 
under: 
'It is proposed to amend the existing Census Act in order to ensure that the 
Central Government and through it the Census Commissioner of India is vested 
with sufficient authority to take action against any person who refuses to cooperate 
with the requirement of conducting national census. The need for this has been felt 
as the penalties already prescribed under Section 11 of the Census Act do not 
appear to be exhaustive or adequate for the purpose of ensuring smooth conduct of 
census operation in future ... 
The list of penalties under the present Act does not, for instance, cover cases of 
requisitioning premises, vessels, vehicles or animals needed or likely to be needed 
for the conduct of census. The present Act also does not safeguard the interest of 
persons who are asked to perform census duties, inasmuch as under the existing 
Act there is no obligation cast on the deputing organisations to treat the deputed 
staff as on duty. The rule making power under the existing Act would be of no 
avail to meet the chasm in such cases since, a rule cannot stand without support of 
express statutory provisions. It is precisely for this reason that amendments to the 
original Act have become necessary ... 
Partly to fill these lacunae and partly to bring the Census Act more in line with 
the realities of today's situation, amendments to the Act are proposed .... In future, 
because of the changing socio-economic climate more and more such occasions may 
arise and it would not do at all to be found wanting in adequate legal protection to 
back the direction. In this context, it needs to be pointed out that the purpose of 
introducing penal provision cannot be served by resorting to disciplinary proceed­
ings. The taking of census is a short period, time-bound programme. Departmental 

3 
proceedings are notoriously time-consuming. They are hardly likely to deter 
delinquent workecl. The proposed amendment provides for sufficient safeguard 
against any possible misuse of penal provisions. It is necessary to obtain previous 
sanction of the Central/State Governments before prosecuting any person. The 
need for seeking Central Government's prior sanction has been introduced only in 
limited cases. It would be easier for the Central Government in those cases to 
ascertain if any mitigating factors exist before deciding to sanction prosecution .... 
The proposed amendments, as pointed out above, are only supplementing and 
modifying the already existing provisions which regulate the conduct of all those 
involved in the Census taking. The amendments are in the nature of forearming 
the census organisation to deal with problems which seem to be in the offing .... It 
can be seen that the thrust of the proposed amendments is clearly and unmistak­
ably in favour of strengthening the perceived authority of the Census Commis­
sioner who is charged with an arduous responsibility of conducting time bound 
census all over the country. It is submitted that the proposed amendments would 
go a long way in stabilising the position of the Census Commissioner in a fast 
changing world where every action of the authorities is being questioned. If such a 
timely step is not taken, it may become difficult for the census organisation to hold 
census in future.' 
6. The Committee having heard the representatives of the Ministries of Home Affairs 
and Law, Justice and Company Affairs and having considered the notes on the subject, 
concludes that in view of the facts placed before it, related to the conduct of population 
census in the country, it has been found necessary to amend the Census Act, 1948 with 
a view to achieving the objectives as set out in the Statement of Objects and Reasons of 
the Amending Bill. Accordingly, Clauses 2 to 15 of the Bill were adopted by the 
Committee without any change. 
7. Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted with. some changes 
which are of consequential or drafting nature. 
8. The Committee recommends that the Bill, as reported, be passed.

STATEMENT ON THE LOKPAL BILL , 1998 
(J) A statement indicat ing the proviSions in the Lokpal Bill, 1996, the 
recommendations of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Home Affairs made thereon and the decision of the Government taken on each of 
the recommendations, which were included in the Lokpal Bill, 1998, is enclosed. 
(2) Apart from the recommendations of the Parliamentary Standing Committee, it was 
decided that in Clause 5 of the Lokpal Bill, 1996, which prescribed that a Member 
of the Lokpal shall be ineligible to hold other Offices, membership of the 
Legislature of a Union Territory should also be incorporated. This has been 
included in the Lokpal Bill, 1998. 
(3) Besides the recommendat ions of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on the 
Lokpal Bill, 1996, the following decision was also taken by the Government: 
"(1) In respect of the tenure and maximum age of the Chairman and Members of 
the Lokpal, the following provisions may be suitably incorporated in the 
Lokpal Bill:-
(i) A person appointed as Chairman shall hold office for a term of 3 years 
from the date on which he enters upon his office or until he attains the 
age of seventy years, whichever is earlier. 
(ii) A person appointed as Member shnll hold o ffice for n term of 3 years 
from the date on which he enters upon his of[icc or until he attains the 
age of seventy years, whichever is earlier. 
(iii) On ceasing to hold office, the Chairman or a Member shall be ineligible 
for funhcr employment under the Government of India or under the 
Government of any State. 
(iv) A person who has been -a Chairman or a Member of the Lokpal shall no.t 
be eligib le Cor re-appointment in the Lokpal. 
(2) In respec t of discharge of the functions of the Chairman owing to his absence 
on leave or otherwise, as also in the event of the occurrence of a vacancy by 
reason of his death, resignation or otherwise, the following provisions may be 
suitably incorporated in the Lokpal Bill:-
(i) In the event of the occurrence of any vacancy in the office of the 
Chairman by reason of his death, resignation or otherv.<ise. the President 
may, by notification, authorise one of the Members to act as the 
CHairman until the appointment of a new Chairman to fill such vacancy. 
(ii) When the Cha irman is unable to discharge his functions owing to absence 
on leave or otherw ise, such one of the .Members as the President may, by 
notificat ion, author ise in this behulf, shall discharge the functions of the 
Chairman until the date on which the Chairman resumes his duties." 
This has been incorporated m the Lokpal Bill, 1998.

11. The Central Vigilance Commission Bill, 1998 aims to provide for the constitution of a 
Cen tral Vigilance Commission to inquire or cause inquiries to be conducted into offences 
alleged to have been committed under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 by certain 
catego ries of public servants of the Central Government, corporations cstnblished by or under 
any Centra l Act, Government companies, societ ies and local authorities owned or controlled 
by the Central Government and for matters CO!)nected therewith or incidental thereto. 
12. Following are the salient features of the Bill:-
(i) The Central Vigilance Commission shall consist of a Central Vigilance Commissioner 
as Chairperson and not more than four Vigilance Commbsioners as Members; 
(ii) The Central Vigilance Commissioner and the Vigilance Commissioners shall be 
appointed from amongst persons:-
(a) Who have been or are man all-India Service or in any civil service of the Union 
or in a Civil post under the Union having knowledge and experience in the 
matters relating to vigilance, policy making and administration including police 
administra tion; 
(b) Who have held office or a re holding office in a corpora tion established by or 
under any Centra l Act or a Government company owned or contro lled by the 
Central Government and persons who have expertise and experie nce in finance 
including insurance und banking, law, vigilance and investigation: 
Subject to the condition that from amongst the Central Vigilance Commissioner and 
the Vigilance Commissioners, not more than three persons shall belong to the 
categories of persons referred to eithe r in (a) or (b) above; 
(iii) The Central Vigilance Commissioner and Vigilance Commissioners shall be 
appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal and their appointment 
shall be made after obtaining the recommendations of a Committee consisting of the 
Prime Minister as Chairperson, the Minister of Home Affairs and the Leader of the 
Opposition in the House of the People as Members; 
(iv) The term of the Centra l Vigilance Commissioner shall be for a period of four years 
from the date on which he enters upon his office or till be atta ins the age of 65 years 
whichever is earlier; 
(v) The term of a Vigilance Commis~io ner sha ll be for a period of three years from the 
date on which be enters upon his office or till he attains the age of 65 years whichever 
is earlier: and 
(vi) On ceasing to hold office, the Central Vigilance Commissioner and every other 
Vigilance Commissioner shall be ineligible for reappointment tn the Commi.ssion and 
further employment to any office of profit under the Government of India or the 
Government of a State.

The Cen tral Vigilance Commission has been made a multi-member body in order to

26 thereof is reproduced below:-
"The re is no doubt that :wo heads are better than one, and particular ly when an 
institution like the Election Comm ission is entrusted with vital functions , and is

desira ble that the powers are not exercised by one individual , however, all-wise he

independence of an institution depends upon the persons who man it and not on

exercised by an institution which is ;,ccounwble to none , it is politic to entrust its 
affairs to more bands than one . It helps to assure judiciousness and want . of 
arbitrariness. The fact, however. remains that where more individuals than one, man 
an institu tion, the ir roles have to be clearly defined , if the functioning of the 
institutio n is not to come to a naught" .

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 
In pursuance to the recommendati o ns of the Commiltcc on Prevention of 
Corruption headed by Shri K. Sanrhan am . the erstwhile Central Vigilance 
Commission was set up vide Resolution No. 2417/64-A VD dated the llth 
Febr uary, 1964. The said Resolution inter alia provide d that the Central 
Vigilance Commissioner would be au·achcd to the Ministry of Home Affi1irs 
(now !be Ministry of Personnel , Public Grievances and Pensions). but in the 
exercise of its powers and functions it will not be subordinate to any Ministry/ 
Department and will have the same measure of independe nce and autonomy as 
the Union Public Service Commission. Paragraph 3 of the said Resolution also 
stipulated that the Cen tral Vigilance Commissioner will be appointed by the 
President by warrant under his hand and seal and that he will not be removed or 
suspended from the office except in the manner provided for the removal or 
suspension of the Chairma n or a Member of the Union Public Service 
Commission. This Resolution was amended in November, 1995 deleting the 
prov ision relating to appointment of tlte Cent ral Vigilance Commissioner by the 
Preside nt by warrant under his hand and seal. 
2 . In September , 1997, the Government constituted an Independent Review 
Committee (IRC) comprisi ng Shri B.G. Deshmukh. Shri S.V. Giri and Shri 
N.N. Vohra tO suggest measu res for stre ngthening inter alia, anti-corrupt ion 
activities as part of its efforts against -corruption . One of the rc.commcndations 
made by the IRC was that the quest ion of conferr ing statutOry sta tus tO the 
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) alongwith the restoration of the provision 
relating to appointmenr of the Central Vigilance Commissioner being made 
unde r the hand and seal of the Presiucn1 may be considered by the 
Government . The fRC also recommended that the Central Vigilance 
Commission sho uld be made responsible for the efficient functioning of the CB!. 
3. Subsequently, the Supreme Court vide its order dated 18th December. 1997 
in Criminal Writ Pctiuons Nos . 340-343193-Vinect Narain and others versus 
Union of India and others (generally known as Jain Hawala case} had imcr alia 
give.n directions that statutory status should be C011ferred upon the Centra l 
Vigilance Commission. Several consequences of the conferment of such status 
were also dkectcd by the Supreme Coun to follow. 
4. While the activo on the formulation of the suitable legislation for the 
conferment of statutory status to the CVC was under way.-thc then Chief 
Vigilance Commissioner in position resigned and hence appointmen t to senior 
posts in Public Secto r Undertaki ngs. National ised Banks and Financial 
Institutions could not be finalised and mndc. Besides. matters relating to grant 
of sanction of prosecution of certain categories of public servants also rema ined 
pending in such a situation. In view o·f the urgency involved in the maucr and 
keeping in mind the fact that the next Session or Parliament was likely to take 
place not earlier than Novetnber, 1998. the Government decided 10 put the 
proposed law in place through an Ordinance . Acording ly, the Central Vigilan ce 
Commiss ion Ordinance. 1998 (Ord. l5 of 1998) was promulgated by the 
President on the 25th August. 1998. 
5. Subsequent to the promulgation of the Ordi nance on the 25th August,

filed certain written objections objecting 10 certain prov ision of the Ordinance. 
In order 10 rectify the position and after obtain ing the views of the Attorney

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Home Affairs, having been authorised by the Committee . to present the Report on its 
behalf, present this Fifty-second Report of the Committee, relating to the Notaries 
(Amendment) Bill, 1997: 
2. In pursuance of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committees, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, in consultation with the Speaker, Lok Sabha, 
referred•• the Notaries (Amendment) Bill 1997, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on the 4th 
August, i997 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report. 
3. The Notaries Act, 1952 (Act No. 53 of 1952) was enacted by Parliament on the 9th 
August, 1952 and came into force w.e.f. the 14th February, 1956. Before the Notaries Act 
came into force, the notarial functions were regulated by the Negotiable Instruments Act, 
1881 (Act No. 26 of 1881). A need was felt to provide a separate Act dealing with all 
aspects of notaries when it was found that the provisions of the negotiable Instruments Act, 
1881 were not sufficient to cater to the needs of developing India. The Notaries Act is a 
Central Act but the subject "Legal Profession" falls in the Concurrent List of the 
Constitution and hence the Central Government as well as the State Governments are 
administratively competent to appoint notaries . 
. 4. No major amendments in the Notaries Act, 1952 have been made .so far. The 
Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs received several references from various State 
Governments to amend the Notaries Act, 1952 regarding renewal of the certificate; fee 
chargeable by the notaries; qualifications prescribed for appointment of notaries; 
standardization of seal used by notaries; and the fee for appointment etc. of notaries. The 
Ministry examined the suggestions/recommendations received from various State 
Governments and also the suggestions received from various Notaries' Associations in India. 
5. With a view to studying all. aspects relating to the functioning of the Act, a 
Committee was constituted by the Ministry under the Chairmanship of Dr. V.K. Agarwal, 
the then Additional Secretary , Department of Legal Affairs. The Committee included 
representatives of the States of Maharashtra, Punjab, Karnat aka, U.P. and West Bengal. 
The Committee recommended* .. the amendment of Section 2(c), i.e. the definition of 'Legal 
Practitioner'; amendment of Section 5, i.e. Renewal of Certificate; amendment of Section 
10, i.e. Removal of names from the Register of Notaries maintained by the CentraVState 
Government; amendment of Section 12, i.e., a person falsely representing as a Notary and 
the penalty prescribed thereof; and amendment of Section 15(2)(a) , i.e. the power to make 
rules to carry out the purposes of this Act. 
*Published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary , Part-II, Section 2 dated the 4th August, 1997. For a copy of 
the Bill, please see Annexure-!. 
••Rajya Sabha Parliamentary Bulletin Part II dated the 5th August, 1997. 
•••see Annexure II for the Report (1994) of the Committee to review all aspects relating to the Administration 
of Notaries Act, 1952, and Notaries Rules, 1956, Ministry of Law, Justice & Company ~ffairs .

2 
6. An All India Notaries' Conference took place at Panjim in Goa on the 16th 
February, 1997. ,The Conference was attended by the notaries from most of the States in 
india. It was .inaugurated by the then Union Minister of State for Law & Justice. The 
Conference considered the Report of the Committee. It disagreed with the recommendation 
of the Committee for the amendment of Section 5. It was stated in the Conference: 'Once a 
notary always a notary is our moto. Rigours of renewal should be dispensed with specially 
when the notaries have already put in professional experience of 10 years and are also 
eligible for Higher Judicial Service.' The Conference was also against prescribing any age 
limit or number of renewals. Similar views were also received from various State Notaries' 
Associations before and after the Conference. The then Minister had accepted the 
suggestion that renewal should be for five years; there should be no limit on renewals; and 
there sho~Ild be no age limit. However, he had also agreed with the view that the renewal 
should not be automatic. 
7. The then Minister had d~sired that the notaries may be involved in the court process 
to ease the burden of courts and tribunals throughout the country; that they could make 
useful contribution in the Alternative Dispute Redressal System by working as arbitrators, 
mediators and conciliators for settling petty cases. He was of the view that with the opening 
of the world economy increase in trade would result in a new regime of legal system and 
notaries would have grea~er role with an increasing demand for documentation. He, 
therefore, suggested that the notaries who have 10 years' experience at the Bar should be 
eligible for appointment as pro tem judges or magistrates in the absence of sitting judge or 
magistrate on being so directed. They should also be able to act as commissioners to record 
evidence in any civil and criminal trial if so directed by any court or authority. 
8. The amendments in the Notaries Act were also considered by the Law Ministers from 
various States in their Conference held on the 301h June and the P1 July, 1997. The Law 
Ministers unanimously accepted the proposed amendments. 
9. The Notaries (Amendment) Bill, 1997 seeks to amend the Notaries Act, 1952 to 
provide inter alia for:-
' 
(a) rationalisation of the procedure for renewal of certificate of practice; 
(b) the exercise of the functions of pro tem judge, magistrate, commissioner, arbitrator 
etc. by a notary when so directed; 
(c) the removal of the name of a notary on convictiOn by a court for any offence 
involving moral turpitude or for failing to get the ~ertificate renewed; 
(d) enhancing the quantum of punishment for falsely representing as a notary or doing 
any notarial act in contravention of Section 9 from three months to one year. 
10. Based on the papers supplied by the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs 
(Department of Legal Affairs), certain questions/issues were framed and comments of the 
Ministry were sought thereon which have been summadsed as follows: 
935 RS F-3·B 

3 
Question/issue 
(I) Which are the circumstances or conditions under which the renewal of certificate 
may be refused by the Government to a notary? Will the Government have 
absolute discretion in such matters or whether it will not be desirable as 
recommended by the Committee on Notaries to provide grounds in the law itself on 
the basis of which the renewal of a certificate of practice may be refused to a 
notary? 
Government's reply 
Discretion is always exercised judiciously. If a notary files his return in time 
requesting Government to renew the certificate, deposits requisite fee for renewal in 
time, no case is pending against him, he is of sound health and is not otherwise 
unfit, normally his certificate will be renewed. For the renewal of a certificate of 
practice he has to follow the above noted procedure. 
Committee's views/observations 
The reply is not at all satisfactory. The pointed question has not been replied. 
Question/issue 
(II) Whether Government has ever conducted any survey to evaluate the performance 
of notaries? Whether it will not be desirable to have some kind of standing 
mechanism to monitor the functioning of the notaries and bring about necessary 
improvements from time to time? 
Government's reply 
The Government has standing mechanism to monitor the functions of the Notaries. 
The District Judges, being the competent authority appointed by State Government, 
have the power to check the notarial register used by a notary while discharging his 
functions . .The competent authority appointed for the purposes of the Act also 
receives the annual return from the notaries and scrutinizes it. The specimen 
signatures and rubber stamps/seals are checked from time to time. These measures . 
are ad.opted to streamline their functions. · 
Committee's views/observations 
The reply is unsatisfactory. 
Question/issue 
(III) The Committee on Notaries Act has made some observations concerning the 
Notaries Rules, 1956, particularly about fixation of upper age limit for Notaries, 
qualifications for their appointment, fees payable to a notary and enlarging , the 
source for appointing. the notaries. What is Government's views regarding these 
observations/recommendations and whether the Notaries Rules are also proposed to 
be amended accordingly? 
Government's ' reply 
The amendment of the Notaries Rules, 1956 will be taken up after the notaries Act, 
1952 is amended. 

4 
Committee's views/observations 
The reply is evasive. 
11. The previous Committee heard the then Law Secretary in its meeting held on the 
29th September, 1997. In the said meeting of the Committee , several queries were put 
relating to provisions of the Bill which were replied to by the then Secretary. The main 
thrust of the discussion in the Committee, however, revolved around clause 4 of the Bill 
proposing to empower the notaries to act as a pro tern judge or magistrate in the absence of 
a sitting judge or magistrate; to act as a commissioner to record evidence in any civil or 
criminal trial; and to act as an arbitrator, mediator or a conciliator. The Committee in 
particular wanted to know as to how and under what circumstances the notaries would be 
required to act as pro tern judge/magistrate/commissioner/conciliator; whether the 
Government would fix responsibility and accountability on them consequent upon giving 
them additional powers which would be in the nature of judicial functions; whether 
Government was contemplating to make rules and regulations more stringent to ensure their 
responsibility and accountability; what would be the additional qualifications concomitant 
with higher responsibility and corresponding accountability attached to the additional power. 
12. A view was expressed in the Committee that the proposed amen·dment would have 
far reaching cpnsequences. An apprehension was also expressed that the proposed 
amendment in Section 8 of the Principal Act ·giving powers to the Government was 
arbitrary. In the same genre a question was posed whether it was proper to give too much 
power to any entity including the Government. What would happen if that person acting as 
pro · tem judge or magistrate pronounced some judgement which was bad in law, was among 
the several other questions posed. 
13. In response to the above questions/queries and apprehensions the then Law 
Secretary inter alia stated that clause 4 of the Bill seeking to amend Section 8 of the 
Principal Act was not recommended by the Committee on Notaries. It was based on the 
suggestion by the then Law Minister in the All India Notaries Conference. It was more• in 
the nature of an enabling provision. If there was any shortage of judges/magistrates or in 
any case the courts did not find time for recording evidence, then they could call a notary 
and ask him to sit and record evidence. It was only to expedite the process. If the court 
decided, then only notaries could be permitted to discharge the functi9ns. 
14. The Secretary went on to explain that the intention behind the proposal was that if a 
judge/magistrate was on leave or unavailable and if the Government thought it proper, it 
could direct a particular notary to record evidence in a civil or criminal trial. The Secretary 
observed that even presently advocates were being given this function under the C.P.C. The 
notaries were also advocates and without this amendment they could be directed to record 
evidence. To act as arbitrators they did not need any authority under the Act. Any person 
can be appointed as an arbitrator. 
15. The Secretary went on to say that so far as the pro tern judge or magistrate was 
concerned, such a ·system was prevailing in Goa sometime back under the Portugese Law 
and this had been included in the Bill on the suggestion of Law Minister. 
16. The Secretary further, observed that the Ministry was ·considering to add a provision 
in the C.P.C. conferring power on Government to appoint a person as a pro tern judge and 
in that case a notary too would be entitled to be appointed as such. The present Bill. only 
makes a notary eligible to be appointed as a pro tern judge. 

5 
17. Thereafter, a Member of the previous Committee while stating that -the Law of 
Notaries in the country was defective in many ways, shared with the Committee at length his 
knowledge of the functioning of notaries during the French Rule in Pondicherry . He inter 
alia requested the Committee to visit Pondicherry and study the institution which was 
prevalent during the French Rule. 
18. In conclusion, the previous Committee felt the need to study in greater detail the 
various aspects related to the proposed amendments and in this context decided to examine 
the system of Notaries prevailing in the U.K., Switzerland, Sweden, France, the U.S.A. and 
Malaysia. In order to facilitate the work of the Committee, the Chairman of the Committee 
had specifically asked the then Law Secretary to furnish notes on the current status of the 
institution of the Notaries as it obtained in the aforesaid countries and how the functions of 
the Notaries were being discharged there. 
19. The pr~vious Committee also decided to visit Pondicherry at a convenient date to 
study the operation of the Law of Notaries there vis a vis the one prevalent during the 
French Rule and interact with some of the persons associated with the a4ministration of the 
Law during that period . The Committee further decided to hear the representatives of Delhi 
Notaries Association in the matter . 
19.1 In this connection , the then Chairman had also asked the then Law Secretary ·to 
study various aspects of the institution of Notary as it obtained in Pondicherry during French 
Rule and send a report thereon to the Committee. 
20. Sub~quent to the meeting of the Committee held on 29th September, 1997 the 
Department of Legal Affairs vide their O.M. dated the 17'h October, 1997 had forwarded 
copies of relevant Acts of England on Notaries. In the said communication that Department 
had stated that the Notaries Act of the various countries like France, Switzerland, Malaysia, 
Sweden, the U.S .A. had not been traced out in any Library. However, that Department had 
been searching for the relevant material. 
20.1 On the 23rd October, 199'7 a communication was sent from the Secretariat to the 
Department of Legal Affairs reminding them to take jmmediate necessary action to furnish 
detailed notes on (i) current status of the institution of Notaries obtaining in the aforesaid 
six countries and whether some of the features thereof could be adopted to suit our needs 
and (ii) Institution of Notary in Pondicherry during French Rule. 
20.2 As no reply was forthcoming, the Department of Legal Affairs was again reminded 
on the 17th November, 1997. Thereafter, there had been no response from the Department 
in the matter. Subsequently, the previous Committee got dissolved consequent upon the 
dissolution of the Eleventh Lok Sabha on the 4th December , 1997. The then Chairman of 
the Committee directed the Secretariat that since the Lok Sabha had been dissolved the 
matter may be placed before the new Committee. 
21. After constitution of the present Committee, a reference was made to the 
Department of Legal Affairs on the 4'h August, 1998 to let the Committee know the 
willingness of the Government in pursuing the Bill in its present form. The Department after 
nearly three months responded on the 29'h October, 1998 stating that the Government 
wanted to pursue the Bill in Parliament in its present form. 
22. The Committee in its sitting held on the 8'h Februar y, 1999 took up consideration of 
the Bill from w.here it was left by the previous Committee . 
23. At the outset, the Chairman apprised the Committee of the decisions taken by the

carried out in the Notaries Act, 1952 were of non-contentious nature, it may dispose of the

clause 4 (a) (ha), relating to exercise of the functions of pro tem judge or magistrate by a 
Notary when so directed, all other provisions were innocuous. With regard to the aforesaid 
clause, the Committee finds it totally incongruent with the uther Jaws of the country. The 
Committee opines that the functioning of a Notary is different from that of a judge or 
magistrate. Since a notary's duty is basically to authenticate, verify, certify documents,

CHAPTER-III 
THE NOTARIES ACT, 1952 
The present Notaries Act, 1952 (Act 53 of 1952) was passed by the Parliament on 
9th August, 1952. Before this Act came into force, the notaral functions were regulated by 
the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (Act 26 of 1881). After India, became independent , it 
was felt that these provisions were insufficient to satisfy the needs of developing India and 
there should be a separate Act comprehensively dealing with all aspects of notaries. Hence , 
iii '19521 Parliament enacted the Notaries Act, 1952. It came into force on 4th February , 
1956. No major amendment has been made in the Act since then. 
2. The Notaries Act, 1952 extends to the whole of India including the State of Jammu 
and Kashmir. It was extended to the State of Sikkim by an order of the Government of 
India No. S.0.210(E) dated 16th May; 1975. 
3. Amendment of Section 2(c) 
3.1 Section 2 of the Notaries Act, 1952 contains definitions. It does not define the word 
'Advocate'. Sub-section (c) of Section 2 defines the word 'legal practitioner'. The said 
definition is as follows: 
" 'legal practitioner' mean S" any advocate or agent of the Supreme Court or any 
ad'o(ocate, vakil or attorney of any High Court or any pleader authorised under any 
law for the time being in force to practise in any court of Jaw." 
3.2 The Committee felt that after coming into force of the Advocates Act , 1961 this 
definition is no more relevant. Various categories of legal practitioners, such as, vakil~ 
pleaders, mukhtars, attorneys do not exist any longer. Now, advocates enrolled under the 
Advocates Act, 1961 alone are entitle to practise law in any courts. In view of the above, 
the Committee is of the opinion that this definition requires to be amended in terms of the 
provisions of the Advocates Act, 1961. 
3.3 The Committee therefore, recommends that the said definition of the word 'legal 
practitioner' may be substituted by the following definition: 
" 'legal practitioner' means an advocate entere·d in any roll under the provision~ of 
the Advocates Ac.t, 1961 (Act 25 of 1961)." 
4. Amendment of. Section 5 
4.1 Section 5 of the Notaries Act, 1952 is an important provision. Sub-section (2) of 
Section 5 gives a right to a notary who wishes to continue practise, after the expiry of the 
period for which he was appointed as notary, that on payment of the prescribed fee, he shall 
be entitled to the renewal of his certificate of practice for three ye.ars at a time. It is as 
follows: 
"Every such notary who wishes to continue to practise after the expiry of the period 
for which his certificate of practise has been issued under this section shall, on 
application made to the Government appointing him and payment of the prescribed 
fee, if any, be entitled to have his certificate of practice renewed for three years at a 
time." 
4.2. The Committee noted that this· provision gives a right to a notary to get his 
30 

31 
certificate of practice renewed for a period of three years. Once a notary submits an 
application for the renewal of his certificate of practice and pays the prescribed fee, the 
certificate of practice has to be renewed. The use of the word "shall" in section 5(2) creates 
a vested right in favour of a person once appointed as a notary. Further the said provision 
does not place any limit on the number of renewals. A certificate of practice can be renewed 
for indefinite number of times. In other words, the extension of the term of a notary is 
automatic and perpetual. The appropriate Government has no discretion in the matter. The 
said provision does not give power to the appropriate Government, even to scrutinise the 
application at the time renewal is sought, with a view to ascertaining whether the certificate 
of practice of a notary deserves to be renewed or not. 
4.3 The experience of some of the representatives of the State Governments has been 
that this provision has not worked well in the past. The Government had no choice in the 
matter of renewal of a certificate of practice even if it is of the opinion, for valid reasons, 
that the ·certificate of practice should not be renewed. 
4.4 The Committee generally agreed that it is necessary to fix a limit beyond which a 
certificate of practice must not be renewed. With this end in view, various options were 
considered. Some members of the Committee were of the view that limit should relate to the 
age of a notary. After the notary has attained a particular age, he should not be eligible for 
seeking renewal of the certificate of practice. In this context various age limits, such 13S 65 
year, 75 years, 80 years were suggested . Other members felt that the fixation of age limit for 
the purposes of renewal of the certificate of practice would not be appropriate, 'the reason 
being that an advocate is more in need of money when he is old and unable to attend the 
court work. To deprive him of the benefit of notaryship at that age will not be appropriate. 
After long deliberations, the Committee came to the conclusion that this provision which 
deals with renewal should not be linked with age. 
4.5 The Committee, therefore, feels that the limit sh9uld be linked to the renewals. A 
certifi'cate of practice should not be renewed for more than three time, each renewal being 
of 3 years. Thus, the total ·period permissible to a person, once appointed as a notary, 
should not be more than 12 years - three years being initial appointment period and nine 
years being three renewals of three years each. Further that such renewals should not be 
automatic and compulsory. The appropriate Government should have a right to. scrutinise an 
application for renewal and may renew the certificate of practice at its discretion. 
4.6 The GovemmeJ.I)t, however, should not have absolute discretion in the matter. The 
said discretion should be· guided or regula ted by law. The law should provide grounds on the 
basis of which the renewal of a certificate of practice may oe refused. Such ground may 
include public interest, medical grounds, ethical grounds, and so on. Further, the principles 
of natural justice demands that before an application for renewal of a certificate of practice 
is rejected, the notary should be given an · opportunity of being heard. · Thus, if a 
Government proposes to reject an application for the renewal of the certificate of practice, 
the notary should be given a show cause notice to reply within 15 days. 
4.7 The Committee has expressed the view that the total period during whfch a person 
can act as notary should be 12 years. The Committee does not wish to debar a person from 
becoming notary again after 12 years, if he is found fit for such an appointment by the 
Government. Hence, it should be specifically provided that after 12 years a notary may be 
eligible for re-appointment. 
4.8 The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that the existing sub-section (2) of 
Section 5 should be repealed and substituted by the following sub-section:-

32 
"Every such notary who wishes to continue to practice after the expiry of the 
period for which his certificate of practice has been issued under this section may 
make · an , application to the Government appointing hil]l for renewal of his 
certificate of practice. On receipt of such application the Government appointing 
him may ' renew his certificate of practice for a further term of three years on 
payment of the prescribed fees, subject to a maximum of three such renewaJs. No 
application of a notary for renewal of a certificate of practice shall be rejected 
unless he has been given a notice to show cause. The notary who has ceased to be 
so may be eligible for re-appointment." 
5. Amendment of Section 10 
5.1 Section 10 of the Act prescribes grounds for removal of name of a notary from the 
Register of Notaries maintained by the Government under Section 4 of the Act. It is a& 
follows: 
"Removal of names from Register:- The Government appointing any notary may, 
by order, remove from the Register maintained by it under Section 4 of the name 
of the notary if he -
(a) makes a request to that effect; or 
(b) has not paid any prescribed fee required to be paid by him; or 
(c) is an undischarged insolvent; or 
(d) has been found , upon inquiry in the prescribed manner, to be guilty of such 
professional or other misconduct as, in the opinion of the Government , 
renders him unit to practise as a notary. " 
5.2 This section contains four grounds. If any of the ground exists, the name of a notary 
can be removed from the Register of Notaries. These grounds do not include conviction of a 
notary, by a criminal court, for an offence. Thus, the name of a notary can't be removed 
from the Register of Notaries even if he commits an offence or is sentenced by a court. The 
conviction of a notary by a court of competent jurisdiction for an offence involving moral 
turpitude is a serious matter. Such a person looses the confidence of the society and should 
not be allowed to practice -as a notary. Further, conviction for an offence involving moral 
turpitude is also a disqualification under various other laws. The Committee, therefore, is of 
the view that conviction by a court for an offence involving moral turpitude should be a 
ground for the removal of his name from the Register of Notaries. 
5.3 While recommending amendment of Section 5(2), the Committee has recommtnded 
that the Government should have a right to scrutinise an application for the renewal of the 
certificate of practice. If for valid reasons, the Government decides that a particular 
certificate of practice should not be renewed, then, it should be a ground for the removal of 
name of the notary from the Register of notaries. In fact this is a consequential amendment. 
If the certificate of practice has not been renewed, he cannot practice as a notary and his 
name has to . be removed from the Register of Notaries. 
5.4 Another ground which needs to be added in this section is a failure to renew a 
certificate of practice. If a notary does not apply for the renewal of the certificate of practice 
and the period for which it was issued or previously renewed has expired, his name has to be 
removed fro~ the Register of Notaries. Though in the normal course also when a certificate 
of notary is not validly in existence, the notary ceases to be so. Nevertheless, the Committ ee 
feels that since amendments to the Notaries Act, 1952 are being considered, it is better to 

33 
make a specific provision rather than to leave it for future dispute~ and varying court 
interpretations. 
5.5 The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that the existing section 10 should be 
substituted by the following:-
"Removal of names from Register:-The Government appointing any notary may, 
by order, remove from the register maintained by it under section 4 of the name of 
the notary if he-
(a) Makes a request to that effect; or 
(b) has not paid any prescribed fee required to be paid by him; or 
(c) .is an undischarged insolvent; or 
(d) has been found, upon inquiry in the prescribed manner, to be guilty of such 
professional or other misconduct as, in the opinion of the Government, 
renders him ·unfit to practise as a notary; 
(e) is convicted by any court for an offence involving moral turpitude; 
(f) ·does not get his certificate of practice renewed; and 
(g) the certificate of practice is not renewed by the Government appointing him." 
On the removal of the name, the person shall cease to be a notary from the day the order 
is passed removing the name from the Register of notaries. 
6. Amendment of Section 12 
6.1 Existing Section 12 provides for punishment to a Notary who falsely represents that 
he is a notary without being appointed as such or practices as a notary or does any notarial 
act in contravention of Section 9. The punishment provided is imprisonment for a term 
which may extend to three months or with fine or with both. It is as follows: -
"12. Penalty for falsely representing to be a notary, etc. - Any person who -
(a) falsely represents that he is a notary without being appointed as such, or 
(b) practises as a notary or does any notarial act in contravention of section 9, 
shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to three 
months, or with fine, or with both." 
6.2 The Committee feels that the period of imprisonment of three -months is inadequate. 
It does not have sufficient deterrent effect. In order that this provision should act as a 
deterrent for a person to commit the offence mentioned above, the quantum of punishment 
should be increased. Some Members of the Committee were of the opinion that in order 
that this provision really acts as a deterrent, a minimum punishment of six months should be 
provided. A discretion should be given to the court to provide a punishment of less than six 
months for reasons to be recorded in writing. The other Members were of the opinion that 
the ··nature of offence prescribed by Section 12 is not such as to warrant a minimum 
punishment. After a long deliberation, the Committee decided against prescribing a 
minimum punishment. On the question of maximum punishment, the views of the Members 
were unanimous. It was agreed that the punishment should be increased from three months 
to one year. " 
6.3 The Committee is, therefore, of the opinion that in Section 12, quantum of 
punishment should be increased to one year thus the words by "one year or with fine or with 

34 
both" may be substituted for the words "three months or with fine or with both. The 
amended Section 12 should read as follows: 
"12. Penalty for falsely representing to be a notary, etc. - Any person who­
(a) falsely represents that he is a notary without being appointed as such, or 
(b) practises as a notary or does any notarial act in contravention of Section 9, 
shall be punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one 
year, or with fine, or with both." 
7. Amendment to Section 15. 
7.1 Section 15(1) of the Act enables the Central Government to make rules to carry out 
the purposes of the Act: Sub-section (2) of Section 15 enumerates matters in respect of 
which rules can be made. 
Clause (a) of Sub-section (2) of Section 15 enables the Central Government to make 
rules regarding qualification of a notary, the form and manner in which applications for 
appointment as, a notary !Jla.Y be made and the disposal of such applications. 
This sub-section does not provide for prescribing age limit' for the purposes of eligibility 
for appointment as a notary. The Committee is of the view that this sub-section .should be 
suitably amended to enable the Central Government to frame rules to prescribe the age limit 
for the purpose of eligibility for appointment as a notary. 
7.2 Clause (e) of Sub-section (2) of Section 15 enables the Central Government to make 
rules regarding fees payable by a notary to the appropriate Government for appointment as 
a notary for issue and renewal of a certificate of practice. This suh-sedion reads as follows: 
-"(c) The fees payable for appointment as a notary and for the~issue and renewal of a 
certificate of practice, and exemption, whether wholly or in part, from such fees in 
specified classes of cases." 
7.3 Sometimes, the notaries submit applications seeking extension or enlargement of the 
area of practice. There may be various reasons for a notary seeking enlargement of the areas 
of practice. In many such cases the Government also does not have any objection to such an 
enlargement of the area of practice . However, as there is no provision for levying fees for 
such services the Governments have in the past been reluctant in doing this service or 
charging fees for such service without authority of law. 
7.4 The Committee is, therefore,' of the view that Section 15(2)(a) and 15(2)(c) may he 
amended so as to read as follows: 
"(a) The qualifications of a notary, age limit for the purpose of eligibility of 
appointment as a notary, the grounds for refusal for renewal of a certificate of 
practice, the form and manner in which applications for appointment as a notary may 
be made and the disposal of such applications; 
(c) the fees payable for appointment as a notary for the issue and renewal of a 
certificate of practice and for the enlargement of the area of practice, and exemption, 
whether wholly or in part, from such fees in specified classes of cases." 

CHAPTER-IV 
THE NOTARIES RULES, 1956 
1.1 After having examined the provisions of the -Notaries Act, 1952, the Committee 
desires to make use of this opportunity to consider the Notaries Rules, 1956 also. In 
pursuance of the power conferred by Section 15 of the Notaries Act, 1952 (Act 53 of 1952) 
the Central Government has made the Notaries Rules, 1956. These rules were notified on 
14th February, 1956. 
1.2 Section 3 of the Act gives a power to the Central Government to prescribe 
qualifications of the persons who may be appointed as notaries. Section 15(2)(a) of the Act 
also gives a power to the Central Government to ma~e rules prescribing the qualifications of 
a notary, the form and manner in which applications for appointment as a notary may be 
made and the disposal of such applications. In pursuance of the aforesaid provision , rule 3 
has been made prescribing qualifications for appointment as a notary. It is as follows: 
"Qualifications for appointment as a notary - No person shall be eligible 
for appointment as a notary unless on the date of the application for such 
appointment - (a) he is notary to be appointed by the Master of Faculties in 
England; or (b) he has been practising as a legal practitioner for atleast 10 years." 
1.3 The Committee feels that clause (a) has become redundant and may be deleted. 
1.4 The Committee felt that one of the important objective of the Notaries Act, 1952 is 
to provide facilities to the public to get their notarial functions performed without much 
difficulty. The provision limiting the appointment of notaries from the legal practitioners of 
atleast 10 years standing has restricted the choice of the Government. Tl)ere is a need for 
enlarging the source from where the notaries can be appointed. The Committee also felt that 
officers working in the Law Ministries of the Central and the State Governments are also 
adequately qualified and should be appointed as notaries. This will help the Governments as 
well as the public in easy availability of notaries. 
1.5 The Committee observed that at present there is no age limit for the appointment of 
a person as a notary. At a very old age, a person may be unable to function as a notary. His 
faculties may not be that alert as are necessary for functioning as a notary. The Committee, 
therefore, felt that some age limit should be prescribed beyond which a person should not be 
eligible for appointment as a notary. During the discussion, various age limits were 
suggested by the members. Some members were of the view that the maximum age of 
eligibility for appointment as a notary should be 60 years. Since the Committee has 
suggested in para 5 of Chapter III that no person should be allowed to function as a notary 
for more than 12 years (three years on appointment and three renewals of three years each 
i.e. nine years making the total to twelve years), this will ultimately mean that a person can 
practise as a notary up to the age of 72 years. Other members were of the view that the age 
limit of 72 years for a man to stop practising as a notary will be too short. They were of the 
view that age at the time of appointment plus the 12 years period should be fixed in such a 
way that the person should not exceed 80 years of age. After much deliberations, the

Committee felt that maximum age limit of 75 years as eligibility for appointment as a notary 
will be reasonable. The reason being many persons at that age do not come forward for 
appointment as a notary. Generally, the appointment as a notary takes place at a young age. 
Therefore, the limitation of 75 years will be more or less observed by way of upper limit. 
1.6 The Committee, therefore, recommends that rule 3 may be substituted by the 
following: · 
"No person shall be eligible for appointment as a notary unless on the date of the 
application for such appointment:-
(a) he has been practising as a legal practitioner for atleast ten years; and 
(b) he is or has been a member of Indian Legal Service under the Central 
Government or has been a member of judicial service for atleast 10 years or has 
been an officer under any CentraVState Government for · atleast 10 years 
· requiring special knowledge of law. 
Provided that no person shall be eligible for appointment as a notary on 
attaining the age of 75 years."
