Reservation Benefits to Scheduled Castes Residing in Chandigarh
59. While discussing the Demands for Grants (1998-99) of the Ministry, the Committee had deliberated on
the issue of non availability of reservation benefits to the members of the Scheduled Caste Community who
migrated to Chandigarh after 1.11.1996. The Committee in its 43
rd Report had expressed its dissatisfaction
with the views of the Ministry in the matter. The Ministry had, however, assured to take up the matter again
with the concerned Ministries so that the issue could be resolved. The Committee had hoped that necessary
steps would be taken by Government to ensure that the members of scheduled castes communities who
migrated to Chandigarh after 1.11.1996 be provided reservation benefits.
60. The issue again came up in the meeting of the Committee held on the 23
rd March, 1999. Explaining the
matter the Ministry has submitted that in accordance with provisions contained in Article 341 of the
Constitution of India, the President may with respect to any State or Union Territory specify the castes, races
or tribes which shall for the purpose of the Constitution be deemed to be Scheduled Castes in relation to that
State or Union Territory, as the case may be. The castes so specified under the Presidential Notification
relate to the State or Union Territory concerned and not to other States or Union Territories. This position has
been upheld by the Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Pradeep Jain Vs. Union
of India.
61. The Ministry of Home Affairs has accordingly laid down in its letter No.35/1/72-RU (SCTV) dated the 2
nd
May, 1975 that where a person migrates from one State to another, he can claim to belong to a Scheduled
Caste or Scheduled Tribe only in relation to the State to which he originally belonged and not in respect of
State he had migrated. It has been further clarified in the Ministry of Home Affairs’ letter No. BC 12055/2/76-
SCT(1) dated 22
nd March, 1977 that the inter-state area restrictions have been deliberately imposed so that
the people belonging to the specific community residing in a specific area, which has been assessed to
qualify for the Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe status, only benefit from the facilities provided for them.
62. The Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court of India in the case of Pradeep Jain Vs. Union of India has
clearly stated that merely because a given caste is specified in State A as a Scheduled Caste does not
necessarily mean that if there be any caste bearing the same nomenclature in another State, a person
belonging to the former would be entitled to the rights, privileges and benefits admissible to a member of the
Scheduled Caste of the latter State. The said ruling was given by the Supreme Court of India in the

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
background of Dr. Ambedkar having stated in answer to a question put to him in the course of debates in
Parliament that "a member of a Scheduled Tribe going outside the scheduled area or tribal area would
certainly not be entitled to carry with him the privileges that he is entitled to when he is residing in a
scheduled area or in a tribal area.
63. The Ministry further submitted that the issue whether a person who belongs to a Scheduled Caste in the
State of his origin on migration to Chandigarh after 1
st November, 1966 (the date on which Presidential
notification in respect of the Union Territory of Chandigarh was issued) is entitled to carry the benefit and
privilege of being a member of Scheduled Caste in case the same Caste is included in the list of notified
castes in respect of Chandigarh also was nonetheless specifically referred to Ministry of Law for advice. The
Ministry of Law has opined that where a person belonging to a Scheduled Caste in the State of his origin has
migrated to Chandigarh after 1.11.1966, he is not entitled to carry the benefit and privilege of being a
member of Scheduled Caste even if the same caste is included in the notification in respect of Chandigarh.
This legal advice is based on the judgements of the Hon’ble Supreme Court of India in Action Committee Vs.
Union of India (1994 5 S.C.C. 244) and in Marri Chandra Shekhar Rao Vs. Dean Seth G.S. Medical College,
(1990 3 S.C.C. 130).
64. The Ministry pointed that it is therefore clear that in accordance with existing constitutional scheme, a
member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe who migrates from a State in which he was specified to be
a member of Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, as the case may be, can not carry with him the rights,
privileges and benefits if he migrates to another State or a Union Territory. The Ministry, however, submitted
that it cannot at the same time be over-looked that the said provision does act harshly against the interests of
those members of Scheduled Castes who migrated for permanent residence to Chandigarh after the
notification of the Presidential Order specifying the list of Scheduled Castes in respect of the Union Territory
of Chandigarh was issued. The Ministry informed the Committee that the Ministry of Social Justice &
Empowerment, which is the nodal Ministry for this purpose, has indicated that the issue of extending the
privileges and benefits of reservation to SC/ST migrants is under consideration of the Government along with
similar cases received from other States/Union Territories in the context of comprehensive revision of
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes lists.
65. The Committee notes the reply furnished by the Ministry. It hopes that Government would be able
to arrive at a judicious decision soon. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry that it may be
apprised of the progress of the consideration of the subject from time to time. 
  
  
Punjab Aided Schools (Security of Service) Act, 1969 As extended to Union Territory of Chandigarh
66. The Committee while considering the Demands for Grants (1998-99) of the Ministry had deliberated on
the issue of repealing the `Punjab Aided Schools (Security of Service) Act, 1969’ as extended to the Union
Territory of Chandigarh in August, 1971 and replacing it with the `Punjab Privately Managed Recognised
Schools Employees (Security of Service) Act, 1979’. The Committee was informed on the issue by the
Ministry that while Section 87 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966 empower the Union Government to
extend with such restrictions or modifications as it thinks fit to the Union Territory of Chandigarh, it does not
give power to it to repeal any enactment which is in force in the Union Territory of Chandigarh. Such a repeal
could be done only by a law of Parliament. The Ministry had also informed the Committee that the matter has
been referred for appropriate action to the Union Ministry of Human Resource Development (Department of
Education), being the Ministry concerned with the subject matter. The Committee in its 43
rd report had
expressed the hope that appropriate action would be taken in the matter.
67. The issue was again discussed by the Committee in its meeting held on the 23rd March, 1999. Some

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
members expressed unhappiness over tardy progress in the matter.
68. The Ministry in a detailed reply informed the Committee that section 87 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act,
1966 provided that the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, extend with such
restrictions or modifications as it thinks fit, to the Union Territory of Chandigarh any enactment which is in
force in a State at the date of the notification".
69. In exercise of the powers conferred by section 87 of the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966, the Central
Government extended to the Union Territory of Chandigarh, the Punjab Aided Schools (Security of Service)
Act, 1969, as was in force in the State of Punjab. The State of Punjab enacted a new law on the subject
known as "The Punjab Privately Managed Recognised Schools Employees (Security of Service) Act, 1979".
This Act also repealed the Punjab Aided Schools (Security of Service) Act, 1969 in the State of Punjab.
70. The Chandigarh Administration examined the matter in view of the new law enacted in Punjab and
recommended the repeal of the Punjab Aided Schools (Security of Service) Act, 1969, as in force in the
Union Territory of Chandigarh and simultaneously to have the Punjab Private Managed Recognised Schools
(Security of Service) Act, 1979 extended to the Union Territory of Chandigarh in terms of section 87 of the
Punjab Reogranisation Act, 1966.
71. The matter was examined in the Ministry and it was felt that whereas section 87 of the Punjab
Reorganisation Act, 1966 empowers the Central Government to extend, with such restrictions or
modifications as it thinks fit, to the Union Territory of Chandigarh, any enactment which is in force in a State
at the date of the notification, it does not confer on the Central Government any power to repeal such an
extended law by an executive order and that it would therefore be necessary to have the Punjab Aided
Schools (Security of Service) Act, 1969, repealed through a Parliamentary legislation before extending to the
Union Territory of Chandigarh the Punjab Privately Managed Recognised Schools (Security of Service) Act,
1979. The Committee was informed that since the subject-matter of secondary education is alloted to the
Department of Education, that Department was requested to process the matter further for repealing the
1969 Act and its substitution by the 1979 Act through a Parliamentary legislation.
72. In order to have the matter expedited in pursuance of the reocmmendation made on the subject by the
Committee in its 43
rd Report, a meeting with the Officers of the Department of Education was convened on
the 17th August, 1998 in which the representatives of that Department agreed to process the matter further
after the Chandigarh Administration/Ministry of Home Affairs furnished certain clarification as regards the
scope of the 1979 Act proposed to be extended to the Union Territory along with a draft Bill. The Chandigarh
Administration was accordingly advised to furnish the requisite clarifications along with a draft "Bill" and the
same were received in November, 1998. A self-contained proposal containing the comments of Ministry of
Home Affairs was forwarded to the Department of Education on the 11
th December, 1998 alongwith a draft
Bill on the subject.
73. The Department of Education informed the Ministry in March, 1999 that the matter had been examined in
consultation with the Ministry of Law and that the Legislative Department in that Ministry had opined that the
purpose could be achieved by superseding the earlier notification (under which 1969 Act had been extended)
by issue of a fresh notification for extension of 1979 Act. A draft notification for extending the 1979 Act was
accordingly prepared and forwarded to the Ministry of Law on 18
th March, 1999 for vetting from legal angle.
The proposal was, however, returned by the Ministry of Law on 30th March, 1999 with the observation that
the 1979 Act could not be extended to the Union Territory of Chandigarh unless the existing Act of 1969 was
repealed through a Parliamentary Legislation.
74. The above advice of the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs, however, does not appear to be
correct in view of Section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897, which reads as under:-

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
"21. Power to issue, to include power to add to, amend, vary or rescind notifications, orders, rules
or bye-laws, - where, by any Central Act or Regulation, a power to issue notifications, orders,
rules or bye-laws is conferred, then that power includes a power, exercisable in the like manner
and subject to the like sanction and conditions, if any, to add to, amend, vary or rescind any
notifications, orders, rules or bye-laws so issued."
75. The Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs, therefore, are being requested to reconsider the
matter and clear and vet the draft notification for repeal of the existing Punjab Aided Schools (Security of
Service) Act, 1969 and extension of the Punjab Privately Managed Recognised Schools Employees (Security
of Service) Act, 1979 to the Union Territory of Chandigarh by a notification.
76. The Committee notes the reply furnished by the Ministry. It hopes that the Ministry of Law, Justice
and Company Affairs will arrive at a decision soon regarding appropriate legal way for repealing the
Punjab Aided Schools (Security of Service) Act, 1969 and extending in its place the Punjab Privately
Managed Recognised Schools (Security of Service) Act, 1979 to the Union Territory of Chandigarh.
The Committee also hopes that the concerned Ministry would take necessary action for repealing and
extending the two Acts soon after getting informed by the Ministry of Law about the correct legal
procedure to be followed in the matter. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry that it may be
apprised of the progress of the case from time to time.
SCHEME FOR RESETTLEMENT OF KASHMIRI MIGRANTS IN KASHMIR
77. In the meeting of the Committee held on 23
rd March, 1999, the issue of Kashmiris who migrated from the
valley to different parts of the country in the wake of militancy in the State was raised. Members regretted
that lakhs of such migrants are living in inhuman conditions in different parts of the country. While
Government is making claims that the situation in the State has improved, no effort is seems to be made for
early return of these migrants, some of whom want to go back to their native places. There should be some
concrete plan for the purpose and funds should be made available in the budget for implementing such plan.
78. The Ministry in this regard has apprised the Committee that Government is conscious of the fact that
return of Kashmiri migrants to their homes would signify restoration of complete normalcy. Accordingly, no
permanent rehabilitation of migrants at any other place has been envisaged. The Ministry has been
constantly urging the State Government to work out a detailed Action Plan.
79. In response to this , the Government of J&K has informed that the matter of safe and honourable return
of migrants to their native places in the valley is of top-most priority for the State Government and that the
Government is drawing a detailed plan in this regard. As the matter has to be dealt on politico-economic
basis, finalisation of this plan is likely to take some time. It has also been intimated by the State Government
that a Social Interaction Programme was started under which groups of migrants visited their native Districts
in the valley. This programme was launched with a view to enable the migrants to meet the members of the
majority community and their old neighbours and interact with them.
80. The Ministry further submitted that it has been in constant touch with the State Government regarding
finalisation of the Action Plan. The State Government in a letter dated 8.6.1998 has intimated that they have
constituted a Sub-Committee of Ministers comprising Ministers for Revenue, Law, Finance and Tourism
under orders of the State Cabinet to examine the whole issue and make recommendations thereon. The
Ministry has requested the State Government to ensure that the exercise is completed at the earliest. As and
when the Action Plan is finalised, necessary financial assistance would be provided either by re-appropriation
or placing the requirement in RE.
81. The Committee notes the reply furnished by the Ministry. It strongly feels that the issue of
Kashmiri migrants is of significant importance and deserve utmost attention. It feels sorry for the

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
plight of these migrants who are facing all kinds of problems and living in miserable conditions due
to the proxy war unleashed by Pakistan in Kashmir. Of their no fault they were forced to leave their
homes and properties in their native places. The Committee feels that it is of urgent necessity that
these migrants return to their home land, but at the same, it should be ensured that conditions are
conducive enough there to make them lead peaceful and honourable life. The Committee in this
regard appreciates the Social Interaction Programme started by the Government of J&K under which
groups of migrants visit their native districts in the valley to meet with the people living in the vicinity
of their residence and interact with them. The Committee feels that this programme will definitely
help these migrants in judging the present situation in their native places and in deciding whether
conditions have improved enough for having a safe return. The Committee hopes that the State
Government will be able to expedite preparation of a comprehensive Action Plan for rehabilitation of
these migrants in Kashmir. The Committee urges upon the Ministry to extend every possible help to
the State Government as soon as the Action Plan as prepared by it is received in the Ministry.
DELHI POLICE
82. The Committee in its meeting held on the 31st March, 1999, considered the Demands for Grants of Delhi
Police and heard Commissioner of Police on the funds allocated to it, performance of Delhi Police during the
year and the support, if any, Delhi Police require from the Committee.
83. The Commissioner of Police in his presentation informed the Committee that as per census figures the
population of Delhi now stood at 1.3 crores. However, according to voters’ figure, it is more than 1.6 crores.
Everyday more than ten lakh people come or go by trains in Delhi, and more than 20,000 passengers come
to Delhi by air. Every ten years, the city of Delhi multiplies itself by one-and-a-half times. Though this city has
the highest per capita income, the number of people living below the poverty line is about 17 lakhs. This
underlines the difference in the economic status of people living in Delhi the Commissioner explained. He
further stated that the persons in the age-group of 15-25, which is supposed to be more vulnerable to crime,
and who committ most of the crimes are more than 20 per cent in Delhi, which is highest in the country. The
Commissioner submitted that the performance of Delhi Police should be judged against this background.
84. The Commissioner of Police further informed the Committee that if the number of crimes committed
during the first three months of year 1999 were compared with those of the last three months of year
1998, then it can be observed that almost under every head the crime had come down. This is not a
common feature to occur. The Commissioner stated that it is, however, true that certain sensational
cases have taken place and Delhi Police has not been able to work them out. In this connection he
narrated certain impediments which the police was experiencing. He, however, assured that every
effort is being made to solve them and nab the culprit. He stated that Delhi Police has significantly
higher detection of crime percentage with comparison to the All India average. After the Committee’s
recommendation made in its 43
rd Report 17 Police Stations have been sanctioned. The recruitment has
also been done and the candidates selected are under training. At present, we have been able to post
there only about 40% to 50% of the sanctioned strength. As office building for these Police Stations are
not currently available, they are functioning from make-shift shelters. It will take some time to provide
regular buildings. The Commissioner recalled that in the last presentation also he had suggested about
a study may be done on Delhi Police to find out whether its functioning is all right, what is expected of it,
whether its sanctioned strength is adequate to fulfil its obligations or not. Delhi Police has been able to
get two reliable agencies to conduct this study. One is the Tata Consultancy Services and the other is
Arthur and Aderson, who are supposed to be experts in man-power studies. They have submitted their
project reports and these would be submitted to the Government of India for consideration. The
Committee requests that early action should be taken by the Ministry of Home Affairs on the suggestion
made by the Delhi Police for this study.
85. The Commissioner opined that the sanction of police stations should be on the basis of future

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
requirements, after taking into consideration growth rate of the city, setting up of new colonies and
industrial estates etc. If planned so, it would help Delhi Police in utilising the sanction as soon as it is
received by it, because activities like acquisition of land, recruitment of personnel etc. take time. He
stated that Delhi Police has been working under very heavy pressure to give excellent performance. On
the level of satisfaction in providing dwelling units to its personnel, the Commissioner stated that the
situation was very unsatisfactory and currently only about 19 per cent of the total police personnel have
been provided houses.
86. The Commissioner further stated that about 1,20,000 cases concerning Delhi Police are currently
pending in courts and almost 20,000 cases are added every year, he stated. The prosecution of cases
in the courts takes place at very slow pace because in many cases witnesses do not come forward to
depose before the courts. The dehumanizing level in Delhi is very high and is one of the reasons for
many heinous crimes. Delhi Police is trying to convince the residents for forming resident associations.
Some resources are available with them. It is dovetailing the resources available with public with police
resources to provide them better security. A beginning has been made but it is not as satisfactory as it
should be. ‘Thana Committees’ are also functioning and he hoped that with their help and efforts, Delhi
Police would be able to force some kind of community feeling into them.
87. The Additional Commissioner of Police (Traffic) then made a presentation before the Committee on
situation of traffic on Delhi roads. She said that the number of vehicles in Delhi has increased significantly
and presently there are 32 lakh vehicles. But, the road space has not grown correspondingly. There is
congestion in many areas of the city. In the walled city, it has been estimated that during peak hours the
average speed of a vehicle is 6.1 kilometers per hour. Added to this is the problem that drivers are normally
not trained prior to coming on the roads. The training as well as testing of drivers before licensing is almost
non-existent. About 1500 driving licences are being issued on a daily basis, but we don’t have the facilities in
the city for their training or their proper testing, she stated. There is, therefore, the necessity of having some
sort of Government controlled training institutions, under the Traffic Police or any other institution where
training and testing of drivers before their coming on the roads become possible. In the absence of
education, prior to licensing, traffic police have to rely on prosecution to educate. The challanning amount
needed to be raised suitably because the current level of challan of Rs.100 hardly makes a difference in a
city like Delhi. Traffic Police has also made a proposal for raising the quantum of fine to the level existed in
other cities of the country. In fact, a special punitive fine in a city like, Delhi is needed, she submitted. To
ensure optimum utilisation of the road space modern technology is required to be brought in she added. A
pilot project in this respect has been approved for the Central business District of Delhi which includes
Cannaught Place.
88. The Committee agrees with the suggestion made by Commissioner of Police for having
prospective planning for sanction of new police stations. It feels that with the increase in population
and other criminogenic factors, there has to be regular review of the strength of Delhi Police as per
norms accepted by Government. When new colonies come up, there should be a system of automatic
increase in the police strength. It feels that such planning may be made at least two years in advance
for sanction of the manpower as well as setting up of Police Stations/Police Posts, because finding
location of a site for Police Station and construction of buildings takes considerable time. The
Committee notes that this point is evident from the recent sanctioning of 17 Police Stations. The
whole process has begun much after the growing of colonies where these stations have been set up.
These police stations are currently functioning with 50% of their sanctioned strength which is made
available to them from the existing strength of Delhi Police, which thereby must also have affected
the functioning of Police Stations from where they have been withdrawn. The full new batch will likely
to be made available to it for performing duties only by the end of year 1999-2000.
89. The Committee also notes from the presentation of Commissioner of Police that Government of
India is contemplating to engage and expert body to study about the functioning and component of

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
additionality to the existing strength of Delhi Police. The Committee is in full agreement with such a
study to be conducted by an expert body. In this connection it notes that on an earlier occasion also,
a Committee was set up by Government of India under the Chairmanship of S.D. Srivastava. This
Committee had recommended along with other recommendations criteria for setting up of police
stations in Delhi. As per recommendation of this Committee to be effective, a police station has to be
a compact unit and the population in the jurisdiction of it should not exceed 75,000 and the incidence
of crime it is expected to deal with in a year should not be more than 500. The Committee had further
recommended that when population under jurisdiction of any Police Station exceeds one lakh and/or
when the number of crime in a year exceeds 750, bifurcation of the police station should be
considered. Further to ensure proper organisation and supervision of beats, the Committee
recommended that jurisdiction of the police station even in a semi urban or rural area in Delhi should
not be more than 20 kms. In densely populated area, the area would be much less.
90. The Committee has noted from the papers submitted to it that there should have been 165 police
station in Delhi as per Srivastava Committee. However, the total number of police stations which
Delhi currently has is only 122. The Committee in this background feels that when a Committee or an
expert body is set up for examining a particular issue, the recommendations made by it should be
given due consideration and action taken accordingly. The Committee is not aware whether these
recommendations of the Committee were accepted by Government or not and if accepted why there
is such a large gap between the required and existing number of police stations in Delhi.
91. The Committee also notes from the evidence of the Commissioner that housing for Delhi Police
personnel is another sector where the situation is quite unsatisfactory . From the information
submitted to it, the Committee notes that the satisfaction level in Type-II, III, IV and V quarters are
only 19.80%, 10.50%, 12.02% and 85.29% respectively. This makes the overall satisfaction level at
18.29%. In this context, the Committee notes with concern that one of the reasons for this low
satisfaction level is the underutilisation of funds allocated for construction of residential houses. Out
of total amount allocated at the BE stage for the years 1994-95, 1995-96, 1996-97 and 1997-98 there
was a saving to the tune of Rs.9.91 crores. The Committee feels that if that amount could have been
utilised, the position would have definitely been much better. Further, it notes that in R.E. 1999-2000,
due to increase in allocation for construction of office buildings, the allocation for residential
buildings has been reduced to Rs.23.70 crores. The Committee feels that making available dwelling
units for its personnel is very crucial for any force to keep their morale high. The Committee,
therefore, urges upon the Government to suitably raise the allocation under this head at the RE
stage. The various reasons for non utilisation of fund allocated for construction of residential
quarters, which have been put forth by Delhi Police include multiplicity of authority and slow
progress of work by PWD. The Committee in this context has noted that in the year 1998-99, Delhi
Police has purchased 250 ready built flats from DDA. The Committee feels that it is a good option to
purchase ready built flats than to surrender funds. The Committee also feels that the situation could
be improved if a Police Housing Corporation on the lines of similar Police Housing Corporation in
other States be constituted for Delhi. The Committee urges upon the Ministry to examine the
feasibility of setting up of such Housing Corporation for Delhi Police.
92. The Committee notes the various measures taken by the Police Commissioner for maintaining
law and order in the capital city and fully supports the endeavour of Delhi Police in seeking
cooperation of general public in maintaining peace and prevention of crime in the capital as
highlighted by the Commissioner in his presentation. The Committee feels that Commissioner of Police
is doing a good job despite heavy odds. The Committee wanted to know the various steps taken by Delhi
Police in soliciting cooperation of general public for the purpose. The Committee has been informed that
following steps have been taken to solicit cooperation of general public:-

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
i. District Level Committees/Thana Level Committees have been constituted in every District/Police

ii. "Neighbourhood Watch Scheme" is functioning in some of the localities wherein vigilant members
of the public have been organising themselves to ensure area security under the police guidance.
iii. "Crime Watch Scheme" has been revived. Under this scheme anyone can pass on information to
police regarding crime/criminals without disclosing his/her identity.
iv. "Helpline Scheme" for women in distress is functioning since June 3
rd 1997 and a separate

issued directions to contact the aged persons living alone in his beat and to take all steps for their

directed not to put any question to the person who brings the victim to hospital, against his will.

help the stranded passengers to reach their destination.
viii. Regular interaction takes place between the Police and Resident Welfare Associations/Market
Associations.
ix. Special Police Officers are nominated from the public to help/interact with the Local Police.
x. It is emphasised upon every police officer/man to maintain human dignity and to protect "human
rights" of every citizen while dealing with them.
xi. From time to time service oriented activities such as de-addiction camps, blood donation camps
and juvenile aid camps etc. are organised by Delhi Police.
93. The Committee acknowledges the importance of these schemes and feels that if sincere efforts
are made by Delhi Police for involving larger section of society in cooperating with it, the situation on
the law and order front and curbing the incidents of crimes can be improved significantly. For this,
the Committee feels that the public need to be informed/educated about these schemes and the
electronic and print media can play a big role in achieving this. While the task of ensuring peace and
law and order primarily is the task of police, but the active cooperation of citizens is very vital and
Committee hopes that the citizens of Delhi will extend all cooperation.
94. The Committee also acknowledges the importance of having training institutions for imparting
driving skills to persons who want to have driving licences. The Committee strongly feels that if such
institutions are established, the number of accidents on roads can be reduced to a large extent.
Keeping in view the fact that almost 1500 driving licences are issued every day, it will definitely
require large infrastructure for imparting training to the licence seekers. The Committee urges upon
the Ministry to take appropriate action in the matter.

rd Report on the Demands for Grants (1998-99) of the Ministry had noted that the
casualty rate in road accidents in Delhi was very high and thousands of persons die every year in such
accidents. In many cases accident victims die due to non-availibility of immediate medical first-aid. The
Committee had felt that if a rudimentary knowledge of medical first aid was made mandatory for acquiring
driving licence then in the event of road accidents the driver/owner of the vehicle can render valuable aid, to
the victim and many lives could be saved. The Committee, therefore, urged upon the Ministry to take
necessary action in the matter and make knowledge of medical first aid compulsory for all persons holding

96. In its comments on the recommendation of the Committee, Delhi Police has stated that it endorses the

97. The Committee notes the reply furnished by the Ministry. It however, impresses upon the Ministry
to pursue the matter with Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi as the knowledge of

101. The Committee, in view of the fact that Delhi is the city where there is Parliament House, State

HOUSING FOR CPMFs

 its letter dated 8.9.97 that the

relaxation under GFR 136 for being able to engage agencies other than CPWD for construction of
residential quarters for CPMFs. The Committee hopes that with periodical reviews of the construction
work by the Ministry with CPWD and CPMFs it will be able to ensure better utilisation of the allocated
amount.
CENTRAL INDUSTRIAL SECURITY FORCE (CISF)
106 The Director General, CISF in his presentation before the Committee on 7th April, 1999 informed that
CISF was made an armed force of the Union of India on 15th June, 1983. The role of CISF is to protect and
safeguard Industrial Undertakings owned by the Central Government together with such other installations as
specitied to be vital by the Government which includes state Government Undertakings and its employees.
The CISF has also been performing the all important role of Internal Security duties and Election duties as
and when called upon by the Government, although the same is beyond the purview of the CISF Act. The
CISF is a force of over 94,000 sanctioned strength.
PERSONNEL POLICES FOLLOWED IN CISF
107. Several Members raised the issue of discriminatory personnel policies being followed in CISF. The force
has been following the Personnel Polices in line with those of Para Military forces officers of the gazetted
ranks starting from the rank of Assistant Commandant, filled through promotion from the rank of Inspector,
absorption of security officers from PSUs, reemployment of Ex-army officers and direct recruitment through
Civil Services Examination. The post of AC was a group ‘B’ post and was elevated to the status of a group ‘A’
post in 1987-88. The direct recruitment at the level of group ‘A’ started from Civil Services Examination 1987.
The rank structure of the force at Group ‘A’ level is as under:-
AC
Deputy Commandant
Commandant
DIG
IG
DG
108. In addition to promotion a provision for deputation exists at all these levels. Besides, Ex-army officers
are also given lateral entry into the force at the levels above the Assistant Commandants. Provision for

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
deputation widen as we move from AC to DG with the latter being filled exclusively by deputation.
  
 
SERVICE CONDITIONS VIS-À-VIS GROUP ‘A’ CIVIL SERVICES
109 As per the V Central Pay Commission Report – chapter 48, the following attributes characterise a group
‘A’ Civil Services, recruited through the Civil Services Examination:-
(i) Highest Cadre Post is not below the level of 5900-6700;
(ii) It has all the standard grades namely 2200-4000; 3000-4500; 3700-5000; 4500-
5700; and 5900-6700;
i. Total 50% of the vacancies in Junior Time scale (2200-4000) are required to be filled by direct
recruitment;
(iv) All vacancies above Junior Time scale and upto Senior Administrative Grade
(5900-6700) are filled by promotion from the next lower grade.
110. As per the report officers joining a Central Group ‘A’ Civil Service have certain expectations from these
services in terms of going up the ladder through different stages of the heararchy within a reasonable period
of time.
111. Career planning in all group ‘A’ Civil Services follow these broad parameters. Broady, the new entrants
in all group ‘A’ services are assured of promotions to Senior Time scale around 4
th to 5th year of service and
J.A.G. by 9th year of service. They assure selection grade in 14th year and SAG after 17th year, with some
minor directions depending upon the steepness of the cadre pyramid of the services.
112. All these services also undergo periodical cadre reviews (roughly once every 3-5 years) aimed at
providing reasonable promotional avenues to the cadre officers.
Scales indicated in para 109 are pre-revised scales.
113. With the upgradation of post of AC of group ‘A’, the service rules of CISF were amended in 1988,
however, the Committee observed that the new rules framed for CISF were no way near the guidelines
mentioned above. In the new rules no provisions for Time scale were made. Further the direct recruits at
entry level remained at 30% and the eligibility period for promotions were considerably enhanced.
Deputations also continued at all levels.
114. Contrary to DOPT norms the seniority of direct recruits were placed below those of all other officers
every year. These irregular practices continued ever since, with there being no cadre review since 1988.
115. In reply to a query, the CISF has claimed that deployment for internal secutiry, election duty and VIP
duties is as per order of Ministry of Home Affairs under provisions of the Article 355 of the Constitution read
with Section 7 and 10 of CISF Act. The force having been constituted only for the better protection and
security of industrial undertakings and employees therein as envisaged in the preamble of the CiSF Act,
1968 (Act No. 50 of 1968) does not include performance of internal security duties, VIP and election duties
by the force. Section 7 of the Act only mentions that the superintendence of the force rests with the Central
Government and subject to such superintendence and the provisions of the Act the command, supervision
and administration of the force rests with the DG.

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
116. Thirdly administration of the force within local limits has also been vested in the other supervisory
officers.
117. Section 10 mentions the duties of member of force which, includes obeying and executing promptly all
orders lawfully issued by superior authorities, to protect and safeguard the industrial undertakings, the
employees therein and to do any other act conducive to the better protection of industrial undertakings and
employees therein.
118. These sections do not confer adequate powers on Central Government to use the force for the
purposes other than security and protection of the industry and its employees. It also fails to show how a
force trained specifically for protection of industrial undertakings and employees therein can be suitably
trained for these duties which, are outside its structure of duties, except in a generalised way.
119. The Committee has found the reply of CISF with regard to deployment of forces on IS duties
evasive. A perusal of CISF Act and Rules clearly proves that the deployment for internal security
duties are outside its charter of duties. The fact cannot be denied that CISF as a Para Military Force
meant for secutity of industrial undertaking is being pulled out of some PSUs to carry out duties like
Internal Security etc. thereby naturally affecting the security of these undertakings.
120. The Committee takes very strong exception of the evasive, incorrect and misleading replies
furnished by the CISF with regard to the cadre policies like ROTA QUOTA etc. While the CISF has
admitted to the existence of ROTA QUOTA System in CISF, it has evaded answers of other aspects
raised in the question. The contention that seniority of direct officers is not affected by the ROTA
QUOTA System, and that they are placed on top of the seniority list appear to be misleading and
factually incorrect. A perusal of the seniority list with reference to the year of vacancy in case of
promotees and year of examiniation in case of direct recruits clearly shows the placement of five
promotees, one optee (opned from PSU security service) and one ex-army (reemployed) above a
group of 3 direct officers, in a group of 10 officers. The factual position is thus a total contradiction of
the stand taken by CISF.
121. Contrary to the experience of various Group ‘A’ Services, it is observed that in CISF which is
also a Group ‘A’ Service, a Group ‘C’ level has been the feeder category to Group ‘A’, as Group ‘C’
officials get promotions directly to Group ‘A’. Further, existing Group ‘B’ officers of CISF were also
upgraded to Group ‘A’ retrospectively enmasse when the CISF itself was upgraded to Group ‘A’.
ROTA QUOTA System also envisages first – 5 positions in the seniority list for promotee officers. The
Committee thus fails to understand as to how the career prospects of direct officers is not seriously
disadvantaged, when promotee officers have been given priority over direct recruits, over the years.
122. The Committee also notes that the faulty policies and no cadre review since 1988, the direct
Group ‘A’ officers of CISF get a raw deal vis-à-vis the other Group ‘A’ services like IPS, RPF etc.
selected through the same exam. A mere comparision with scales as submitted by the CISF clearly
indicates the casual approach to the significance of rank in the legitimate career aspirations of these
young officers.
123. The CISF has also enlisted a list of proposals for amendment with an aim at improving the career
prospects of cadre officers. The Committee observes that the proposed promotions and their time period are
at variance with other Group ‘A’ Civil Services. The CISF also proposes to introduce the concept of
Residency Period in each rank which is not in existence in a majority of the Group ‘A’ Civil Services. Further,
the Committee having been apprised of the stagnation of the direct officers (having rendered 8-9 years of
service and yet to get even one promotion) it fails to see how these prospects can be effected in a need
based force. With the CISF facing mounting dues from 21 major PSUs and withdrawal from them being

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
imminent, the possibility of having vacancies in the existing set up appear to be limited. Already the direct
officers as seen in the paragraphs above have been placed unfairly in their seniority. These
recommendations/proposals by CISF thus appear to be faultering on the point of actual implementation and
as to whether they will really make a difference to the plight of the young Group ‘A’ entrant of the force.
124. The new proposals thus appear to be an eyewash as along with the delayed promotions (vis-à-vis
Group ‘A’ Services) and the residency periods envisaged – the service conditions are bound to deteriorate.
The CISF has in its reply indicated that there have been no shrinkage of vacancies in any rank. However,
with list of 21 major PSUs having dues greater than 322 crores and withdrawals from them imminent, the
Committee fails to see how the posts will remain unaffected.
125. The Committee takes note of the fact that on the ground of parity of all Group ‘A’ Services, officers
allotted CISF were subjected to negative restrictions in the subsequent attempts in Civil Services as per Civil
Services Examination Rules. However, the fact that there are glaring discrepancies between the other Group
‘A’ Civil Services and the CISF is also not hidden from the Committee. Haphazard cadre governing policies
like distorted from of ROTA QUOTA being operational in CISF, Group ‘C’ as a feeder to Group ‘A’ Service,
new clauses in the proposals proposed for remedy of career prospects like residency period etc. lead the
Committee to the view that Ministry of Home Affairs seems to have overlooked the basic aspects of career
planning in CISF. While the anomalous position vis-à-vis Group ‘A’ Services is evident, there has been no
word to the same by the affected Department i.e. the CISF. It appears that it considers Group ‘A’ as a mere
categorisation of its officers in names like only, and that consideration of proper promotional avenues as a
constant process rather than ascribing to them the basic prerequisites of a Group ‘A’ Services as envisaged
by DOPT.
126. An examination of the records with the Committee clearly establishes that recruitment to CISF started
through C.S.E. in 1983 as a Group ‘B’ Service. The upgradation to a Group ‘A’ service started w.e.f. C.S.E. in
1987. It is surprising that the CISF indicates in its reply that service conditions did not require to be changed
to accommodate Group ‘A’ officers. This itself lends credence to the fact that this service i.e. the CISF treats
Group ‘A’ categorisation in namesake only. While the Act by Parliament did not require amendment, all
changes in recruitment rules appear to have worsened the conditions in the service till the present state –
affecting the very morale of these bright officers.
127. The reply has been found to be extremely evasive and there seems to be an attempt to divert the
members. Instead of accepting its failure to give Group ‘A’ service conditions to a group of officers recruited
through the Civil Services Examination, even after having prevented them from improving to other services,
the Committee finds all norms governing Group ‘A’ Civil Service to be simply overlooked in the CISF. 
  
  
  
 
128. The Committee strongly felt that MHA should ensure that these officers do not lose their morale
and that service conditions due to them are provided in order to enable them to give their best to the
organisation. The Committee also noted that the decision to delink the recruitment of CISF officers
through Civil Services Examination has been withdrawn by Ministry of Home Affairs. 
  
 
129. The Committee feels that due to faulty and skewed personnel policies followed in CISF (e.g. Rota
Quota System etc.) taking it’s toll, and due to lack of initiative on the part of CISF/MHA in the last 10-
12 years to rectify these faults, an irreparable damage has already been done to these officers which
cannot be reversed by Cadre Review as stated by the special Secretary before the Committee. Their

Fifty Fourth Report-Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/54_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:25]
promotions will continue to remain vacancy based due to the need based deployment pattern of
CISF. Further, the non direct officers of CISF cannot be circumstanced adversely at such a late stage.
This would invite prolonged litigation, ultimately leading to these direct officers continuing to
stagnate. 
  
  
  
 
130. The Committee expresses its deep concern over the issue and strongly recommends
reallocatipon of these direct Group ‘A’ officers of CISF who were recruited through Civil Services
Examination into Indian Police Service (IPS) or in other Group ‘A’ services in order to settle their
grievances. In the past officers of Indian Frontier Administrative Service (a Group ‘B’ Service) were
merged/reallocated to the Indian Administrative Service (IAS). Even the latest National Police
Commission has recommended for allocating 16 2/3% of the posts of IPS for the officers of Central
Police Organisations (CPOs) subject to their clearing an exam conducted by the U.P.S.C. These
direct CISF officers have already cleared the combined Civil Services Examination which is also the
source of recruitment for direct IPS officers. Further, the MHA should end this ambivalence of
recruitment of officers for Central Paramilitary Forces under MHA through the Civil Service
Examination.
General Observation
131. The Committee at its sitting held on the 15th April, 1999, noted with concern that some of the
recommendations made by it from time to time have not been taken by Government with seriousness they
deserve. There has been inordinate delay in their implementation and when recommendations have not been
accepted, no detailed and cogent reasons were given for not accepting them. The Committee, therefore,
strongly feels that Government may take earnest action in respect of such recommendations pending before
it for decision/implementation.

REPORT
The management of personnel policies in Government of India, to begin with, was the joint responsibility of the
Ministries of Home Affairs (Services and Establishment Wing) and Finance (Establishment Division) with Union Public
Service Commission playing an important advisory role. The Establishment Officer to the Government of India,
functioning under the Cabinet Secretary had an important role to play in the senior appointments under the Government
of India. All this made for improper division of responsibility and lack of a unified central didrection.
2. To plug this organisational loophole, the Estimates Committee of the Third Lok Sabha in its 93
rd Report (April 1966)
observed that "the ever expanding role of the Government in a welfare state with its natural concomitant of a large civil
service calls for effective personnel control through a single agency". The Administrative Reforms Commission too
urged upon the Government to set up a separate Department of Personnel, to be placed directly under the Prime Minister
to serve as a nodal agency for the personnel functions of the Government.
3. The Union Government accepted this recommendation and as a consequence the ‘Department of Personnel’ was set
up in August, 1970 and placed within the Cabinet Secretariat. In February 1973, the Department of Administrative
Reforms, till then with the Ministry of Home Affairs, was amalgamated with the Department of Personnel and the
newly created department was christened, the ‘Department of Personnel and Administrative Reforms’. In 1977, this
department was transferred to the Ministry of Home Affairs. In March, 1985 a full fledged ‘Ministry of Personnel,
Public Grievances and Pensions’ was created. The Ministry comprises three departments, namely :-
1. Department of Personnel and Training.
2. Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances.
3. Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare.
4. The Ministry is under the overall charge of the Prime Minister, assisted by a Minister of State. All the three
departments are functioning under the charge of Secretary (Personnel) assisted by seven additional Secretaries/Joint
Secretaries and other officers and staff.
5. Functionally, the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions is divided into the following seven divisions

:-
Establishment Officer
Services and vigilance

6. DEPARTMENT OF PERSONNEL AND TRAINING AND THE VARIOUS AGENCIES UNDER ITS
ADMINISTRATIVE CONTROL
1. The role of the Department of Personnel and Training can be conceptually divided into two parts. In its
larger nodal role, it acts as the formulator of policy and the watch dog of the Government ensuring that
certain accepted standards and norms, as laid down by it, are followed by all Ministries/Departments in the
recruitment, regulation of service conditions and deputation of personnel as well as other related issues.
Towards this end, guidelines are issued by it for the benefit of all Ministries/Departments and it monitors
the implementation of these guidelines. It also advises all organisations of the Central Government on
issues of personnel management. At a more immediate level, the Department has the direct responsibility of
being the cadre controlling authority for the Indian Administrative service (IAS) and the Central Secretariat
Service (CSS). The Department also operates the Central Staffing Scheme under which suitable officers
from All India Services and Group ‘A’ Central Services are selected and then placed in posts at the level of
Under Secretary on the basis of tenure deputation. The Department also deals with cases of appointment to
posts of Chairman, Managing Director, full-time functional Director/Member of the Board of Management
of various public sector undertakings/enterprises, corporations, banks and financial institutions. It also deals
with the assignment of Indian experts to various developing countries.
Recruitment Agencies
2. The two organisations through which the Department ensures recruitment of personnel for the Government
are the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC) and the Staff Selection Commission (SSC). The former
is constituted under a provision of the Constitution and is responsible for conducting examinations for
appointment to the higher civil services and civil posts under the Union Government, including recruitment
to the All India Services. There is a mandatory provision for consulting the Commission on all matters
relating to methods of recruitment, principles to be followed in making promotions and transfers from one
service to another and all the disciplinary matters. The SSC is responsible for making recruitment for Group
‘B’ non-gazetted posts of Assistants, Stenographers, etc.
Training Institutions
3. Two major training institutions directly under the administrative control of the Department are the Lal
Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration (LBSNAA), Mussoorie and the Institute of
Secretariat Training and Management (ISTM), New Delhi. The former is mainly responsible for providing
induction training to recruits to the Indian Administrative Service and other all India Services and Central
Services. The Institute of Secretariat Training and Management provides induction as well as in-service
training to members of the Central Secretariat Service.
Senior Appointments under the Government of India
4. All proposals for senior appointments under the Government of India, which require the approval of the
Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC) are processed through the Establishment Officer as
Secretary of the ACC. These include board level appointments to Central Public Sector Undertakings and

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/55_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
appointments of Joint Secretaries, Directors and Deputy Secretaries in the Ministries/Departments. In
additional, all appointments by promotion, which require the approval of the ACC are also processed
through the Establishment Officer.
Public Enterprises Selection Board
5. The Public Enterprises Selection Board (PESB) is entrusted with the responsibility of making
recommendations for appointment to the full-time Board level posts of Chief Executive and functional
Directors and part-time Chairman in the Central Public Undertakings.
Administrative Vigilance
6. The Department of Personnel and Training determines Government policy for the maintenance of integrity
of the public services and eradication of corruption and coordinates the activities of various
Ministries/Departments in that area.
Central Vigilance Commission (CVC)
7. Advice on all vigilance matters is provided by the Central Vigilance Commission. It has jurisdiction and
power in respect of all matters to which the executive power of the Union Government extends. The
Commission enjoys the same measure of independence and autonomy as the Union Public Service
Commission.
Central Bureau of Investigation
8. The CBI is the premier investigating agency of the country. Originally set up as an anti-corruption agency
of the Government of India, the role of CBI has undergone a sea change. It is now dealing with a variety of
offences which include anti-corruption, special crimes, economic offences, major financial frauds, terrorist
crimes and other serious crimes having inter-state and international ramifications. A large number of such
areas are now referred to the CBI by High Courts and the Supreme Court.
Joint Consultative Machinery
9. There is a well-structured machinery for joint consultation between the Central Government and its
employees on a wide variety of service matters having a bearing on the administration and the general
interests of the Government employees. It is a three-tier machinery consisting of the National Council, the
Departmental Council and the Regional/Office Council. Service matters pertaining to the interests of the
generality of employees or specific groups of them are dealt with by this machinery.
Central Administrative Tribunal
10. In order to provide speedy and inexpensive justice to employees aggrieved by Government decisions, the
Government set up the Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) in 1985, which now deals with all cases
relating to service matters which were previously dealt with by Courts upto and including the High Courts.
There are now 17 regular Benches of the CAT functioning in various parts of the Country, including its
Principal Bench in Delhi.
Staff Welfare

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/55_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
11. The Department supports various programmes, which are provided in various Ministries/Departments,
Central Government Employees Welfare Coordination Committee in Central Government offices located
outside Delhi, Residents’ Welfare Associations/Area Welfare Officers; Benevolent Fund and Departmental
Canteens. Department of Personnel and Training is the nodal agency for three registered societies set up for
the welfare of the Government employees and their families. These societies are the Central Civil Services
Cultural and Sports Board, Grih Kalyan Kendra and Kendriya Bhandar. As a welfare measure, the
Government had also decided, during the course of the year, to have a Civil Services Officers Institute in
Delhi which has been set up as a registered society.
DEPARTMENT OF PENSION AND PENSIONERS’ WELFARE
7. The Department of Pensions & Pensioners’ Welfare is the nodal agency of the Government of India for
formulation of general policy on pension and other retirement benefits, as also for redressal of grievances on
retirement benefits. The Department was set up in 1985 as a part of Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and
Pensions and has been rendering service for the benefit of pensioners since then. Department has taken a number
of steps over the years for streamlining the pension administration system, for greater convenience and welfare of
the pensioners.
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC GRIEVANCES
8. The Department of Administrative Reforms and Public Grievances is the nodal agency of the Government of
India for administrative reforms as well as redressal of public grievances relating to the State in general and
grievances pertaining to Central Government agencies in particular. The Department disseminates information on
important activities of the Government relating to administrative reforms and public grievance redressal through
Management Publications and Documentation. It also undertakes activities in the field of international co-
operation and exchanges to promote public service reforms.
9. Demand No. 64 which pertain to the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances & Pensions includes requirements
of funds for the Department of Personnel & Training, the Department of Administrative Reforms & Public
Grievances, the Department of Pension & Pensioners’ Welfare, the Central Administrative Tribunals, the Staff
Selection Commission the Central Bureau of Investigation (including Interpol and Coordination Wing), the
Institute of Secretariat Training & Management, the Lal Bahadur Shastri National Academy of Administration,
Training Scheme, the Central Vigilance Commission, the Public Enterprises Selection Board, and loans to State
Government for payment of Home Building Advance to All India Services Officers.

ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS
16. Responsive and responsible administration is the need of the hour especially in the Age of Information.
Transperancy and accountability in the machinery of Government is bladly needed for ensuring the basic objective of
clean and citizen friendly administration. Transperacy could be effected only after sharing information with the public.
FREEDOM TO INFORMATION
17. The Committee lauds the endeavour of the Government for drafting a Bill on Freedom of Information in pursuance
of recommendation of "Working Group on Right to Information and Promotion of Open & Transparent
Government" under the Chairmanship of Shri H.D. Shourie. But the Committee at the same time, note that the
Ministry has not taken any measures with regard to amendments in Official Secrets Act, 1923, Indian Evidence Act,
1972, Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, Criminal Procedure Act, 1973, CSS Rules, 1964 and the Manual of Departmental
Security Instructions relating to classification of Information, as recommended by the above working group.
18. Further, the Action Plan prepared for the conference of Chief Ministers held on 24th May, 1997 also inter-alia
emphasised the `Right to Information'. The Committee in its 44
th Report had recommended for the explicit
provision of "Right to Information", which would enable the citizenry to ensure accountability in administration.
The Committee again reiterates its stand taken earlier on the matter and suggests that access to information
must be accorded the status of Fundamental Right.
 INFORMATION FACILITATION COUNTERS
19. Information Facilitation Counters (IFCs) are set up outside the security zone of each office with a view to
facilitating the dissemination of information pertaining to schemes and procedures of the concerned organisation and
regarding acknowledgement and status report of individual application. In brief, IFCs are the visible faces of Citizen
Charters formulated by the concerned Ministries/Department.

20. Citizen Charters contain the commitments of the concerned organisation alongwith expected standards of service
delivery, grievance system etc. The Ministry had intimated that, of late, 55 Ministries/Departments/Offices have framed
their Charters.
21. The Committee was informed that the opening up of IFCs in Ministries/Departments/Offices having large public
interface were taken up in the phased manner. It is learnt from the Annual Report of the Ministry that 45 Ministries in
coordination with NIC have set up their IFCs but, in the replies to the Questionnaire, the Ministry had submitted list of
31 IFCs only.
22. Further, the Ministry elsewhere had intimated the Committee that two Departments had decided not to open IFCs on
the plea that their Directors (Public Grievances) are accessible to the public. The Committee has been informed that the
Departments of Administrative Reforms & Public Grievances does not maintain the work done by IFCs of individual
Ministries/Departments.
23. The Committee notes with dismay that the approach of the Ministry towards the monitoring of concepts
(IFCs and Citizen Charters) evolved by it is non-committal. The Committee recommends that IFCs should be
opened up in all Ministries/Departments/Offices with corresponding Citizen's Charters. The Ministry being
nodal agency, would monitor the progress report of individual Ministries/Departments for giving effect to such
concepts. The two different figures of IFCs given by the Ministry may be rectified. Most importantly, the
behavioural reform alongwith procedural and structural reform must be taken up vigorously through
appropriate training and supervision.
LAW OF ADMINISTRATION
24. While examining the Demands for Grants (1997-98 and 1998-99) of the Ministry, the Committee in its 38th & 44th
Reports had emphasised the need to evolve law of administration. The Ministry in its ATN on 44th Report of the
Committee had expressed its inability to codify varied extant rules and regulations into a comprehensive legislation.
25. In this regard, the Committee has also been informed that the Commission for Review of Administrative Laws
under the Chairmanship of Shri P.C. Jain in its final Report submitted on 30th September, 1998 has inter-alia
recommended the following points:-
(a) All the Ministries/Departments should compile up-to-date information about rules, regulations, orders
and procedures under different Central Law administered by them including manuals in respect of areas
which are important from the point of view of the general public.
(b) There is a need also for unification and harmonisation of statutes, laws and regulations with reference to
the perspective of domestic and foreign investors, trade and industry, consumers, builders, expoerters and
importers.
(c) Repeal of over 1300 Central Laws of different categories out of about 2500 Laws in force, on the
ground that these laws have become either irrelevant or dysfunctional. The break-up of laws recommended
for repeal are as given below :
(i) 166 Central Acts (including 11 Pre- Nationalisation Acts and 20 Validation Acts).
(ii) 315 Amendment Acts.
(iii) 11 British Statutes still in force.
(iv) 114 Central Acts relating to state subjects.
(v) Approximately 700 Appropriation Act (approximately) passed by Parliament.
(d) Expansion of the system of alternate disputes resolution and more effective utilisation of the Arbitration

MODERNISATION OF GOVERNMENT OFFICES
28. The Scheme of Modernisation of Government offices is linked to the contemplated piece of legislation on 'Right to
Information' as a well equipped office with up-dated information could be in a position to part with that information to
public. In the current phase of liberalisation, the need for boosting the productivity of Government offices is badly felt,
which could be achieved by augmenting the efficiency of the officials through the scheme of mordernisation of offices
and appropriate training. The Committee queried about the slow pace of mordernisation process in Government offices.
It has also observed that most of the Offices have not used fully the amount earmarked for mordernisation scheme. It is
also learnt that the amount earmarked under the Scheme 'Support to State Government for development of
computerised net-work' remained unutilised due to the fact that the scheme could not be materialised.
29. The Ministry has stated that there is a provision of supply of certain equipments like office machines, risographs,
photocopiers and over-head projectors under the Scheme of Modernisation of Government Offices. The provision of
computers both hardware as well as software is, however, not provided under the scheme.The Ministries/Departments
are expected to seek assistance from within their own resources. The Ministries/Departments have been requested to
implement a time bound programme for converting into electronic form all the non-classified rules, regulations,
procedures and circulars etc. They have also been requested to make Five year plans as well as Annual plans for
increasing use of the Information Technology. They have also been permitted by the Planning Commission to allocate
2-3% of their Plan Budget for programmes/schemes relating to Information Technology. A High Powered Committee
under the Chairmanship of Cabinet Secretary has also recommended the increasing use of Information Technology for
more effective and efficient performance of the Government. The Ministry is monitoring the process. As far as non-
materialisation of scheme of "support to State Government for development of computerised network' the Ministry has
informed that the details of "Electronic Government Project" have not been supplied to the Union Government.
30. The Committee lauds the objective of modernisation scheme but at the same time is not happy with the slow
pace of modernisation work in Ministries/Offices, the Committee recommends that the drive for modernising
offices taken in 8O's should be completed before the on set of this new millenium. The Ministry being a nodal
agency for co-ordinating O&M activities of the Ministry has to take a lead role and direct all Ministries to gear
up their respective machinery for putting all rules, regulations, procedures etc. in electronic form. The
Committee also emphasises progressive use of information technology in the place of traditional machine aid to
official work. The Government has to take care for creating appropriate training methods for making use of
information technology in the Government offices. Necessary consultation may be undertaken with the State
Governments to use information technology in their official work also.
31. The Committee in its 44th Report had observed that a set of Administrative Courts may be set up to look into and
adjudicate upon the acts of omission and Commission of the administrative officials. The Ministry in its ATN to the said
Report of the Committee had merely enumerated the existence of Civil Courts, CAT, Consumer Fora for dispensing
justice without mentioning any action taken by it to implement the above recommendation. In this context, the Ministry
feels the need to strengthen/reform Administrative Tribunals to bring greater speed in the disposal of cases relating to
service matters and strengthen Internal Grievance Redressal Machinery (IGRM) of all Ministries/Departments. The
Ministry is also considering on the recommendation of the Commission on Review of Administrative Law in this
regard. The Commission had recommended more effective use of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act and greater use

33. The facilitating role of the Government as compared to its regulatory role has not improved considerably as a result

37. The Committee understands that the backlog of large number of cases relating to grievances in Ministries is a

CENTRAL ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL
38. Pursuant to the provision of Article 323A of the Indian Constitution, the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1985 was
enacted by Parliament to set up Administrative Tribunal for adjudication of disputes and complaints with regard to
recruitment and condition of services of persons appointed to public services and posts in connection with the affairs of
the Union and the States.

39. Administrative adjudication, which is quasi-judicial in nature, is the main function of Administrative Tribunals. The
basic objective of enacting the Administrative Tribunal Act was :
(i) to relieve congestion in the ordinary set of courts; and
(ii) to provide for speedy disposal of disputes relating to service matters.
In brief, the objective of the Administrative Tribunal is to provide for speedy and inexpensive justice to the litigants for
which the procedure followed by Tribunal is made flexible and technically free from the ordinary courts.
40. As on date (1.1.99) it has 17 regular benches, 15 of which operate at the principal seats of High Courts and the
remaining two at Jaipur and Lucknow. The present sanctioned strength of the Chairman, Vice-Chairmen and Members
of the CAT is as given below:
Chairman - 1
Vice-Chairmen - 16
Members - 49
The CAT had jurisdiction over the civilian employees of the Central Government and nine Societies/Corporations. As
per information submitted by the Ministry, twenty nine more organisations have been brought under the purview of the
CAT w.e.f. 1.1.99.
41. The Committee is extremely concerned over the pendency of large number of cases in the different benches of the
CAT. The Ministry has submitted that since its inception 2, 97, 346 cases have been instituted upto 31.12.98, out of
which 2, 47, 825 cases have been disposed of leaving a balance of 49, 521 cases. The break up of bench wise pendency
of cases in the CAT is at Appendix A. The inordinate delay in disposal of cases by the CAT has defeated the very
objective for which it was brought into existence in 1985. The reason given by the Ministry for such delay is that
addition of 29 organisations under the purview of the CAT has led to increase in institution of cases and consequent
pendency of cases.
42. The Committee feels that the reason attributed by the Ministry for the pendency of cases is misleading. The
statement relating to the pendency of cases (49, 521) is before the enlistment of 29 organisations under the purview of

barring only four years (1991, 1992, 1993 and 1994) where the trend remained somehow constant. The increase of cases

several cases two or more than two Ministries are involved. The Ministry being the nodal agency for modernisation
of Government offices has not upgraded its Departments especially in the present age of internet. The Committee
suggests that the pendency of cases (Ministry wise) should be compiled by the Ministry and put the same on the
internet.

SENIOR APPOINTMENTS AND PERSONNEL POLICY AND CADRE MANAGEMENT
47. The Department of Personnel and Training (DOP&T) is charged with the responsibility of senior appointments and
personnel policies in the Government of India. This Department is also responsible for cadre management in respect of
the Indian Administrative Services (IAS) and the Central Secretariat Service (CSS). The Establishment Officer and the
Additional Secretary (EO) in the Department is the nodal officer who oversees the aforesaid functions. The
Establishment Officer also serves as Secretary to the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC). All proposals for
appointments under the Government of India which require approval of the ACC under the Government of India
(Transaction of Business) Rules, 1961, are processed through the Secretary to the ACC.
48. The Committee has been making from time to time various recommendations with regard to the appointment of
Officers belonging to Group `A’ and CSS to man the senior positions at the Centre. The Committee had also in its
earlier reports made recommendations in respect of promotion and posting of CSS officers at the level of Under
Secretary and Deputy Secretary. The Committee in its 44
th Report had made certain recommendations in paras 46
to 51 in this respect.. The Ministry in its Action Taken Note has not commented on paras 46 and 47. In respect of
para 48 of the 44
th Report, the Department of Personnel inter alia gives details of the minimum service required
for promotion of CSS officers to different levels. The Committee has taken note of this. Actual position, however,
appears to be quite opposite to this. The experience has shown that it takes much longer for officers to get
empanelled and the actual placement takes much longer, particularly in respect of senior positions from Director
to Joint Secretary and Joint Secretary to Additional Secretary level. In this connection, the Committee would like
to point out that during the calendar year 1998, although several CSS officers working at Joint Secretary level
were eligible for promotion to next level, that is, Additional Secretary, but no panel was prepared. Even during
the current year till the writing of this report, the Government has not prepared the panel for promotion of
Group ‘A’ and CSS officers from the level of Joint Secretary to Additional Secretary. Therefore, it would not be
wrong to conclude that the minimum service required for promotion from one level to other as detailed in the
Action Taken Note of the Ministry is only a paper provision and is seldom put to practice. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Department of Personnel should have a fixed schedule for bringing out the
panels of CSS Officers for promotion one level to another.
CENTRAL SECRETARIAT SERVICE RULES
49. The Committee in its 44
th Report (para 52) had commented that the Central Secretariat Service Rules, 1962, had
become quite old and felt that there was an urgent need to review these rules. It had, therefore, recommended that
necessary amendments in these rules in the light of their operation during the last 36 years be carried out on priority
basis. The Committee had also recommended that the amendments of rules should include inclusion of Director, Joint
Secretary and Additional Secretary level posts within the purview of these rules as Officers of this service have been
holding post at these levels during the last so many years.
50. The Ministry in its Action Taken Note has mentioned that the CSS Rules, 1962, and regulations issued thereunder
are reviewed in the light of the general policy, guidelines and the matter of recruitment, promotion, etc. issued by the
Establishment Division of that Department from time to time and necessary amendments are carried out, as and when
necessary. It further states that certain proposals for amendment have been finalised recently and those are likely to be
notified shortly, after vetting by the Ministry of Law (Legislative Department).
