51. As regards the Committee’s recommendations for inclusion of the post of Director, Joint Secretary and Additional
Secretary within the purview of the CSS Rules are concerned, it may be stated that the post of the level of Under
Secretary and above under the Central Staffing Scheme are to be filled by taking officers of All India Services who have
a specified central deputation reserve and to that extent the State Governments recruit officers in excess of their actual
requirement and Group `A’ organized services on deputation. Officers of the CSS are also appointed to the posts under
the Central Staffing Scheme. Hence the very nature and spirit of the Central Staffing Scheme does not allow posts at the
Central Secretariat to be specially earmarked for any particular service cadre. The Department, therefore, stated that it
may, therefore, not be feasible to bring the post of Director, Joint Secretary and Additional Secretary within the purview
of CSS Rules.
52. The Committee is not in agreement with the stand taken by the Ministry for not amending the CSS Rules so
as to include the post of Director, Joint Secretary and Additional Secretary in the CSS cadre. The Department’s
stand is that the CSS is a service that starts in Group `B’. The Committee is fully aware of this fact. However, an
important point which the Department has all along been ignoring is the fact that the directly recruited Section
Officers come through the common competitive Civil Services Examination conducted by the UPSC. In a
competitive examination there are no qualifying marks. One may qualify in a competitive examination and yet
may not make the grade so as to enter the service as the number of vacancies for different services vary each
year. Therefore, it would be not only unfair but also against the principles of natural justice to continue archaic
rules which were made nearly four decades ago. Further, it has been brought to the Committee’s notice that in
earlier days before the Second Pay Commission’s recommendations, there used to be two grades for Section
Officers. After couple of years of service, directly recruited Section Officers used to be promoted to Grade-I and
were class one officers.
53. The Committee regrets that the Ministry in its Action Taken Note has not given details of the proposals which
are under consideration for amendment to CSS Rules, 1962. The Committee would have appreciated if the
Department had given details of the proposed amendments in the rules.
54. The Committee would also like to reiterate its recommendations contained in para 42 of its 38
th Report
wherein it had recommended that keeping at par with the eligibility criteria regarding length of service
prescribed for Grade-I, Selection Grade, Director and Joint Secretary of the CSS, the eligibility criteria
regarding length of service for CSS officers for emplanelment to hold post at the level of Additional Secretary
should also be reckoned with effect from 1
st July of the relevant year in which a CSS Joint Secretary is included
in the Joint Secretary’s suitability list irrespective of the actual date of appointment as Joint Secretary In this
connection, Ministry in its Action Taken Note had inter-alia mentioned, that if the recommendations of the
Committee were to be accepted and CSS officers for the post of Director and above such posts would become
cadre posts for the service. Any such provision in CSS Rules will lead to similar demands form other services for
earmarking post for them. In this connection, it is important to bear in mind that it is not relevant to compare
CSS with any other Group ‘A’ services. CSS has been created to man the various posts in the Central Secretariat
alone whereas the Group ‘A’ services have their respective cadres. Their cadre prospects are exclusively in their
respective services, where officers belonging to other services do not compete. Therefore, comparing CSS with
other Group `A’ services is neither relevant nor justifiable.
55. Another reason which warrants immediate amendment of the rules so as to bring the posts of Director, Joint
Secretary and Additional Secretary within the cadre of CSS, is the fact that a number of officers have now
become eligible to hold these middle and senior level posts. Already four officers of the CSS are holding posts at
Additional Secretary level. The amendment of rules will not open the flood gates for the CSS officers nor the CSS
officers are going to grab unusually large number of these posts as only officers those who have joined the
services direct recruit at S.O. level will be in a position to reach to these levels. Number of such officers is quite
small. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its recommendations for amendment of CSS Rules so as to bring the
post of Director, Joint Secretary and Additional Secretary in the CSS cadre and also to reckon officers for
empanelment to hold post at the level of Additional Secretary should be recommended with effect from 1
st July
of the relevant year in which a CSS Joint Secretary is included in the Joint Secretary’s suitability list irrespective
of actual date of appointment as Joint Secretary.

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/55_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
56. It is in this background, the Committee has been recommending that the CSS Rules, 1962, should be
amended on priority basis so as to give justice to the CSS officers which has been eluding them thus far and
reiterates that appropriate action be taken.
57. Promotion refers to the movement of an employee from one position to another having a higher grade and pay in the
hierarchy. The Committee came to know that there is stagnation in the Central Secretariat Service even within the
promotion zone. The vertical promotion in Central Secretariat Service could not be effected within requirement of
minimum service period. The Ministry in its ATN had supplied the following information with regard to promotion of
CSS Officers :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Promotion

retirement. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 58. The career
graph indicated in the ATN to the 44th Report in respect of CSS officers give the very rosy picture which is not
supported by the details furnished by the Ministry in its replies.It is unfortunate that CSS officers, who are
considered the backbone of the Central Secretariat has to wait for 27 years or more for being appointed as Joint
Secretary and that to after waiting in the panel for a period ranging from 3 to 4 years.59. As a cadre controlling
authority of this service, the efforts made by DOPT in ensuring in career advancement of CSS officers are
dismal. Out of 20 officers in the panel of Joint Secretary, 13 names have not been circulated even once in the past
three years. The Department needs to put in greater efforts in a time bound manner and ensure placement of
these officers within a period of six months. It has come on record that DOPT has already taken a decision that
CSS officers empanelled for Joint Secretary will be given mandatory posting if they have two years of service
before superannuation or if they have been in the panel for three years.60. One of the names mentioned in the list
enclosed with the written reply is that of Smt. Neena Garg which appears at Sr.No.3 of the suitability list of CSS
Joint Secretary level officers who are yet to be appointed. Against her name it has inter-alia been stated that
officer has finally been selected. The Committee presumed that all necessary formalities which are required to be
followed for appointment of an officer including approval of the ACC have been completed. Either the formal
orders of her appointment are to be issued or officer has to formally take over her new assignment as Joint
Secretary. It appears that this position is perhaps factually not correct. The Committee would, therefore, like
that DOP&T should examine this matter and furnish it in their note with regard to the process of final
selection/appointment.
61. Since most of the Officers indicated in the list will soon be completing three years of their empanelment.
Immediate steps be taken to issue their posting orders. The Committee suggests that the Department of
Personnel and Training should follow a sound promotion policy. The Committee recommends to implement
dynamic Assured Career Progression (ACP) Scheme which could provide financial upgradation of the next post
in the hierarchy without having functional mobility to the higher post.

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/55_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
CENTRAL STAFFING SCHEME
62. The Secretary, Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions has informed that the Department of
Personnel and Training operates the Central Staffing Scheme (CSS) under which suitable officers from All India
Services and Group A Central Services are selected and placed in posts at level of Deputy Secretary, which has also
been exactly stated in the Annual Report of the Ministry for the year 1998-99. The Committee understands that the said
administrative arrangement is in accordance with the Central Staffing Scheme, as introduced in 1957. The objective of
Central Staffing Scheme, 1957 was extended to provide for systematic arrangements for managing senior administrative
posts at the Centre of and above the rank of Deputy Secretary.
63. The Committee notes that the Central Staffing Scheme which is in operation now is the amended version of Central
Staffing Scheme, 1957. It is mentioned in the amended version that the scope of the Central Staffing Scheme is bound
by the following parameters :
(i) All posts of the rank of Under Secretary and above in the Government of India may be filled
on tenure deputation from the All India Services and the participating Group `A’ services of the
Central Government, excluding such posts of Under Secretary and Deputy Secretary as are
filled by CSS Officers; and
(ii) In so far as the Officers from the Central Secretariat Service (CSS) are oncerned, a
specified number of posts at the level of Under Secretary will be treated as part of their cadre
and posts over and above these will be filled under the Central Staffing Scheme.
64. In the light of above stipulation of Cental Staffing Scheme, 1992, the Committee wanted to know whether Central
Secretariat Service being one of participatory Services participate in the Scheme at Under Secretary level. The
Committee also enquired about the reasons leading to inclusion of the post of Under Secretary in Central Staffing
Scheme. The Ministry in its reply has stated that all 38 participating services except Central Secretariat Service
participate in the Scheme at the level of Under Secretary, whereas Central Secretariat Service which starts at Group `B'
participate at the level of Deputy Secretary after getting elevated to Under Secretary (Group A) in their Cadre. The
Committee was also apprised that due to stagnation in Central Secretariat Services at the level of Section Officer (Group
B, Gazetted), the post of Under Secretary is being filled up by the method of promotion of Section Officers of CSS as
their cadre post. However, only in rare cases, officers of All India Services/Group A services are considered for
appointment at the level of Under Secretary on compassionate grounds/exceptional circumstances. Further, the reason
given by the Ministry for inclusion of the post of Under Secretary in Central Staffing Scheme is quite vague and not in
consonance with the basic objective of the Scheme.
65. The Committee understands that the amended version of Central Staffing Scheme is tilted towards All India
Services and other Group A services as compared to Central Secretariat Service and is discriminatory too.
66. The Committee understands that the post of Under Secretary cannot be considered as senior level
administrative post and the inclusion of such post in Central Staffing Scheme mars the promotional avenue of
Central Secretariat Service as the latter have the career development only in Central Secretariat, it may lead to
frustration amongst Group B Officers of CSS. The scheme violates the ratio of internal promotion to the enternal
recruitment. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the post of Under Secretary in Central Secretariat
must be kept for the Central Secretariat Service exclusively by the way of excluding the post from the Central
Staffing Scheme. The basic objective of Central Staffing Scheme could be served if the original version of the
scheme, 1957 is restored.
POSTING
67. The Ministry in its ATN to 44th Report of the Committee has mentioned that the . Central Government had taken a
decision in 1990 not to post woman officer from All India Services to North-East and Jammu & kashmir in view of law
and order situation prevailing therein at that time, which was subsequently reviewed in 1994 keeping in view cadre-gap
in these states, as a result of which the special dispensation given to woman officers had been withdrawn from 1994
batch onward.

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/55_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
68. In the above context the Committee wanted to know whether cadre-gap still persists in North- Eastern States even
after the review of the decision. The Ministry has furnished the following information :
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
S.N Name of the States Total Strength Officers in Cadre-gap
Position

3. Assam-Meghalay 207 208 (-)1
69. It is evident from the above statement, the cadre-gap is still exists in Manipur, Tripura and Nagaland. The
Committee feels that the slow pace of developmental work in these States is linked to cadre-gap in All India
Services . The Committee recommends that the cadre-gap in the aforesaid States may be filled up at the earliest.
TRANSFER
70. Taking into consideration of the rampant arbitrary transfer of Officers from All India Services manning field post,
the Committee had recommended in its 44th Report to establish Civil Services Board in the States to ensure fixed
tenure for them. The Ministry has informed that the States and the Centre have agreed in principle that institutional
arrangements were required to be evolved to ensure stability of tenures of officers serving under the Government in the
conference of Chief Ministers held on 24th May, 1997. But the States of Gujrat, Haryana, Kerala, Meghalaya, Tamil
Nadu and West Bengal have expressed that they do not feel the need for setting up such Board.
71. The Committee suggests that for ensuring administrative continuity and stability to the incumbents, frequent
transfers should be discouraged and a minimum tenure three to four years) for each officer should be pre-
determined. The Committee recommends that the DOPT may prepare a comprehensive transfer policy to reduce
arbitrariness in transfer and check pre-mature and frequent transfers.
PENSION
72. The Committee in its Thirty-eighth Report on the Demands for Grants (1997-98) of the Ministry had dealt with the
issue of counting of past services for pensionary benefits on mobility of employees from Central Government
Departments to Autonomous Bodies and vice-versa. The Committee had also recommended that the benefit of counting
of past services for pension be countinued to be allowed to employees who had joined Union Government services after
putting in services in Nationalised Banks/L.I.C etc. and vice-versa. It may also be mentioned that the Ministry in its
Action Taken Notes on the Thirty-eigth Report of the Committee had stated that the matter was being reconsidered.
73. The Ministry in its reply has stated that the issue in also a subject matter of Committee on Subordinate Legislation,
who have also made similar recommendations. The Ministry has further stated that Central Government employees,
who move to State or Central Autonomous organisations, get the benefit of counting the past services for pensionary
benefits and vice-versa as per the existing orders. In case of banks, PSUs, LIC, RBI etc. pro-rata pensionary benefits is
paid in lump-sum to Central Government employees who move over to these organisations. Similarly, persons from
these organisations, if they come to Central Government are free to get pro-rata pensionary benefits from these
organisations at the time of joining Central Government. The question of counting the past service is now under
examination in consultation with the Banking and Insurance Division who are consulting their constituent units. Apart
from this, the present rule regarding extension of benefit is as follows :-
"Central autonomous body" means body which is finance wholly or substantially from cess of Central
Government grants. "Substantially" means that more than 50 percent of the expenditure of the autonomous

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/55_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
body is met through cess or Central Government grants. Autonomous body includes a Central statutory
body or a Central University but does not include a public undertaking.
74. The Ministry has informed that this also covers PSUs, banks, LIC etc. where Government has its investment. This
issue has been referred to the Attorney General of India for his opinion which is still awaited. On receipt of the advice of
the Attorney General and views of Banking and Insurance Division, the issue of counting of past services for pension in
case of employees of nationalised banks, LIC etc. will be decided.
75. The Committee notes that the recommendations of Committee has not been implemented even after the lapse
of two years. The Committee again reiterates its stand taken in 38th Report and suggests that appropriate action
may be initiated to implement the same within a given time frame.
PUBLIC ENTERPRISES SELECTION BOARD
76. The Public Enterprises Selection Board is a recommendatory body vested with the responsibilty of recommending
persons for appointment to Board level posts in the Public Sector Undertakings. The Committee learnt that the panel
recommended by the PESB had been scapped by the Government very often. The Committee wanted to know the
reason behind such move. The Ministry in its ATN to 44th Report had submitted the reasons, which varied from non-
avialability of vigilance clearance to unsuitability of candidate to such post. The Committee enquired how a person not
being cleared from vigilance angle was recommended by the PESB. The Ministry in its reply has delineated the
selection procedure effective from 31.12.1997 which inter-alia states that the PESB while sending its recommendations
to the Administrative Ministry shall endorse a copy to the Central Vigilance Commission so that the latter can initiate
advance action for obtaining vigilance clearance. The CVC is expected to give its clearance within a period of one
month. Further, the Ministry has stated that no criteria has been laid down for declaring a candidate unsuitable once
recommended by the PESB. It varies from case to case in the face of the interest and investment in the particular PSUs.
77. The Committee feels that the existing selection procedure of the PESB should be modified in the way that the
vigilance clearance in respect of the candidate must be obtained by the Board before recommending his name for
the post in PSUs. the Committee reiterates that the ratio between Generalist and Specialist should be maintained
in the PESB itself.
UNION PUBLIC SERVICE COMMISSION
78. The Ministry could not submit Annual Report of the UPSC for examination and consideration of the Demand No.97
pertaining to the UPSC for the year 1999-2000. The Committee has been apprised of the fact that 48th Report of the
UPSC for the year (1997-98) have been received from the UPSC and the Ministry is preparing Explanatory
Memorandum in respect of non-acceptance of the Commission advice. Soon after the finalisation of Memorandum, the
copies of the report will be submitted to the Committee and also laid before the Parliament.
79. The Committee takes strong exception of the delay in the submission of the report. The Committee suggests
that the UPSC, should present the Report to the President well in advance so that the Ministry could be able to
prepare Explanatory Memorandum and present the same before Parliament during presentation of Demands for
Grants of the Ministry.
80. The Committee wanted to know whether Question papers of all examinations conducted by the UPSC were prepared
bilingually (English and Hindi). The Secretary informed that on the basis of recommendation of Satish Chandra
Committee, the preparation of bilingual question papers are extened to the specified examination. It has not be done in
all examinations conducted by it keeping in view the secrecy and impartiality of examination procedure.
81. The Committee is not satisfied with the answer. The Committee desires that the UPSC may be urged to give
opinion on the fact that why can not the facility of answering question paper be extended to all examinations
conducted by it. Committee suggests that all examinations conducted by the UPSC should be conducted
bilinguially (English and Hindi).
82. The Committee is of the view that a candidate who opts for English as the medium for the written

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/55_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
examination should also have the option to take the interview either in English or in any Indian language of his
choice. This is because a candidate may be good in written English but may not be so in verbal expression and
may like to take his interview in any of the Indian Languages of his choice in which he is able to express more
easily and conveniently.
CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION
83. The Committee enquired why the Annual Report for the year 1997 is not available for the examination of the
Committee. The Committee is informed that in pursuance of Supreme Court direction in Vineet Narain case, the Annual
Report of the Central Vigilance Commission shall henceforth contain a separate para on the functioning of the CBI. The
Committee has since presented its 51st Report on the Central Vigilance Commission Bill, 1998 and desires that a copy
of the Annual Report of the CVC may be supplied to the Committee.
84. The Committee took serious note of the frequent change of the Director, CBI. The Secretary has informed
that CBI Director enjoys tenure of two years. The Committee suggest that the Director of CBI, who is a very
important officer in the Indian investigating hierarchy, should be given full freedom for working, which could be
ensured under the superision of CVC.

REPORT
1. The Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs comprises the following Departments :
i. Department of Legal Affairs
ii. Legislative Department,
iii. Department of Justice, and
iv. Department of Company Affairs
1. The main functions of the Department of Legal Affairs are :-
i. To render advice to the various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India on legal matters.
ii. To carry out the conveyancing work of the Central Government;
iii. To attend to the litigation work in the Supreme Court, High Courts and some of the subordinate
courts;
iv. To handle the treaties and agreements with foreign countries in matters of Civil Law;
v. To authorise officers to execute contracts and assurances of property on behalf of the President
under Article 299 (1) of the Constitution;
vi. To sanction grants-in-aid to certain institutions engaged in research in the field of law.
2.1. The Department of Legal Affairs is further concerned with appointment of the Law Officers, namely the
Attorney-General of India, the Solicitor-General of India and the Additional Solicitors-General of India, etc. The
Department of Legal Affairs administers the Advocates Act, 1961 and the Notaries Act, 1987. The Department is
also administratively incharge of the Foreign Exchange Regulation Appellate Board, Income Tax Appellate
Tribunal, Indian Legal Service and Law Commission of India.
2.2 The Department has a two-tier organisational set-up, namely, the main Secretariat at New Delhi and the
Branch Secretariats at Mumbai, Calcutta, Chennai and Bangalore.
1. The Legislative Department deals with the following matters:-

i. Scrutiny of Notes for the Cabinet in relation to all legislative proposals
from drafting and constitutional points of view.
ii. Drafting of all Government Bills including Constitution Amendment Bills before introduction in
Parliament; translation of all such Bills into Hindi and forwarding both English and Hindi versions
of the Bills to the Parliament Secretariats; drafting of non-official amendments and rendering of
assistance to Administrative Ministries to decide on the acceptability or otherwise of non-official
amendments;
iii. Drafting of Ordinances to be promulgated by the President;
iv. Drafting of legislations to be enacted as President’s Acts in respect of States under President’s rule;
v. Drafting of Regulations to be made by the President;
vi. Drafting of Constitution Orders, i.e. Orders required to be issued under the Constitution;
vii. Scrutiny of all statutory rules, orders and notifications and their translation into Hindi;
viii. Scrutiny of State Legislations in the concurrent field which requires assent of the President article
254 of the Constitution;
ix. The Department of Justice deals with the Constitutional organisation of the Supreme Court and the
High Courts and the appointment of Judges thereto, conditions of their service and with the
administration of judicial services in the Union Territories. Besides, it is the nodal Department in so
far as the administration of justice in States is concerned, Scrutiny of legislations to be enacted by
Union Territory Legislatures;
x. Elections to Parliament, Legislatures of States and Union Territories and Offices of the President and
Vice-President;
xi. Election Commission; Electoral Reforms;
xii. Apportionment of expenditure on elections between the Centre and the States/UTs with Legislatures;
xiii. Publication of Central Acts, Ordinances and Regulations and their authorised translations in Hindi
and other languages specified in the Eighth schedule to the Constitution.
4. The main functions of the Department of Justice include the appointment of judges of Supreme Court and
High Courts, their service conditions; Constitution and Organisation of Supreme Court and High Courts;
establishment of benches away from the principal seat of the High Courts; reviewing of strength of the judges in
the High Courts; administration of Contempt of Court Act, 1971 and Family Court Act of 1984; the
administration of justice in Union Territories, monitoring of pendency of cases in the courts; the National
Judicial Pay Commission and National Judicial Academy.
4.1. Though this Department forms a part of Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs, it is under the
administrative control of Ministry of Home Affairs.
5. The Department of Company Affairs is the primary agency responsible for the development and efficient
functioning of the corporate sector comprising the Joint Stock Companies. Functions of the Department include
administration of the Companies Act, 1956 and the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969
(MRTP Act), Indian Partnership Act, 1937, and the Societies Registration Act, 1860, and to exercise supervision
over the activities of the Institute of Chartered Accountants. It also holds administrative control over the
Institute of Company Secretaries and the Institute of Costs and Works Accountants.

General Observations
9.1 The Committee at its sitting held on the 15th April, 1999, noted with concern that some of the
recommendations made by it from time to time have not been taken by Government with seriousness they
deserve. There has been inordinate delay in their implementation and when recommendations have not
been accepted, no detailed and cogent reasons were given for not accepting them. The Committee,
therefore, strongly feels that Government may take earnest action in respect of such recommendations
pending before it for decision.
10. The Committee having considered all aspects makes recommendations/observations in respect of the
following:
DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS
10.1. The Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs made a presentation before the Committee on 30th
March, 1999. The salient points of his presentation are as follows:
National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) and Lok Adalats
10.2 The National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) a statutory body constituted under the National
Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 ( as amended by the Act of (1994) is responsible for extending free
legal assistance to poor and weaker sections of the society entangled in litigation before various courts
including Supreme Court . Rs.4.00 crore has been provided as grants-in-aid for the various functions of the
NALSA which inter alia
 include organising Lok Adalats and legal aid to the persons declared eligible

under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
10.3 The Committee , in its 45th Report on the Demands for Grants (1998-99) of the Ministry of Law,
Justice and Company Affairs had recommended to lay the Annual Report and Audited Statement of
Accounts of NALSA on the Table of the Houses of Parliament. In its Action Taken Note the Department
of Legal Affairs had stated that the action for submission of Annual Audited Statement of Accounts of
NALSA would be possible only after the form and the manner in which the Accounts were to be
maintained as well as the modalities of the Legal Aid Fund are finalised in consultation with the
Comptroller and Auditor-General of India and the Comptroller-General of Accounts . On being asked
about the latest position in that regard, the Department replied that as decided in the first annual meeting of
NALSA held on 13.9.97, the modalities for handling and operation of the Legal Aid Fund were worked out
by a Committee and submitted to the Ministry of Finance (Department of Expenditure) as far back as 29
th
January, 1998 and the matter had still been pending with them even after being constantly persued by the
Department of Legal Affairs.
10.4 The Committee is constrained to note that the matter relating to the modalities for handling and
operation of the Legal Aid Fund, which is a pre-requisite before laying of the Annual Report and
Audited Accounts of NALSA before Parliament, has not been attended to by the Ministry of Finance
with the expedition that it deserves. Had this not been so the matter would not have been pending with
them for over a year. The Committee however, reiterates its earlier decision and recommends that the
Annual Report and Audited Statement of Accounts of the NALSA should be laid before the Parliament
without further delay.
10.5 When the funding of the NALSA came up for discussion in the Committee, it wanted to know from

10.9. Several different and newer ways of settling disputes both quickly and inexpensively have come up
to avoid long, expensive and enormously complicated procedures for seeking legal redress through judicial
courts. One such method is Lok Adalat. Lok Adalats which were initially started and encouraged by a few
judges of the Supreme Court in October-November, 1985 as a way of promoting voluntary settlement of
disputes inexpensively and expeditiously have got the statutory status under the Legal Services Authorities
Act, 1987 which covers Legal aid, Lok Adalats and Legal assistance services and intends to secure the
operation of the legal system in order to promote social justice , particularly for the weaker sections of the
society who because of economic and other disabilities can’t afford the costs or delays involved in normal
court procedures. The juridiction of Lok Adalats is very wide. They can determine and arrive at
compromises or settlements between the parties to a dispute in respect of any matter falling within the
jurisdication of civil, criminal or revenue courts or tribunals. The award of the Lok Adalat can be enforced
in law as it is deemed to be a decree of a civil court or tribunal and such award is final and binding upon all
parties in dispute to avoid further costs, expenses and delay. No appeal has been provided from such an
award to any court. The Lok Adalat has been given the powers of civil court under the Civil Procedure
Code while trying disputes and the proceedings before the Lok Adalat are deemed to be the proceedings of
a court as provided in Indian Penal Code.
11.1 The Committee was informed that the working of the Lok Adalats was being reviewed and monitored
from time to time by the National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) and a further innovative scheme has
been introduced by the NALSA aftger the first Annual Meet of the State Legal Services Authorities held
on 12.9.1998 at Vigyan Bhawan, New Delhi at which a resolution was passed that separate Lok Adalats
should be established within the premise of those Government Deapartments, Public Sector Undertakings
and Statutory bodies which, on account of the nature of their activities , are involved in large scale
litigation with general public. Pursuant to the resolution, NALSA has introduced a scheme to resolve the
disputes in the Departments ifself without incurring any expenditure.

Appointment of Notaries
14. The Committee has been informed that there are 815 applications for appointment of Notaries pending

applications are pending for more than one year. The norms for appointment of a Notary are prescribed
under the Notaries Rules, 1956, under which an advocate having 10 years of practice may apply for
appointment as Notary on the prescribed form (memorial), which has to be countersigned by persons of
locality including a Magistrate, a Bank Manager, a Merchant and other local residents. Thereafter the
Competent Authority examines the application and may ascertain from State Bar Council, Bar Association
and other authority in the area where the applicant proposes to practice as Notary, the objections, if any, to
the appointment of the applicant as Notary. The applicant is also given an opportunity of hearing against
the objections, if any. After considering the objections and the various factors mentioned in Rule 7 of the
Notaries Rules, 1956 a decision to recommend appointment or rejection of the applicant is taken by the
Competent Authority.

avoided and the Department should expedite the process in a particular time frame.

Legislative Department
19. The Secretary, Legislative Department in his presentation before the Committee on 30th March, 1999
inter alia stated that the Legislative Department is basically concerned with drafting of all Government Bill

CONFIDENTIAL
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/56_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
including Constitution Amendment Bills before their introduction in Parliament, Ordinances , Legislations,
Constitution Orders etc. It is also entrusted with publication of Central Acts, Ordinances and Regulations
and their authorised translations in all the Languages specified in the 8th Schedule to the Constitution.
During the presentation , the Secretary, Legislative Department stated that the Legislative Department was
one of the oldest limbs of the Government of India. The origin of the Department dates back to 1833. The
principal job of the Legislative Department happens to be drafting of all sorts of central legislations . In
certain eventualities, it also drafts State legislations when there is President’s Rule in a particular State.
The second important function of the Department is to undertake scrutiny of subordinate legislation . The
draft of the subordinate legislations under various Central Legislations are prepared by the respective
Ministries and Departments of the Government of India. They send it to the Legislative Department for its
scrutiny from drafting and legal angle. In view of the Official Languages Policy of the Government and in
view of the provisions of the Official Language Act of 1965, all Bills which are introduced in Parliament,
would be accompanied by Hindi version . Similarly, in the matter of subordinate legislation, if certain rules
are to be framed, they should have a Hindi version also. The Legislative Department has a full-fledged
Official Languages Wing. The principal job of the Wing is to undertake translation of all those instruments
into Hindi for publication purposes. The Department has been given certain administrative responsibilities
like electoral reform matters, Elections of the President of India and the Vice President of India. Besides
that, as many as 75 Legislations are the responsibility of the Department which is the maximum number of
legislations to be administered by a single Department in the entire Government set up. Those legislations
pertain to List III subjects, like divorce, marriage, infant guardianship, transfer of property, Registration
Act, Civil Procedure Code, Bankruptcy, Arbitration etc. The policy formulation in respect of the
legislations are initiated by the Legislative Department. If any changes are required in the Acts, then the
Bills are drafted by the concerned Departments. The Legislative Department has also been giving training
to the officers of the State Legislative Departments since1905. As late as in 1989, the Cabinet took a
decision that there should be a formal institution for legislative drafting and training and thus the Institute
of Legislative Drafting and Research was established . The Institute imparts certain training courses for the
officers of the State Governments. The Institute does not have any regular faculty and the officers in the
Legislative Department form the faculty. They visit the Bureau of Parliamentary Studies and Training
(BPST), Lok Sabha Secretariat and deliver lectures. Besides the above functions, another important
function of the Department is to bring out in the print form all sorts of legislations, be it principal
legislations or sub-ordinate legislations so as to make it available to the society at large. All Acts of
Parliament, both in English and Hindi and in the regional languages are printed. A couple of months back,
the Department has initiated the task of putting together the entire material relating to principal legislations
on on-line computers and now one can have any Indian Legislation, all Central unrepealed Acts on the
Internet. The Department has undertaken one more project to put the entire subordinate legislations on on-
line computers. The subordinate legislation happens to be a huge volume. The compilation was, hitherto,
being done by respective Departments, the Secretary informed the Committee.

sufficient to prove to the world that India is an independent Nation/State. An independent Nation/State is

23.5. In a written reply to the Questionnaire regarding the service conditions of the officers working for
Hindi side, the Legislative Department informed the Committee that Indian Legal Service Rules, which
comprise of four Grades viz., Gr. IV (equivalent to Under Secretary), Gr. III (equivalent to Deputy
Secretary), Gr. II (equivalent to Director) and Gr. I (equivalent to Joint Secretary) dates back to the year
1957 and include officers of both the Legislative Department and Department of Legal Affairs. The said
Rules have been framed for the recruitment of officers in the Legislative Department and Department of
Legal Affairs. The primary function of Legislative Department is to draft all Government Bills,
Ordinances, Rules & Regulations and the main function of the Department of Legal Affairs is to tender
legal advise to various Ministries and to handle litigation. Accordingly, Indian Legal Service Rules were
framed in 1957.
23.6 On the other hand, the primary function of the Official Languages Wing is to prepare and publish
standard legal terminology for use in all Official Languages and to prepare authoritative texts in Hindi of
all Central Acts and Ordinances and Regulations promulgated by the President and to arrange for
translation of the same. The Official Languages Wing came into being in the year 1976 and accordingly,
the Recruitment Rules for various Officers in the Official Languages Wing were framed keeping in mind
the duties and functions performed by the said Wing. The entry grade in the Group ‘A’ Service in the
Official Languages Wing is the Assistant Legislative Counsel (Hindi) [equivalent to Under Secretary]; the
next promotional post to that of Deputy Legislative Counsel (Hindi) [equivalent to Deputy Secretary],
Additional Legislative Counsel (Hindi) [equivalent to Director] and Joint Secretary & Legislative Counsel
(Hindi) [equivalent to Joint Secretary]. Since the duties and functions performed by the Officers of the
Hindi side are entirely different from those of the Officers belonging to Indian Legal Service, hence, as
already stated above, there is a separate set of Recruitment Rules for recruitment of the Officers of the
Hindi side in the Legislative Department.
23.7 The Committee feels that both the officers viz. Indian Legal Service Officers and Officers of Hindi
side in the Department are working for the same wing of the Government i.e. the wing assisting the
Government in Legislation work. The Committee recommends that the Indian Legal Service Rules
which were framed in 1957 should be arranged so as to include the officers working in the Official
Languages Wing in the Indian Legal Services. The Committee feels that the discrimination perpetrated
against Official Language Wing officers is absolutely unjustified.

DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
25. The Additional Secretary, Department of Justice in his presentation before the Committee on 31st
March, 1999 , inter alia stated that the Department was created in the year 1971 and the subjects handled
by the Department are constitution and organisation of the Supreme Court and the High Courts,
appointment of Judges in the High Courts and the Supreme Court and their service conditions, Judges
strength, administration of Justice in Union Territories and monitoring of pendency of cases in courts.
Courts in the country are at three levels. At the district level, there is subordinate judiciary, at the state
level, High Courts and finally the apex court at the Union level. As per provisions of Articles 233, 234 and
235 of the Constitution, the supervision, control and appointment of subordinate judiciary is done at the
level of the State Governments and the concerned High Court. The Union Government is concerned only
with the appointment of Judges in High Courts and the Supreme Court. At present there are 18 High
Courts in the country. 11 States and one Union Territory have separate High Courts. Six High Courts,
namely, Punjab and Haryana, Bombay, Kerala, Madras, Calcutta and Guwahati High Courts have
jurisdiction over more than one State, the representative of the Department apprised the Committee.

25.1. The Committee, in its 17th, 31st, 34th 39th and 45th Reports had taken a serious view of the anomaly
to the effect that the Demands for Grants of the Department of Justice is met from that of the Ministry of
Law, Justice and Company Affairs whereas the Department is under the administrative control of the
Ministry of Home Affairs. In the latest ATN on the recommendation of the Committee, the Department of
Justice has stated that the Government has again examined the recommendation of the Committee
regarding transfer of the Department from the administrative control of the Ministry of Home Affairs to
the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs, but has decided to continue with the existing system in
view of the reason inter alia that the administrative linkage of the Department of Justice with the Ministry
of Home Affairs ensures better coordination in the appointment of Judges and the administration of
Criminal Justice with the States. In a written reply to the pointed questions as to in view of the reasons
furnished for status quo what is the rational for keeping the Department of Justice under the Law Ministry
only for budgetary purposes, the Department has replied that the Department of Justice was carved out of
the Ministry of Home Affairs as the Law Commission had suggested that all work relating to the subject of
justice should be unified into a separate Ministry of Justice for judicial administration should be handled in
a Ministry that should be immune to political pressures. Accordingly, Department of Justice was created
with transfer of 7 items of work from Ministry of Home Affairs to Department of Justice and placed in the
then Ministry of Law. Ministry of Law was also reconstituted with Department of Justice as a Department
under that Ministry.
25.2 The arrangement then made by retaining the administration and house keeping functions in Ministry
of Home Affairs while budget of the Department of Justice being in the Demands for Grants pertaining to
Ministry of Law, Justice & Company Affairs, has worked well. In 1972, a proposal for Department of
Justice being a self contained Department by having its own administration, house keeping functions, etc.,
without depending on Ministry of Home Affairs was examined and it has decided that there was no need to
change it especially in view of the need for economy in Government expenditure, the Committee has been
informed.
25.3 The cardinal point to be considered in any change in the existing arrangement is the expenditure
involved on account of capital cost as well as cost of development of infrastructure facilities. Besides that,
it would also upset the close coordination that exists now between the Department of Justice and Ministry
of Home Affairs. Even though the Budget is voted in Demands for Grants for Ministry of law, Justice &
Company Affairs, the allocation is operated by Ministry of Home Affairs on behalf of Ministry of Law,
Justice & Company Affairs since 1971.
25.4 The Committee is not at all convinced with arguments put forth for maintaining to status quo.
Here, the Committee wishes to point out that the Law Commission had suggested for a separate
Ministry of Justice that should be immune to political pressures. The Committee fails to understand as
to how the Department of Justice could be insulated from political pressures so long as its
administrative functions remain with Ministry of Home Affairs. Having regard to all the points
explained by the Government having considered all the functional aspects of the Department, the
Committee reiterates it earlier stand and recommends that either the Department of Justice may be
made a full fledged Department under the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs, headed by a
Secretary like other three Departments in the Ministry or alternatively the Demands for Grants of the
Department of Justice may be accounted for in the Ministry of Home Affairs.

USE OF HINDI IN SUPREME COURT AND HIGH COURTS
30. A point was raised in the Committee regarding the use of Hindi in the Supreme Court and High Courts.
The Department of Justice in their written reply has informed the Committee that Article 348 (1) of the
Constitution provides that all the proceedings in the Supreme Court and every High Court shall be in
English until Parliament by law otherwise provides. No law has been made by the Parliament so far in this
regard. Under Article 348 (2) of the Constitution, the Governor of a State, may with the previous consent
of the President, authorise the use of Hindi language or any other language used for any official purpose of
the State, in proceedings of the High Court having its principal seat in the State, provided that decrees,
judgements or orders passed by the High Court shall be in English. Under Section 7 of the Official
Language Act, 1963, the use of Hindi or official language of a State in addition to English may be
authorised, with the consent of the President, by the Governor of the State, for the purpose of judgements
etc. made by the High Court for that State. So far, the Governors of the four Northern States namely,
Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh have authorised the use of Hindi in addition to
English language in the proceedings as well as the judgements, decrees etc. for the High Court of their
State. The Chief Justice of India had reported in October, 1991 that replacement of English at lower levels
of the judiciary by the State Language had already been implemented throughout India.
31.1. The Committee notes the factual position in this regard.
VACANCIES OF JUDGES IN SUPREME COURT AND HIGH COURTS
31. The Committee in its 45th Report had felt concerned over the number of vacancies of judges in the
High Court which had a direct co0relation with the increasing pendency of cases in the Courts.
31.1 The Department, in its Status Note on the position of vacancies in the High Courts, has stated that
certain differences in perception on scope and the extent of ‘consultation’ in appointment of Judges both in
the Supreme Court and the High Courts and transfer of Judges and Chief Justices of the High Courts, arose
in 1998. To resolve the matter, a Presidential Reference under Article 143 of the Constitution of India was
made to the Supreme Court. The following 9 points of law were referred to the Supreme Court:
i. Whether the expression consultation with the Chief Justice of India in articles 217 (1) and
222(1) requires consultation with a plurality of judges in the formation of the opinion of the
Chief Justice of India or does the sole individual opinion of the Chief Justice of India constitute
consultation within the meaning of the said articles;
ii. Whether the transfer of judges is judicially reviewable in the light of the observation of the
Supreme Court in the aforesaid judgement that "such transfer is not justifiable on any ground"
and its further observation that limited judicial review is available in matters of transfer, and the
extent and scope of judicial review;
iii. Whether article 124(2) as interpreted in the said judgement requires the Chief Justice of India to
consult only the two senior most Judges or whether there should be wider consultation
according to past practice;
iv. Whether the Chief Justice of India is entitled to act solely in his individual capacity, without
consultation with other Judges of the Supreme Court in respect of all materials and information
conveyed by the Government of India for non-appointment of a judge recommended for
appointment;
v. Whether the requirement of consultation by the Chief Justice of India with his colleagues, who

CONFIDENTIAL
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/56_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
are likely to be conversant with the affairs of the concerned High Court refers to only those
Judges who have that High Court as a parent High Court and excludes Judges who had
occupied the office of a Judge or Chief Justice of that court on transfer from their parent or any
other Court;
vi. Whether in light of the legitimate expectations of senior Judges of the High Court in regard to
their appointment to the Supreme Court referred to in the said judgement, the ‘strong cogent
reason’ required to justify the departure from the order of the seniority has to be recorded in
respect of each such senior Judge, who is overlooked, while making recommendation of a
Judge junior to him or her;
vii. Whether the Government is not entitled to require that the opinions of the other consulted
Judges be in writing in accordance with the aforesaid Supreme Court judgement and that the
same be transmitted to the Government of India by the Chief Justice of India along with his
view;
viii. Whether the Chief Justice of India is not obliged to comply with the norms and the requirement
of the consultation process in making his recommendation to the Government of India;
ix. Whether any recommendations made by the Chief Justice of India without complying with the
norms and consultation process are binding upon the Government of India?
31.2 The Supreme Court disposed of the Presidential Reference by its Advisory Opinion on October 28,
1998 as under:
i. The expression "consultation with the Chief Justice of India’ in Articles 217(1) and 222(1) of
the Constitution of India requires consultation with a plurality of Judges in the formation of the
opinion of the Chief Justice of India. The sole, individual opinion of the Chief Justice of India
does not constitute ‘consultation’ within the meaning of the said Articles.
ii. The transfer of puisne Judges is judicially reviewable only to this extent: that the
recommendation that has been made by the Chief Justice of India in this behalf has not been
made in consultation with the four senior most puisne Judges of the Supreme Court and/or that
the views of the chief Justice of the High Court from which the transfer is to be effected and of
the chief Justice of the High Court to which the transfer is to be effected have not been
obtained.
iii. The Chief Justice of India must make a recommendation to appoint a Judge of the Supreme
Court and to transfer a Chief Justice or puisne Judge of a High Court in consultation with the
four senior most puisne Judges of the Supreme Court. In so far as an appointment to the High
Court is concerned, the recommendation must be made in consultation with the two senior most
puisne Judges of the Supreme Court.
iv. The Chief Justice of India is not entitled to act solely in his individual capacity, without
consultation with other Judges of the Supreme Court, in respect of materials and information
conveyed by the Government of India for non-appointment of a Judge recommended for
appointment.
v. The requirement of consultation by the Chief Justice of India with his colleagues who are likely
to be conversant with the affairs of the concerned High Court does not refer only to those
Judges who have that High Court as a parent High Court. It does not exclude Judges who have
occupied the office of a Judge or Chief Justice of that High Court on transfer.
vi. ‘Strong cogent reasons’ do not have to be recorded, as justification for a departure from the
order of seniority, in respect of each senior Judge who has been passed over. What has to be

CONFIDENTIAL
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/56_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
recorded is the positive reason for the recommendation.
vii. The views of the other Judges consulted should be in writing and should be conveyed to the
Government of India by the Chief Justice of India along with his views to the extent set out in
the body of this opinion.
viii. The Chief Justice of India is obliged to comply with the norms and the requirement of the
consultation process, as aforestated, in making his recommendations to the Government of
India.
ix. Recommendations made by the Chief Justice of India without complying with the norms and
requirements of the consultation process, as aforestated, are not binding upon the Government
of India.
31.3 The Committee has been informed that the Memoranda of Procedure on appointment of Judges in the
Supreme Court/Chief Justices and Judges of High Courts, as also the transfer of Chief Justices and Judges
of the High Courts are being revised incorporating the Advisory Opinion of the Supreme Court.
32. The Department has informed that as on March 23, 1999, the sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court
is 26 Judges out of which 25 Judges are in position, leaving 1 vacancy to be filled up. Seven vacancies
were filled up after receipt of the Advisory Opinion on October 28, 1998. The Government has, as on
March 26, 1999, not received proposal from the Chief Justice of India for filling up the sole vacancy in the
Supreme Court.
33. The Department has further informed that as on March 1, 1999, against the sanctioned strength of 587
Judges/Additional Judges, 448 Judges/Additional Judges were in position, leaving 139 vacancies to be
filled up. 31 new posts of Judges/Additional Judges have been agreed to in various High Courts. After
receipt of the Advisory Opinion of the Supreme Court, 48 Judges have been appointed in various High
Court. For filling up the existing vacancies of Judges/Additional Judges in the High Courts, 53 proposals
have been received from the State constitutional authorities and these are at various stages of
consideration.
34. The Committee has been informed that the Government, in its part, requests the Chief Justices to
initiate proposals/recommendations for filling up vacancies of Judges in the High Courts expeditiously. As
the procedure involves consultation with various constitutional authorities, it is not possible to indicate the
time by which all the vacancies would be filled in. Procedurally, unless recommendations/proposals are
made to the Government, posts would continue to remain unfilled as initiation of proposal for appointment
rests in Chief Justices and the Chief Justice of India for the High Courts and the Supreme Court
respectively.
35. Regarding the procedure for appointment of Judges the Committee has been informed that according to
the judgement of October 6, 1993, read with the Advisory Opinion of October 28, 1998, of the Supreme
Court of India the proposal for appointment of a Judge of a High Court shall be initiated by the Chief
Justice of the High Court. The Governor, as advised by the Chief Minister, should forward his
recommendation to the Union Law Minister as early as possible but not later than six weeks from the data
of receipt of the proposal from the Chief Justice of the High Court. If the comments are not received within
the said time frame, it should be presumed that the Constitutional authorities of the State has nothing to
add to the proposal. The Union Minister of Law, Justice and Company Affairs would consider the
recommendations in the light of such other reports as may be available to the Government in respect of the
names under consideration. The complete material would then be forwarded to the Chief Justice of India

file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/56_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
for his advice. The Chief Justice of India would, in consultation with two senior most Judges of the
Supreme Court, form his opinion in regard to a person to be recommended for appointment to the High
Court. The Chief Justice of India and the collegium of two Judges of the Supreme Court would take into
account the views of the chief Justice of the High Court and of those Judges of the High court who have
been consulted by the Chief Justice as well as views of those Judges in the Supreme court who are
conversant with the affairs of that High Court. After consultations, the Chief Justice of India is expected to
send his recommendation to the Union Minister of Law, Justice and Company Affairs within four weeks.
The Union Minister of Law, Justice and Company Affairs would then put up as early as possible,
preferably, within 3 weeks, the recommendation of the Chief Justice of India to the Prime Minister who
will advise the President in the matter of appointment. The Department added that it would be observed
that the time-frame for the constitutional authorities in the matter of appointment of Judges of the High
Court has already been proposed. The Government, on its part, requests the Chief Justices to initiate
proposals/recommendations for filling up vacancies of Judges in the High Courts expeditiously. As the
procedure involves consultation with various Constitutional authorities, it is not possible to indicate the
time by which all the vacancies would be filled up , the Department further added.
36. The Department has intimated that the observation of the Committee during the consideration of the
Demands for Grants, on the vacancies of Judges has been noted and the Chief Justices of the High Courts
would be apprised of this with a request to initiate proposals in time so that the vacancies are filled in
expeditiously.
37. The Committee has also been apprised that the transfer of a Judge from one High Court to another is
made by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India (vide Article 222(1) of the
Constitution). The Government had accepted, as a policy, the recommendations of the Law Commission in
its 80
th Report that there should be a convention according to which 1/3rd of Judges in each High Court
should be from any other State. The Government has decided that this may be implemented either by
making initial appointments from outside or by effecting transfers. Pursuant to this policy,
transfer/appointment of Judges and Chief Justices of the High Courts are being made on the
recommendation of the Chief Justice of India.
37.1. The Committee has been further apprised that prior to the judgement of the Supreme Court in
Advocates-on-Record Association vs. Union of India and others on October 6, 1993, proposal for
appointment of Judges could also be initiated by the Government. However, according to the Judgement of
October 6, 1993, read with the Advisory Opinion of October 28, 1998 of the Supreme Court of India the
initiation of the proposal for appointment of the Judge in the Supreme Court must be by the Chief Justice
of India, and in the case of a High Court by the Chief Justice of that High Court. For transfer of a
Judge/Chief Justice of a High Court to another High Court, the proposal has to be initiated by the Chief
Justice of India. This is the manner in which proposals for appointments to the Supreme Court and the
High Courts as well as for the transfers of Judges/Chief Justices of the High Courts must invariably be
made, the Committee has been informed by the Department.
38. In this context the Department has stated that one of the items of the National Agenda for Governance
is to set up a National Judicial Commission to make recommendations for Judicial appointments in the
Supreme Court and the High Courts and draw up a code of ethics for the judiciary.
39. Having considered all the aspects of the matter regarding appointment of Judges of Supreme Court
and High Courts and transfer of Judges of High Courts and the delay in filling up the vacancies of

High Court Judges, the Committee feels that the time has come when the basic substantial issues should
be deliberated at the highest level of the Government so that there could be an over all improvement in
the situation.
Accountability of Judges
40. Regarding the accountability of Judges the Committee has been informed by the Department that the
issue of judicial accountability was discussed in the Conference of Chief Justices held in 1990 and on the
basis of the broad consensus emerging out of the deliberations, the Chief Justice of India summed up the
position as follows:-
i. The Chief Justice of the High Court has the competence to receive complaints against the
conduct of the Judges of his court and when he receives any he would look into it for finding
out if it deserves to be closely looked into. Where he is satisfied that the matter requires to be
examined, he shall have facts ascertained in such manner as he considers appropriate keeping
the nature of allegations in view and if he is of the opinion that the matter is such that it should
be reported to the Chief Justice of India, he shall do so.
ii. The Chief Justice of India shall act in a similar manner in regard to complaints relating to
conduct of Judges of the Supreme Court and in regard to conduct of Chief Justices of the High
Courts.
iii. On the basis of the facts ascertained, the Chief Justice of the High Court or the Supreme Court,
as the case may be, shall take such appropriate action as may be considered proper, keeping the
interests of the judiciary as the paramount consideration.
41. The Department has further informed that in this regard the following resolution was also passed in the
Chief Justices’ Conference held on October 26 and 27, 1996:-
"Resolved that the Hon’ble CJI may constitute a Committee of Judges to finalise the
‘restatement of values’ of judicial life in the light of the suggestions made by the
various High Courts."
In view of above, necessary action with regard to accountability of the Judges of
High Courts and Supreme Court has to be taken by the Chief Justices of High Courts
and the Chief Justice of India respectively.
With regard to accountability in lower judiciary, it is stated that under Article 235 of
the Constitution of India, the administrative control over the members of subordinate
judicial service vests with the concerned High Court. Further, in exercise of powers
conferred under proviso to Article 309 read with Articles 233 and 234 of the
Constitution, the State Government frame rules and regulations in consultation with
the High Court exercising jurisdiction in relation to such State. The members of the
State judicial service are governed by these rules and regulations. Thus, the members
of subordinate judiciary are subject to disciplinary and conduct rules framed by the
State Governments and the High Courts".
42. The Committee recommends that like Legislative and Executive there should be code of conduct for
the judges and some mechanism or arrangement like Lokpal Type should be worked out.

Pendency in Courts
43. The Additional Secretary, Department of Justice in his deposition before the Committee stated that the
pendency of Supreme Court is decreasing. There were 1,04, 936 cases as on 31st December, 1991. The
pendency has come down to 20,306 as on 1st February, 1999 (See Annexure-C). The Supreme Court has
noted that the decrease is due to the categorisation and grouping of cases, non-accumulation of defective
matters, reservations of more time for old pending cases. The pendency with High Courts is increasing
(See Annexure-D). there were 26.5 lakhs case pending as on 31st December, 1993. The pendency has
increased to 32.03 lakhs as on 30th June, 1998. The increase in pendency is due to various complex factors
e.g. more institution of cases, awareness of the rights on the part of the utilizers, population explosion,
industrial development in the country, increase in trade and commerce, emergence of socio economic
measures, grant of frequent adjournments by the Courts, frequent strikes by the advocates etc. The
Committee in its 45th Report, had recommended that measures taken by the Supreme Court should be
suggested to the High Courts also to bring down the pendency. Accordingly, the Minister of Law, Justice
and Company Affairs addressed letters to the Chief Justices of all the High Courts requesting them to
follow the some measures which were undertaken by the Supreme Court. Some of the High Courts have
responded that they have stated taking up those measures. However, the impact of taking those measures
on the pendency is not known because the overall pendency in all the High Court has increased. The
pendency in the subordinate courts,as on 31
st December ,1995 was 2.18 crores. It has gone down to 2.02
crores as on 30th June , 1998. The decrease in the pendency of cases in subordinate courts is mainly due to
classification of cases involving minor offences pending for two years or more in which proceedings have
not commenced and also due to appointment of special magistrates/special metropolitan magistrates under
sections 13 and 18 of Criminal procedure code, the steps taken by the State Governments for increasing the
number of judicial officers etc.
44. Regarding the various steps taken by the Government for expeditious disposal of cases in courts, the
Department of Justice has, in written reply, stated that the various Law Commissions of their Report have
made suggestions regarding speedy disposal of pending cases in Courts such as amendment in procedural
Laws, increase in Judge strength, establishment of more Special Courts/Tribunals, provision of modern
office equipments, etc. Government has taken a series of steps for speedy disposal of pending cases. These
include amendment of Civil Procedure Code and Criminal Procedure Code. The Code of Civil Procedure
(Amendment) Bill, 1997 inter-alia contains a number of provisions which will facilitate speedy disposal of
all cases. Further, steps are being taken to increase the number of posts of Judges in the High Courts,
appointment of Special Judicial/Metropolitan Magistrates for disposal of petty criminal cases,
computerization in courts etc. The Government has also adopted alternative modes of dispute resolution
such as arbitration and conciliation . Lok Adalats have been given a statutory base with the enforcement of
the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, as amended, w.e.f. 9.11.1995. Lok Adalats have proved to be an
effective and successful supplementary forum for resolution of disputes. Free legal aid is available for the
poor litigant. The Law Commission in its 154
th Report has made several recommendations with regard to
speedy disposal of cases viz. Separate and exclusive cadre for investigating agency, timely attendance of
witnesses, protection and facilities to witnesses, setting up of a separate Directorate of Prosecution,
addition of new sub-section 41A on custodial crimes, Protection of under trial prisoners, empowering all
the criminal courts to take bail, appointment of Special Magistrates under Section 13 and 18 of the
Criminal Procedure Code for disposal of petty cases, compensation to crime victims, summary trial
procedure for recording evidence, etc. The Report has been circulated to all the State governments for

CONFIDENTIAL
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/56_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
soliciting their comments/views. Views of some State Governments/UT Administrations have been
received and are being processed.
45. The Department has further stated that "the Supreme Court of India in the case of Common Cause Vs.
Union of India on 1st May, 1996 directed for closing of few categories of criminal cases which were
pending for more than 2 years in Subordinate Courts and in which the trial had not commenced. Further,
the Supreme Court, in Writ Petition No.559 of 1994 – R.D. Upadhyay Vrs. State of A.P. and others is also
seized of the matter regarding pending criminal cases and under trial. The Supreme Court in the said Writ
Petition, in its order dated 10th December, 1998 has directed for releasing of the under trial prisoners
languishing in jail for more than six months for offences under section 107/151 of the Criminal Procedure
Code, on bail, on furnishing personal bonds to the Chief Judicial Magistrate concerned". The Department
has further informed that on the basis of the recommendations made by the various
authorities/Committees/Law Commissions etc., the High Courts have been requested from time to time to
take various measures to expedite the disposal of pending cases in the Subordinate Courts. Recently, the
Chief Justice of India has addressed a letter to the Chief Justices of all the High Courts impressing upon
the need to deal with the problem of delay in disposal of cases in the Subordinate Courts and to initiate
action for filling up the vacant posts of Judges/Judicial Officers so as to make the year 1999 as an "Year of
Action".
46. The Committee takes strong exception to the huge pendency of cases in courts which has shaken the
confidence of the people in the administration of Justice. The Committee is also is seized of the efforts
of the Government on that account for streamlining the procedure of courts by proposing to amend the
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 which will go a long way in bringing down the pendencies in Courts.
Even then, the Committee feels that the Government should make all possible efforts for quick disposal
of cases.
All INDIA JUDICIAL SERVICE
47. The Committee has been informed that in the light of the recommendations of the First, Eighth and
Eleventh Law Commissions and also in pursuance of a recommendation of the Supreme Court of India
vide its judgement dated 13.11.1991 in the matter of All India Judges Associated vs. Union of India &
others (Writ Petition No.1022 of 1989), the question of creation of an All India Judicial Service is already
under consideration of the Government. An All India Service can be created only through a resolution to
be passed by the Rajya Sabha by not less than two-thirds of the Members present and voting, followed by
an enactment by the Parliament under Article 312 of the Constitution. The matter relating to creating of All
India Judicial Service is being processed accordingly.
48. The Committee recommends that the decision with regard to the creation of All India Judicial
Service may be taken at the earliest,
SETTING OF BENCHES OF SUPREME COURT AND HIGH COURTS
49. The Committee has been informed that representations have been received from time to time from
various Bar Associations, other bodies, Members of Parliament, etc. for establishment of Benches of
Supreme Court in various parts of the country. The Governments of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and
Karnataka suggested that a Bench of Supreme Court may be established in the respective State capitals for
south India. The Chief Minister of Tripura sent in August 1983 a copy of the resolution passed by the Bar

file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/56_rep.html[30-06-2016 17:34:26]
Association, High Court of Calcutta, requesting for establishment of a Bench of Supreme Court at

Association. The Law Ministers of the eastern and the north-eastern States adopted a resolution
unanimously in their meeting held on 4.10.96 in Calcutta that it is essential for the Supreme Court to sit at
a suitable place in their regions to promote equal opportunity to all in operation of our legal system.
According to article 130 of the Constitution, " the Supreme Court shall sit in Delhi or in such other place
or places as the Chief Justice of India may, with the approval of the President from time to time, appoint."
The Government has further informed that the matter has accordingly been referred to the Chief Justice of
India from time to time for his views. It has been intimated many a time by the Registry of the Supreme
Court and the Chief Justice of India since 1982 and as recently as 1997 that the suggestion for the
establishment of Benches of the Supreme Court outside Delhi was considered and was not agreed to by the
Full Court in a meeting presided over by the Chief Justice of India.
50. The Committee has not been informed about the reasons communicated by the Registry of the
Supreme Court for disagreement on establishment of benches of Supreme Court in different part of the
country. The Committee recommends that Government should think for setting up benches of Supreme
Court in Southern, Western and North-Eastern parts of the country.
51. The Additional Secretary, Department of Justice in his deposition before the Committee stated that
`proposals’ have been received from Bar Associations, State Governments and other persons for
establishing a bench apart from the principal seat of the High Courts. When a proposal was received from
the Uttar Pradesh Government for setting up of a Bench of the Allahabad High Court in the Western U.P.,
the Central Government set up a Commission known as the Jaswant Singh Commission in 1981 to
examine the issue. Later on, the terms of reference of the Commission were enlarged to include the
demand of a Bench of the Guwahati High Court, Benches of the High Courts of Karnataka, Madhya
Pradesh and Madras. The Commission was also requested to suggest the broad principles of criteria to be
followed for setting up of the Benches of the High Courts. The Commission submitted its report to the
Government of India in 1985 recommedning, inter alia, establishment of a permanent bench of the
Allahabad High Court at Agra and a circuit bench at Nainital and Dehra Dun. The Commission also
recommended the setting up of a circuit bench at Raipur of the Madhya Pradesh High Court and
consideration of its coversion into a permanent bench after five years. Similarly, the Commission also
recommended the setting up of a circuit bench of Madras High Court at Madurai and its conversion into a
permanent bench after five years. The Commission also recommeded the broad principles and the criteria
to be followed for assessing the desirability of setting up of benches of High Courts away from their
principal seats and the factors to be kept in view in selecting the venue of such benches. The report of the
Commission was also laid on the Tables of the Rajya Sabha and the Lok Sabha on 20.4.1987 and 21.4.87
respectively. The specific recommendations of the Commission regarding the Allahabad, the Madhya
Pradesh and the Madras High Courts were referred to the concerned State Governments in October, 1986
for their views and comments in consultation with the Chief Justices of the respective High Courts, as also
the Governors of those States. In 1989, the Government of Uttar Pradesh sent the proposal for the setting
up of a permanent bench of the Allahabad High Court at Agra. At that time the Chief Justice of the High
Court was totally opposed to the setting up of this bench, He mentioned that as a result of this, the High
Court might even break up. There were agitations and counter agitatios by bar associations. The bar
association of Allahabad was against the setting up of a bench at Agra, whereas the district bar association
of the Western UP demanded the setting up of benches of the High Court at various places in Uttar
Pradesh, even away from Agra. In 1994, the then Chief Minister again wrote to the Government of India
