lower level administrative post playing supporting role in decision making process in the Secretariat. Further, the CSS being one of the participating services in Central Staffing Scheme does not participate for the post of Under Secretary, which was viewed
by the Committee  as discriminatory and the amendment was designed  to  bring officers  of  All India   Services  and Group ‘A’  Services at   the  post  of  Under Secretary so as to stifle the career progression of  Section Officer (Group-B Gazetted) within
Central Secretariat Service. Thus, the Scheme in operation is not  in consonance with the basic objective of the original scheme. The Committee, therefore, had recommended in its 55 th Report to honour the original scheme of 1957 by keeping the post of
Under Secretary in Central Secretariat for the Central Secretariat Service exclusively.
 
20.3     The Ministry in its Action Taken Replies to 55 th Report of the Committee has stated that  though the post of Under Secretary is included in the Central Staffing Scheme, officers belonging to All India Services and other Group ‘A’ Services are not
generally appointed at that level. Rarely are the posts of Under Secretaries filled by All India Services/Group ‘A’ Services officers. The Ministry advanced the logic that if the post of  Under Secretary is taken out of the Central Staffing Scheme, it may
become difficult to fill such posts located at places other than Delhi, where CSS Officers may be reluctant to go, while it may be possible to post officers of other services participating in the Central Staffing Scheme at those places.
 
20.4     The Committee fails to understand how come Section Officers of Central Secretariat Service, who are experiencing stagnation in his/her grade and having housing problem will be  reluctant to accept promotion to the post of Under Secretary located at
places other than Delhi. In this context, the Committee intended to know whether the  Section Officers of CSS have ever been offered the post of Under Secretary located outside Delhi.
 
20.5     The Ministry in its reply  stated that posts of Under Secretary level located outside Delhi have been offered to Central Secretariat Service e.g., a post at US level in SSC Bangalore Regional Office,
a CSS cadre post, could not be filled from CSS as there were no optees from CSS. It was proposed to ex-cadre the post for other services, but when it got upgraded to DS level a CSS officer joined the post; one post of US in Department of Agriculture and
Cooperation at Nagpur remained vacant, despite being a CSS cadre post, as it could not be filled for absence of optees. Department of Personnel and Training had to advise that Department to make its own arrangements for filling the post; two posts of Under
Secretary in the Department of Atomic Energy at Mumbai when circulated had no optees from amongst the CSS and were filled by an IAS officer of Bihar cadre and one UTCS officer; one post each of Under Secretary at SSC, Chennai, in Department of
Agriculture and Cooperation at Faridabad and in the Department of Ocean Development at Cochin have been filled by CSS officers.
20.6     The Committee understands that the vacancies of the posts might not have been given wide publicity among the Section Officers of CSS. In that context, the Committee wanted to know whether any post of Under Secretary located in Delhi have ever
been filled up by the officers of All India Services and Group ‘A’ Services and sought details thereof for the period form 1993 to 1999.
20.7     The Ministry has supplied Ministry wise information regarding appointment from AIS and Group ‘A’ Services  to the post  of  Under Secretary  located at Delhi  under Central Staffing Scheme.
The Ministry has also mentioned that an on 1.3.2000 out of 552 Under Secretary level officers working at the Centre, 533 belong to the CSS and the rest is occupied by the officers belonging to AIS/Group ‘A’ Service.
20.8     The Ministry has mentioned, in this context, that it invites nominations from State Governments/Centre Authorities for Central deputation each year for filling the posts of Deputy Secretary level and above upto Joint Secretary/equivalent under the
Central Staffing Scheme. However, considering cadre management requirements whenever the State Governments or Group ‘A’ Cadre Authorities suo motu forward the names of officers for the appointment at Under Secretary level, they are considered for
placement at that levels. Hence, posts of Under Secretaries other than those held by CSS Officers are considered to be well within the scope of the Central Staffing Scheme.
20.9     To     the    another   question   on   the   Central   Staffing   Scheme   –   What   are      the
reasons/circumstances prompting the Ministry to include the post of Under Secretary under Central Staffing Scheme by the way of supersession of the resolution of 1957 by an O.M. of the Ministry dated 15.7.1992, the Ministry has replied that the pay scale
attached to the post of Under Secretary is Rs. 10,000-15,200 and hence it is a Group ‘A’ post and therefore brought within the purview of the Central Staffing Scheme. The Committee was  informed that the post of Under Secretary was included in the
Scheme way back in 1970 by O.M. No. 33(1)-E.O./70 dated 27
th October, 1970.
20.10   In this context, it may be mentioned that the O.M. under reference of the Ministry speaks less about the Central Staffing Scheme and more about constitution and functions of ‘Senior Selection Board’, ‘Central Establishment Board’ and
‘Establishment Officer’. The O.M. does not reflect the picture of Central Staffing Scheme as has been depicted in the Original Resolution of 1957 and in the latest Office Memoranda of 1992 and 1996.
20.11   The Committee takes serious note of the flippant replies submitted by the Ministry on the Central Staffing Scheme. The replies are also ambiguous and misleading. The Committee does not appreciate the logic that the post of Under Secretary is Group
‘A’, thus included in the Central Staffing Scheme. The Committee understands the post of Under Secretary is Group ‘A’ all along  even before the formulation of Central Secretariat Service Rule, 1962. Why the post was included in the Central Staffing
Scheme in 1970, why not at the time of giving shape to original version of the Central Staffing Scheme.
20.12
      The Committee understands  that  the concept of the Central Staffing Scheme was tailored to keep hold on the post of Under Secretary in Central Secretariat by the Officers of AIS and Group ‘A’ Services which is totally against the
objective of the Central Staffing Scheme and reiterates  its stand taken in its 55th Report to keep the post of Under Secretary in Central Secretariat out of the purview of the Central Staffing Scheme.
20.13   As per the CSS Rules, 1962 the composition of Central Secretariat Services is from Assistant (Group B) to Deputy Secretary (Group A). The Committee feels that the post of Deputy Secretary should be reserved for the CSS Officers.
20.13   The Ministry in its reply has mentioned that not less than 25% of the posts of Deputy Secretaries in the various Ministries/Departments are, as far the extant policy, filled by CSS Officers only. The rest 75% of the posts of Deputy Secretaries are filled
by officers of 37 other services participating in the Central Staffing Scheme. If Officers of these services are excluded from manning posts of Deputy Secretaries, that would mean exclusion of these officers below 14 years of service from appointment to post
under the Central Staffing Scheme. Such an exclusion has not been intended or provided in the Central Staffing Scheme or even in the CSS Rules. Further, the Government will be deprived of the benefit of the expertise and experience of the Officers of the
various services at the level of Deputy Secretaries if appointment at that level is made of only CSS officers. It is also pertinent to point out that there is a specific Central Deputation Reserve (CDR) built in the cadres of the various States, in respect of the
three All India Services, namely, the IAS, the IPS and the Indian Forest Service. The CDR level is based on the need of the Central Government in respect of the officers of the three All India Services for manning its posts at various levels. The CDR of IAS
alone stood at 1111 as on 1.3.2000. Officers to the extent   of the number covered in the CDR of the three All India Services have been recruited for the affairs of the Central Government on tenure deputation basis. If AIS officers are to be considered for
placement at the level of Director and above only, their appointments will be confined to posts at Director level and above, and since the number of posts available at those levels as on 1.3.2000 was only 1220, it may not be feasible or desirable to fill 1111
posts out of the total 1220 posts  at Director level as it stood on 1.3.2000, by IAS officers only.
20.15   The objective of the Central Staffing Scheme that has been in existence for over four decades is the Centre’s need for fresh inputs at senior levels in policy planning, formulation of policy and implementation of programmes from diverse sources,
namely the All India Services and the Group ‘A’ Central Services participating in the Central Staffing Scheme, as also the scientific and technical personnel and professionals, all borrowed on tenure deputation basis. The objectives of the Central Staffing
Scheme would be defeated if the posts at certain levels are exclusively reserved for the offices of any particular service.
 
 
20.16
      The Committee agrees with the basic objectives enumerated in the Central Staffing Scheme. The Committee also understands that when the scheme was originally introduced the post of Deputy Secretary was at the bottom level for
decision making process or otherwise treated as one of the senior administrative posts. But, subsequently, when the post of Director was introduced, it took the place of Deputy Secretary in the decision making process making the post of
Deputy Secretary middle management level rendering supporting role in the decision making process. The other 37 participating services have career progressions in their respective cadres whereas the CSS which has career progression only
in the Central Secretariat is affected by the Central Staffing Scheme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the post of Deputy Secretary should also be part of CSS cadre as per the statutory provision of CSS Rules, 1962. But keeping in
view of the reasons stated by the Ministry, in the preceeding paras, the Committee recommends that 50% of the post of Deputy Secretary instead of extant 25% should be reserved for the officers of CSS.

RECRUITMENT
22.0     The Committee was apprised that vacancies in Government Departments/Undertakings are published in the National dailies only and such employment notices are not being published in local language dailies as a result of which many candidates are
being deprived of a chance to apply for the said vacancies.

22.2     The Ministry has also stated that advertising the recruitment notices in local newspapers has been dropped. The Ministry has, further, informed that in terms of Official Language Policy of the Union, a person who is unable to read and write either

22.3     The Committee agrees with the Official Language Policy of the Union but the aspirants residing in remote hinterland and far-flung areas such as North-East who happen to know Hindi and English but cannot get ready access to the

provide easy access to the candidates residing in the remote areas where national newspapers are not easily accessible.
 22.4    In view of the analysis made in the preceding paras, the Committee suggests the Ministry  to ensure that all recruitment notices of  Government are published in local newspapers also.

26.0     The Committee has been informed that at present a retiring civilian employee has to surrender his Identity Card. Once this Identity Card is surrendered, the retired employee has no other document for establishing his identity to the effect that prior to

recommended that the said O.M. was discriminatory and unreasonable and should be withdrawn forthwith. The matter had been under consideration of the Ministry of Personnel since then and a lot of correspondence has taken place in between the
Secretariat of Parliament and the administrative Ministry. The issue was again raised with the administrative Ministry in relation to Demands for Grants of 2000-2001. The Ministry of Personnel have come forward with a cryptic reply that in a case before the
Central Administrative Tribunal, Mumbai, the said Bench has upheld the legal validity of the clarifications issued by the Government excluding Life Insurance Corporation of  India/General Insurance Corporation of India/Nationalised Banks from the
purview of the order dated 29
th August, 1984. No further details of the case, namely, parties involved, issues and material placed before the Tribunal including mentioning of the recommendations made by the Parliamentary Committees and legal opinion, if

27.1     Various Committees of Parliament, including this Committee and the Committee on Subordinate Legislation, are the constituents of the legislative limb of the Government. Judicial limb of the Government operates in the sphere allotted to it under the
Constitution. In spite of the fact that a judicial organ has given an opinion in a particular matter in some regard, the Legislature continues to exercise legislative power to give shape to the legislative policy as it feels reasonable and desirable for the society.
27.2     Notwithstanding the fact that Ministry of Personnel in their answers have not provided the details of the case as aforesaid, on merit as well, this Committee does not subscribe to the proposition of excluding nationalized sector belonging
to insurance and banking including Reserve Bank of India for the purpose of entitlement of counting of service on movement to Government Departments and vice-versa. The Committee urges upon the Government to give effect to the
recommendations made by it in this regard in its 38
th Report at the earliest.
CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION
28.0     The Committee had recommended in its 55th Report to ensure functional autonomy of the CBI under the Central Vigilance Commission and also a fixed tenure for the Director of CBI.
28.1     The Committee has been informed that in accordance with the directions of the Supreme Court,  the CBI Director has been given minimum tenure of two years regardless of the date   of his superannuation, which also finds a place in the Central
Vigilance Commission, Bill, 1999. This would ensure that an officer suitable in all respects is not ignored merely because he has less than two years to superannuate from the date of his appointment.   The transfer of an incumbent Director, CBI in an
extraordinary situation, including the need for him to take up a more important assignment, should have the approval of the Selection Committee.
 
28.2     The Committee has also been further informed that in pursuance of Supreme Court judgement in the Vineet Narain case,  CBI Selection Board with Central Vigilance Commissioner as Chairman and the Home Secretary   and the Secretary
(Personnel) as Members have been constituted for inter alia  making recommendations for the appointment of Director, CBI. While making recommendation, the Board draws up a panel of IPS officers on the basis of their seniority, integrity, experience in
investigation and anti-corruption work.  The incumbent Director, CBI is also consulted in the matter of suggesting a list of suitable persons for preparation of such panels by the Board. However, the consideration of suitable persons is not restricted to the list
suggested by the incumbent Director.
 
28.3     The Selection Board suggests a panel of three names in descending order of preference for consideration by the Appointments Committee of the Cabinet (ACC). The final selection is made by the ACC from the panel recommended by the Selection
Board. If none among the panel is found suitable, the reasons thereof shall be recorded and the Board shall be asked to draw up a fresh panel.
 
28.4     For making the functioning of the CBI efficient and impartial, Independent Review Committee setup in 1997 to examine the structure and functioning of the CBI has inter-alia given the following main recommendations:-
 
(i)
                 The CVC to overview CBI’s functioning and CBI’s reporting to Government to be streamlined without diluting its functional autonomy.
(ii)               Constitution of Selection Committee for identifying a panel of names for selection of Director, CBI; final selection to be made by ACC from such panel.
(iii)             The Director, CBI to have minimum tenure of two years. Transfer of incumbent Director, CBI should have endorsement of the Selection Committee.
(iv)             The Director, CBI to be ensured full freedom for allocation of work within the agency, including constitution of investigation teams.
(v)        Selection/extension of tenure of officers upto the level of Joint Director (JD) shall be decided by a Board comprising  the Central Vigilance Commissioner, Joint Director and above would need the approval of ACC.
(vi)       Director, CBI to be responsible for ensuring time limits for filing chargesheets in courts.
(vii)      Secretary of Administrative Ministry to convey a decision regarding registration of Preliminary Enquiry (PE)/Regular Case (RC) within 2 months of receipt of request. If not satisfied with decision, Director, CBI free to make fresh reference to the 
Committee headed by Cabinet Secretary within a period of four weeks and the latter to decide thereon within a period of four weeks.
 (viii)    Time limit of three months for according sanction for prosecution. Where consultation is required with the Attorney General or the Solicitor General, additional time of one month could be allowed.
(ix)       Cases falling within the jurisdiction of the State Police which do not have inter-state or inter-national ramifications should not be handed over to CBI by States/Courts.
(x)        Government to establish special Courts for the trial of CBI cases.
(xi)       Director, CBI to conduct regular appraisal of personnel to weed out the corrupt and inefficient, and maintain strict discipline within the organization.
 
28.5     The Supreme Court in the Vineet Narain case had directed the Government that Central Vigilance Commission shall be responsible for the efficient functioning of the CBI, while the Government shall remain answerable for the functioning of CBI
primarily to introduce visible objectivity for over viewing the CBI’s working. Following the directions of the Supreme Court the provision of exercising superintendence over the functioning of the CBI, in so far as it relates to  the  investigations  of  offences 
alleged  to  have  been  committed  under  the  Prevention   of Corruption Act, 1988 has been given to CVC. The Central Vigilance Commission Bill, 1999, is currently under the consideration of Joint Parliamentary Committee. The CBI shall report to the
CVC about cases taken up by it for investigation; progress of investigation; cases in which charge sheets are filed and progress thereof. The Central Vigilance Commission shall review the progress of all cases moved by the CBI for sanction of prosecution of
public servants which are pending with the competent authorities especially those in which sanction has been delayed or refused. However  Clause 19 of the Bill, provides that the power of superintendence of the CVC shall not extend to its giving directions
to the CBI to investigate or dispose off a particular case in a particular manner.
 
28.6     Thus, the superintendence of the CVC over the CBI is limited to the investigation of offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act only. The superintendence of CVC shall not extend to investigation of cases relating to general crime and economic
offences. As a result, a clear cut demarcation of the area of superintendence over the functioning of the CBI  has been drawn to ensure
impartial, and efficient functioning of the CBI. However, the stability of the tenure of the Director, CBI  will help infuse full freedom in  its functioning.
 
28.7     Further, the CBI shall have full freedom for constituting team for investigations. Any change made by the Director, CBI in the Head of investigative team should be for cogent reasons and for improvement in investigation, the reasons being recorded
which has also been communicated to the CBI through letter No. 142/1/98-AVDI dated 3.2.1998 for necessary action.
 
28.8     The extension of tenure or premature repatriation of officers upto the level of Joint Director shall be with the final approval of Board comprising Central Vigilance Commissioner, Home Secretary and Secretary (Personnel), which is also approved by
the ACC.
28.9     Keeping in view the ever increasing cases pertaining to  economic offences being handed over to CBI for investigation and the Supreme Court’s direction to strengthen CBI’s in house expertise, professionals from the revenue, banking and security
sectors shall be inducted into the CBI. The Government has sanctioned a total number of 183 posts including technical posts for augmenting the Special Crime division and the Economic Offences Wing of the CBI. The experts/professionals so inducted will
play an advisory role and give expert advice in the investigation of complicated cases of specialised nature pertaining to economic offences.
28.10   CBI has also recently set up an investigating unit designed as Cyber Crime Investigation Cell (CCIC) at New Delhi under the Economic Offences Division (EOD) of CBI for taking up investigation of offences involving computer crimes, crimes
committed in computerized environment and other high-tech crimes in areas like telecom etc.
28.11   In accordance with the CBI Crime Manual, in case of adverse remarks or strictures passed by the courts, it will be incumbent upon the CBI to take action   against the officers found guilty, after obtaining explanation from the affected officers. Reports
in every such case where adverse remark has been made is sent to the Head Office of the CBI for taking strict action against the officer found guilty of dereliction of duty.
28.12   CBI  has  also  prepared  a  panel  of  competent  lawyers  having  experience  and  impeccable reputation to be appointed as prosecuting counsel in significant cases of CBI.
 
28.13   The Committee recommends intensive training for the rank and file in the CBI so as to cope up with new trends in crime particularly in the cases of white collar crimes – cyber, electronics and economic crimes.
 
28.14   The Committee expresses its deep  concern about the cases pending  in courts and cases pending investigation with the CBI as a consequence of which the credibility of the CBI is suffering.

28.16   It  has been stated by the Ministry  in the replies to the questionnaire that the cases under investigation are constantly monitored by  senior supervisory officers as per provisions in the CBI Crime Manual. Cases pending investigation for more than two
years are regularly reviewed, in the meeting taken by Director, CBI with the Joint Directors and DIs G concerned from time to time. The cases pending investigation for over two years are now being centrally monitored at the CBI Head Office. As to cases
pending investigation for more than five years, Letters Rogatory have to be executed in three cases after issuance by competent courts for investigation abroad. Although, these are being constantly pursued through the Indian Mission abroad, execution of
such Letters Rogatory depends on the legal system of the country, which is very often time consuming. In the four of such cases, stays have been granted by the High Courts and vacating of stay takes a long time.
 
28.17   As to cases pending trial in the courts, instructions have been issued for Superintendent of Police to  monitor these cases personally  and to attend to important hearings in the court. The senior supervisory officers during their visit to the Branches/units
from time to time review the progress in these cases. As disposal of cases pending trial depends upon the functioning of the courts, efforts are also made by the senior supervisory officers to call on the presiding officers of the courts and also the Chief  
Justices   of  various  High   Courts   during   their  visits  to  outstation field units. The Central Vigilance Commission, has also called for court-wise details of cases pending trial for analysis during its monthly review meetings with CBI and the CVC has also
taken up the matter with the Chief Justices of various High Courts. Further, proposals for creation of courts of Special Judge/Magistrate, exclusively for trial of CBI cases are also being vigorously pursued with the respective State Governments and High

28.23   From the perusal of table titled  “Disposal of Court Cases” it appears that No. of cases ended  in acquittal   in  1999  is  41.7%  whereas  the  same  was  33%  during the year 1997. The reasons attributed for such acquittal are that the trial proceedings
take a long time during which some of the important/vital witnesses either expire or are not available for deposition in the court. Further, some of the witnesses become disinterested over a period of time or won over by the accused and turn hostile. Some of
the cases also result in acquittal as the courts take a view that the evidence adduced was insufficient to prove the allegation beyond doubt.
 
28.24   The Committee is of the view that CBI prosecutors should be impressed upon to prepare a strong case and lacunae, if any, should be pointed out  to the CBI before filing the chargesheet so that CBI can collect the required evidence in
this regard and the accused is not acquitted on the ground of insufficient evidence.
 
28.25   The Committee understands that the CBI does not have its own cadre of officers and the officers on deputation have their loyalty to their parent cadre. The question of CBI’s own cadre comes to lime light in  the Priyadarshini Mattoo Case wherein 
the court has reprimanded the CBI for biased investigation as a son  of DIG police was involved in the case.
 
28.26   The Ministry has stated that the CBI is the premier investigating agency of the country and is handling various types of cases of very complicated and technical nature. Investigation of these cases requires specialised knowledge and expertise in
various fields. There are experienced officers of the State Police Forces and other enforcement agencies who have wealth of experience in investigation of various kinds of cases, particularly cases relating to conventional crime. Hence it is considered
necessary to draw  officers from  the State Police Forces  and  other enforcement agencies so that their experience is utilized by the CBI. The officers coming on deputation to CBI acquire experience in investigating cases relating to corruption, while collar
crimes and other cases having national/international ramifications during their tenure in CBI. After returning to their parent cadre, they share the knowledge/experience acquired in CBI with their colleagues in their parent Department which is beneficial to

29.1     There is no provision in the existing  Recruitment Rules for direct recruitment of Inspectors in the CBI. Posts in the grade of Inspector are either filled by promotion or by deputation. The feeder grade for promotion to the rank of Inspector is that of
Sub-Inspector.
 
29.2     Sub-Inspectors in the CBI recruited through Staff Selection Commission (SSC) as well as through the Limited Departmental Competitive Examination (LDCE) from within the CBI. Sub-Inspectors recruited through SSC are required to be Graduates
whereas those recruited through the LDCE are required to be Graduates with three years of service or Matriculations with 8 years of service. But there is no minimum qualifications prescribed as such for deputation to the grade of Inspector.
 
29.3     The Ministry   further  informed  that  the  Recruitment  Rules for the  posts  of  Inspector and
Sub-Inspector in the CBI are under revision subsequent to the recommendations of V Central Pay Commission. It has been proposed that for deputation to the post of Inspector in the CBI a minimum qualification of graduation should be made compulsory. It
is also proposed that Sub-Inspectors recruited through LDCE should be graduates. The proposed Recruitment Rules are under the consideration of the UPSC whose concurrence  has been sought.
 
29.4     As the Sub-Inspector and Inspector are required to go to the field for investigation, the minimum educational qualification of graduation is very much essential for them. The Committee recommends  to amend the Recruitment Rules of
the CBI for introducing minimum qualification of graduation for the deputationist to the both Sub-Inspector and Inspector. Inspector recruited through LDCE should also be graduate. The Committee also recommends that officers who are
on deputation to the post of Sub-Inspector and above in the CBI and have no graduation degree should be repatriated forthwith.

Asstt. Secretary to the Government of  India.  The Committee understands that only Section Officer grade will be given  Group ‘A’ status and not the service of CSS as it starts with Asstt, which is Group ‘B’ non-gazetted.  The
Committee, therefore, recommends necessary amendment to Rule 3 of CSS Rules, 1962.
(Para 19.8)
 
 
*          The Committee feels that CSS as a whole (Assistants, Section  Officers, Under Secretaries and   Deputy Secretaries) is facing a common problem of stagnation and lack of promotional avenues for its various grades.  No doubt, the
Government have taken some remedial measures for two grades which also need to be taken for 3 rd grade also. The Committee, therefore, recommends upgradation of equal number of posts of Assistants to that of Section Officers as
has been done for the grades of Section Officers, Under Secretaries and Deputy Secretaries on ‘in-situ’ basis.
(Para 19.17)
             CENTRAL STAFFING SCHEME
 
*          The Committee understands   that  the concept of the Central Staffing Scheme was tailored to keep hold on the post of Under Secretary in Central Secretariat by the Officers of AIS and Group ‘A’ Services which is totally against the
objective of the Central Staffing Scheme and reiterates  its stand taken in its 55th Report to keep the post of Under Secretary in Central Secretariat out of the purview of the Central Staffing Scheme.
(Para 20.12)
*          The Committee agrees with the basic objectives enumerated in the Central Staffing Scheme. The Committee also understands that when the scheme was originally introduced the post of Deputy Secretary was at the bottom level for
decision making process or otherwise treated as one of the senior administrative posts. But, subsequently, when the post of Director was introduced, it took the place of Deputy Secretary in the decision making process making the post
of Deputy Secretary middle management level rendering supporting role in the decision making process. The other 37 participating services have career progressions in their respective cadres whereas the CSS which has career
progression only in the Central Secretariat is affected by the Central Staffing Scheme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the post of Deputy Secretary should also be part of CSS cadre as per the statutory provision of CSS
Rules, 1962. But keeping in view of the reasons stated by the Ministry, in the preceeding paras, the Committee recommends that 50% of the post of Deputy Secretary instead of extant 25% should be reserved for the officers of CSS.
(Para 20.16)
 
             CENTRAL DEPUTATION OF IAS OFFICERS
 
*          The Committee is of the view that ‘public interest’ criterion should not be used in cases of granting extensions to the officers of the levels of Under Secretary, Deputy Secretary and Director.
 
(Para 21.0)
 
 
*          The Committee feels that the guidelines laid down for Central Deputation of IAS Officers should be followed in letter and spirit.  In normal course, the extension should not be granted as it presupposes the indispensability of the
incumbent to the post which checks the flow of better inputs to the organisation.
(Para 21.1)
             RECRUITMENT
 
*          The Committee agrees with the Official Language Policy of the Union but the aspirants residing in remote hinterland and far-flung areas such as North-East who happen to know Hindi and English but cannot get ready access to the
Employment News and the National dailies. The local newspapers have large number of readerships in the areas of their publications and can be accessed easily by the candidates  in those areas. Further, the Committee   does    not  
want  the recruiting office to advertise the recruitment notice in the language in which the local newspaper is published.  The Committee is of the view the recruitment/employment notices should also be published in English/Hindi in
local newspapers to provide easy access to the candidates residing in the remote areas where national newspapers are not easily accessible.
(Para 22.3)
*          In view of the analysis made in the preceding paras, the Committee suggests the Ministry  to ensure that all recruitment notices of  Government are published in local newspapers also.
(Para 22.4)
            TRAINING
 
*          In this context, the  Committee feels that the extant training policy needs  review so as to inculcate basic values in the administrators.
(Para 23.1)
            TRANSFER
 
*          The Committee does not agree with the period of five years of an incumbent in a sensitive post, as stipulated by the Ministry.  The Committee recommends that such posts should be identified and put in a place and the incumbents

occupying such posts for more than three years  may be transferred immediately.
(Para 24.2)
 
             STAFF WELFARE
 
*          The Committee feels that the grants-in-aid of Rs.3000/- for Residents Welfare  Association is meagre and not sufficient to maintain activities of the Associations.  It is suggested that the grant may be augmented considerably.
(Para 25.1)
 
 
              PENSIONERS’ WELFARE
 
*          The Committee feels that it would be in fitness of things  if the civilian exployees are also issued Identity Cards indicating the details such as last post held before retirement, pay-scale of the post last held, period of service rendered etc,
which the retired employee can carry on his person for identification as and when needed.
(Para 26.2)
 
*          The Card may also include on the reverse the retired employee’s Blood Group, his residential address and telephone number, if there is one.
(Para 26.3)
*          The Committee  strongly recommends that the Government should favourably consider on priority the desirability of issuing such cards on retirement to each Central Government employee.
(Para 26.4)      
             COUNTING OF PAST SERVICE FOR PENSION
 
*          Notwithstanding the fact that Ministry of Personnel in their answers have not provided the details of the case as aforesaid, on merit as well, this Committee does not subscribe to the proposition of excluding nationalized sector belonging
to insurance and banking including Reserve Bank of India for the purpose of entitlement of counting of service on movement to Government Departments and vice-versa. The Committee urges upon the Government to give effect to the
recommendations made by it in this regard in its 38
th Report at the earliest.                                                                                                  (Para 27.2)
 
             CENTRAL BUREAU OF INVESTIGATION
 
*          The Committee is not satisfied with the explanation given for the pendency of CBI trial cases and  reasons advanced for speedy disposal of cases. In spite of existing arrangements, the pendency is witnessing an upward trend. This lack-
lustre performance calls for in-depth examination at the top.  The Committee wants the Ministry to take bold steps to expedite investigation and strengthen the inner
Mechanism of CBI for quick disposal of cases. The Committee also suggests to establish more special Courts in States for the trial of CBI  cases so as to instill confidence in public at large.
(Para 28.21)
*          The Committee is of the view that CBI prosecutors should be impressed upon to prepare a strong case and lacunae,  if any, should be pointed out to the CBI before filing the chargesheet so that CBI can collect the required evidence in
this regard and the accused is not acquitted on the ground of insufficient evidence.
 (Para 28.24)
 
*          The Committee suggests that the officer held responsible for biased investigation must be   punished  at     once   in order to restore faith in the premier investigating
agency of the Country.   The Committee also recommends to maintain transparency in the investigation conducted by the CBI.  The Ministry may also take measures to infuse professionalism in the existing cadre of the CBI and create
a permanent cadre in the long run.
(Para 28.29)
            RECRUITMENT POLICY OF CBI
 
*          As the Sub-Inspector and Inspector are required to go to field for investigation, the minimum educational qualification of graduation is very much essential for them. The Committee recommends  to amend the Recruitment Rules of the
CBI for introducing minimum qualification of graduation for the deputationist to the both Sub-Inspector and Inspector. Inspector recruited through LDCE should also be graduate. The Committee also recommends that officers who
are on deputation to the post of Sub-Inspector and above in the CBI and have no graduation degree should be repatriated forthwith.
(Para 29.4)
             PUBLIC ENTERPRISES SELECTION BOARD
 
*          The committee understands that the individual Ministries/Deptts are taking the issue causally.  In that context, it suggests that all Ministries/Deptts should implement the recommendation of PESB in letter and spirit.
(Para 30.2)
             LOK PAL
 
*          The Committee desires that the Government while considering its recommendations on the Lok Pal Bill, 1998 may also keep in view the recommendations as contained in the First and Second Reports of Ethics Committee of the Rajya
Sabha, adopted by that House on 15  December 1999.
(Para 31.1)

REPORT
 
1.                  The Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs comprises the following Departments
(i)                 Department of Legal Affairs
(ii)               Legislative Department,
(iii)             Department of Justice, and
(iv)             Department of Company Affairs

2.                  The main functions of  the Department of Legal Affairs are :-
(i)                 To render advice to the various Ministries/Departments of the Government of India on   legal matters.
(ii)               To carry out the conveyancing work of the Central Government;
(iii)             To attend to the litigation work in the Supreme Court, High Courts, Tribunals and some of the subordinate courts;
(iv)             To handle the treaties and agreements with foreign countries in matters of Civil Law;
(v)               To authorise officers to execute contracts and assurances of property on behalf of the President under Article 299 (1)
of the Constitution and to sign and verify plaints and written statements in suits by or against the Union of India;
(vi)             To sanction grants-in-aid to certain institutions engaged in research  in the field of law.
2.1.      The Department of Legal Affairs is further  concerned    with appointment  of the Law Officers, namely the Attorney-General
of India, the Solicitor-General   for India and the Additional Solicitors-General for India, etc.   It administers the Advocates Act,
1961,  the Notaries Act, 1952 and the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.  The Department is also administratively incharge of the
Foreign Exchange Regulation Appellate Board, Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Indian Legal Service and Law Commission of 
India.
2.2       The Department has a two-tier  organisational set-up, namely, the main  Secretariat at  New Delhi and the Branch Secretariats
at Mumbai, Calcutta, Chennai and  Bangalore.
3.                  The Legislative Department  deals with the following  matters:-
(i)                 Scrutiny of Notes for the Cabinet in relation to all legislative proposals  from drafting and constitutional points of
view.
(ii)               Drafting of all Government Bills including Constitution   (Amendment) Bills  before  introduction in Parliament;
translation of all such Bills into Hindi and forwarding both English and Hindi versions of the Bills to the  Parliament 
Secretariats; drafting of official  amendments to Bills, Scruting of non-official amendments and rendering   assistance
to Administrative Ministries to decide on the acceptability or otherwise of non-official amendments;
(iii)             Rendering assistance to Parliament and Joint Select or Standing Committees of Parliament at all stages through
which a bill passes before enactment.   This includes scrutiny of and /or preparation of reports of such Committees,
and Hindi translations of such reports and minutes of dissent;
(iv)             Drafting of Ordinances to be promulgated by the President;
(v)               Drafting of legislations to be enacted as President’s Acts in respect of States under President’s rule;
 
(vi)             Drafting of Regulations to be made by the President;
(vii)           Drafting of Constitution Orders, i.e. Orders required to be issued under the Constitution;
(viii)         Scrutiny of all statutory rules, orders and notifications and their translation into Hindi;
(ix)             Scrutiny of State Legislations in the concurrent field which requires assent of the President under Article 254 of the
Constitution;
(x)               Scrutiny of legislations to be enacted by Union Territory Legislatures;
(xi)             Elections to Parliament, Legislatures of States and Union Territories and Offices of the President and Vice-
President;
(xii)           Apportionment of expenditure on elections between the Centre and the States/Union Territories  with Legislatures;
(xiii)         Election Commission; Electoral Reforms;
(xiv)         Publication of Central Acts, Ordinances and Regulations and their authorised translations in Hindi and other
languages specified in the Eighth schedule to the Constitution.
4.         The Department of Justice deals with the constitutional organisation of the Supreme Court and the High Courts and the
appointment of Judges thereto, conditions of their service and with the administration of Judicial services in the Union Territories. 
Besides, it is the nodal Department in so far as the administration of justice in States is concerned, although the actual responsibility
of judicial administration below the High Court level rests with the concerned State Governments and High Courts.  Though this
Department forms a part of Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs, it is under the administrative control of Ministry of
Home Affairs.  Till 1992-93 the budget of the Department of the justice was salary oriented.   From 1993-94,  the Demands of the
Department of Justice also included provision for the Centrally Sponsored Scheme relating to infrastructural   facilities for the
judiciary and National  Judicial Academy.  From the financial year 1996-97 provision has also been made for the First National
Judicial Pay Commission, in the year 2000-2001, Rs.63.00 lakhs has been allocated for the Commission.
5.         The functions of the Department of Company Affairs in the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs includes
administration of the Companies Act, 1956 and the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act, 1969 for development and
efficient functioning of the Corporate Sector comprising Joint  Stock Companies.  The Department also exercises supervision  over
the activities of Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, Institute of Company Secretaries of India and Institute of Cost & Works
Accountants of India.  These Institutes, which are self-supporting, are concerned with the proper growth of profession of Chartered
Accountants, Cost Accountants and Company Secretaries.   The Department also has the responsibility of carrying out the functions
of the Central Government relating to the Administration of the Partnership Act, 1932, the Companies (Donations to National Funds)
Act, 1951 and Societies Registration Act, 1860.  Certain essential amendments to the Companies Act, 1956, initiation of modern

DEPARTMENT OF LEGAL AFFAIRS
10.1     The Secretary, Department of Legal  Affairs made  a presentation   before  the Committee on 30th March, 2000. 
Appointment of  Notaries
11.       The  Committee, in its 56th Report on the Demands for Grants  of the Ministry for the year 1999-2000, had recommended   to
avoid long and undue delay in the appointment of Notaries and expedite the process in a definite time frame.  In its action taken reply
the Department  has  informed the Committee that it  has set up a separate Notary  Cell   to curtail the delay in appointment   of
Notaries.  In order  to assess suitability  of the applicants  for  appointment  as Notaries, the competent   authority  in this Department
earlier  used  to interview   the applicants.   However, this practice has since been dispensed with.  This step has been taken with a
view to curtailing  the delay in appointing Notaries.  On being asked whether with the setting   up of a  separate Notary Cell and with
the simplification of the procedure for appointment of Notaries, the pendency   has gone down  the Committee has been informed
that  prior to the  implementation of
 
the new decision for appointment   of Notaries, 935 applications were pending.  At present, 1693 cases for appointment of Notaries
are pending out of which 958 applications have been received during the period from June, 1999 to till date.   So far 200  Notaries
have been appointed.  With the dispensing of holding of interviews and with the gearing of the administrative   machinery, the time
taken for processing  the applications   for appointment of Notaries, has been reduced   considerably.   However, large number of
applications for appointment  of Notaries are being received  as  a result of which the pending applications have increased.  Since the
new system was introduced only in June, 1999, it would gradually knock  down  the pendency.
11.1     The Committee does not find the pending position with regard to the applications for appointment of Notaries
satisfactory.  It reiterates its earlier   recommendation  and hopes that the Government would ensure the quick disposal of
applications for appointment of Notaries and feels that if a definite time frame is fixed for disposal of applications it will
considerably reduce the pendency. The Committee further recommends that Government should ensure due representation
of Schedule Castes, Schedule Tribes and Other Backward Classes while appointing Notaries.
Law Commission
12.       The Law Commission of India is a non-statutory body constituted   by the  Government  from time to time.  The Commission
was originally constituted  in 1955.  It is reconstituted  every three years.  The present Law Commission (15th Law Commission) was
constituted  with effect from 1 st September, 1997 for a period of three years i.e. upto 31 August  2000.  The Committee has been
informed that the Commission  has so far submitted 171 reports, 91 of which have already been implemented.   32 reports have not
been accepted by the Government.   One report of the Commission is currently under   process for being laid in the Parliament.   The
remaining  47 reports are pending  for implementation/consideration with various Ministries/Department of the Government which
are administratively concerned with the subject matter of the reports.  The Government has further informed   that the Fifteenth Law
Commission has so far submitted fifteen Reports.  Fourteen reports have already been  laid in  Parliament.   The last Report is the
171st Report entitled “Bio-Diversity Bill”, received on 20.1.2000.
12.1     The Committee in its 45 th Report on Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the year 1998-99 had recommended to ensure
the accountability of the administrative Ministries of the Government for implementation of the accepted recommendations.    The
Committee reiterated  its earlier recommendation in its 56th Report  and desired that the concerned  Ministries/Departments might be 
persuaded and periodical meetings with them may be called once in a month to look into the  progress in that regard .  In any case 
accountability  may be fixed by the Government in cases where the concerned   Ministries/Departments have not started the
implementation  of the accepted reports of the Law Commission.  As regards reports relating to the subjects falling under List III of
the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution  of India, the Committee recommends  that the matter may be  taken up on priority basis
with the State Governments/Union Territories  Administrations  and it should be impressed  upon them to implement those reports in
a time bound manner.  In its action taken reply, the Department has intimated   that  the matter regarding early implementation of the
pending reports of the Law Commission is being pursued vigorously  with the concerned Ministries/Departments at the level of Law
Secretary.

National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) and Lok Adalats
13.0     The National Legal Services Authority (NALSA), a statutory   body constituted   under the National   Legal Services
Authorities Act, 1987 ( as amended   by the Act of 1994) is responsible    for extending   free legal assistance to poor and weaker
sections of the society entangled in litigation before  various  courts including   Supreme Court .  Rs.6.00 crore has been provided as
grants-in-aid for the  various  functions of the NALSA which inter alia
   include   organising  Lok Adalats and legal aid  to the
persons declared eligible under the Act.
13.1     The Committee , in its 45 th Report   had recommended   to lay the Annual Report  and Audited  Statement of Accounts of
NALSA on the  Table of the Houses  of Parliament.   In its action taken reply the Department   had stated    that the action for
submission of Annual Audited  Statement  of Accounts  of NALSA would  be possible only after the form and the manner in which
the Accounts  were to be  maintained  as well as the modalities   of the Legal   Aid Fund  are finalised   in consultation   with the
Comptroller  and Auditor-General of India and the Comptroller-General of Accounts .  The Department   had further replied   that as
decided in the first  annual  meeting of NALSA held on 13.9.97, the  modalities   for handling  and operation of the Legal Aid Fund
were worked  out  by a Committee and submitted to the Ministry  of Finance (Department of Expenditure) as far back as 29 th 
January, 1998 and the matter is still  pending with them even after being constantly  pursued  by the Department.
13.2     The  Committee in its 56 th Report, had reiterated its earlier recommendation and recommended   that the Annual Report and
Audited Statement of Accounts of the NALSA should be laid before the Parliament without further delay. In its action taken reply,
the Department has informed that the NALSA has requested the Ministry of Finance    (Department of Expenditure) to expedite its
recommendations on the modalities for handling and operation of the Legal Aid Fund.  The Member Secretary, NALSA has
addressed a letter on 3.6.1999 to the Additional Secretary, Department of Expenditure to submit their recommendations to the
Executive  Chairman of NALSA at the earliest so that a final decision in regard  to the handling and operation of the National   Legal
Aid  Fund as well as the modalities for submission of accounts and audited report to the Parliament can be taken.   As there has been
no response from the Ministry of Finance to the aforesaid   communication, Law Secretary   has addressed a d.o. letter to the
Secretary, Department of Economic Affairs in the Ministry of Finance on 16.9.99 to look into the matter personally and have 
necessary action in this regard expedited.   The Department has further informed that the Secretary, Department of Expenditure   has
again been reminded vide  d.o. letter dated 28 February 2000 to furnish the  recommendation so that a final decision in regard to
handling and operation of the National Legal Aid Fund as well as modalities for submission of accounts and audited report to the
Parliament, is taken by the National Legal Services  Authority.  However, Department of Expenditure is yet to submit their
recommendations to the Executive Chairman of NALSA.
13.3     The Committee takes serious view of the inordinate delay in taking the decision and  impresses  upon the Government
to lay the  Annual Report and Audited Statement of Accounts of the NALSA before both the  Houses of Parliament without
any further delay.

13.9     There are several different and newer ways of settling disputes both quickly and inexpensively to avoid long, expensive and
enormously complicated procedures for seeking legal redress through judicial courts.  One such method is Lok Adalat.  Lok Adalats
which were initially started and encouraged by a few judges of the Supreme Court in October-November, 1985 as a way of
promoting voluntary  settlement of disputes  inexpensively and expeditiously have got the statutory status under the Legal Services
Authorities Act, 1987 which covers Legal aid, Lok Adalats and Legal Assistance Services and intends to secure the operation of the
legal system in order to promote social justice, particularly for the weaker sections of the society who because of economic and other
disabilities can not   afford the costs or delays involved in normal court procedures.  The jurisdiction of Lok Adalats is very wide. 
They can determine and arrive at compromises or settlements between the parties to a dispute in respect of  any matter  falling within
the jurisdiction of civil, criminal or revenue courts or tribunals.   The award of the Lok Adalat can be enforced in law as it is deemed
to be a decree of a civil court or tribunal and such
 
award is final and binding upon all parties in dispute to avoid further costs,  expenses and delay.   No appeal has been  provided from
such an award to any court.  The Lok Adalat has been given the powers of civil court under the Civil Procedure Code while trying
disputes and the proceedings before the Lok Adalat are deemed to be the proceedings of a court as provided in Indian Penal Code. 
The Committee has been informed that   a scheme for setting up a permanent and continuous Lok Adalat for settlement of disputes
between the Central Government and its
employees and other persons has been framed. Up to 31.12.1999 about 49,415 Lok Adalats have been organised wherein about 97.20
lakh cases have been settled.   In about 5.09 lakh motor vehicles accident claim cases compensation amounting   to over Rs.2306.07
crore has been awarded.  During the calendar   year 1999, about 15,198 Lok  Adalats were held and about 9.68 lakh cases were
settled and in 78,602 Motor Accident Claim Tribunal cases, compensation of over Rs.534.92 crore was awarded.
13.10   In view of the pendency of cases in High Courts and subordinate judiciary the Committee reiterate that more funds
may be allocated for holding Lok Adalats and at the same time the NALSA should be instructed to enhance its output and
more and more Lok Adalats be held in different parts of the country.
13.11   The Committee has been informed that under the Legal Services Authorities Act, even the cases pending before the Supreme
Court can also be referred to Lok Adalats for settlement.   So far two Lok Adalats have been held in which some of the cases were
settled amicably.
13.12   In reply to a query about the number of Lok Adalats held in Daman & Diu and the number of cases disposed of, the
Department has informed that Lok Adalats on old pattern are being organised in the Union Territory of Daman & Diu and so far two
such Adalats have been held and 68 cases have been settled.
Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT)
14.       The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, constituted under the Income Tax Act, deals with second appeals in all matters relating
to direct taxes,  and appeals against orders of revision of Commissioners as well as orders of acquisition of properties under Chapter
XXA of the Income-tax Act.  At present there are 53 Benches of the Tribunal spread over 24 cities.   The Government created 15
additional benches of the Tribunal on 1.4.97.  The  Tribunal is headed by a President and three Vice-Presidents.   The Tribunal
consists  of Judicial Members and Accountant Members.  The sanctioned strength of the Members of the tribunal is 106.  In view of
the amendment   in Section 256 (1) by the Finance Act, 1998 with effect from 1.10.98.  The provision of filing Reference  
Application is now deleted  and the  parties can go in appeal directly to the High Court  against the orders passed by the Tribunal on
or after 1.10.98 on  a pure  question of law instead of reference previously.  Thus as the Law now stands, the appeal lies directly to
the High Courts.
14.1     The Committee in its 45
th Report had expressed its displeasure over the non-functioning of the 14 benches out of 15 newly
created benches of the Tribunal on 1.4.97 and had recommended   to make them functional   without any further delay.  The
Committee has been informed that out of the 15 new Benches, one each at Chandigarh, Rajkot and Jodhpur have been made
functional with effect from May 1997 and October 1999.   The Government  has also informed that the process for making  
remaining 12 Benches fully functional   are at different   stages.  The  Committee has been informed that  the pendency of cases, as
on  1 st March, 2000, before the Income Tax  Appellate Tribunal was 2,64,033 as against 3,02,052 in the corresponding  month

National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution
15.       The Committee has been informed that the Government has constituted   ‘The National Commission to Review the working
of the Constitution’ on 22 February 2000 to review the Constitution  of India  in the light of more than 50  years of its working and to
make suitable recommendations  for any possible changes. The Commission shall consist of a whole-time Chairperson who shall be
a person of distinction with knowledge and expertise of constitutional   issues and in the working of the democratic   institutions   of
the Nation.  In addition to the Chairman, the Commission shall have not more than ten other Members who shall be selected on the
basis of their proven expertise and knowledge in the field of Constitutional law, economics, politics, law, sociology, political science
and other relevant subjects. The Commission shall examine, in the light of the experience of the past 50 years, as to how best the
Constitution can respond to the changing needs of efficient, smooth and effective system of governance and socio-economic
development and to recommend changes, if any, that are required in the provisions of the Constitution   without interfering with its
basic structure or features. The Commission shall decide its own procedure and hear and entertain all persons, representations   and
communications  which in the opinion of the Commission shall facilitate its work and finalise recommendations.   The Commission
shall complete its work and make its recommendations within one year.  The funding of the Commission shall be through separate
budgetary allocation by the Government under the relevant budget heads of the Ministry of Law, Justice and  Company Affairs
(Department of Legal Affairs).
16.       The Committee is of the view that the Government should allay fears, if any, about the setting up of the Commission. 
Further the Committee is also of the opinion that the State Governments should have  been consulted in the process and
recommends that the public should be informed about the  subjects on which the Commission will work so that the basic
structure of the Constitution remains unchanged.
LEGISLATIVE
  DEPARTMENT
Electoral Reforms
 
17.0     The Committee has been informed that  the Government is committed to bring necessary reforms in electoral  laws pertaining
to elections to Parliament and Legislatures of the States.  The President, in his Address to the Parliament, at the commencement of
the first session  after constitution   of the 13 th Lok Sabha, has also stressed the necessity of bringing comprehensive   reforms in the
Electoral Laws of the country as priority subject for the present Government.  The National Agenda for Governance of the previous
Government had also mandated introduction   of necessary electoral reforms on the basis  of recommendations   of the Dinesh
Goswami Committee and accordingly that Government took up on priority basis consideration of unimplemented  recommendations 
of the Dinesh Goswami Committee. The various recommendations of the Committee are being examined  by the Government in
consultation with the Election Commission and State Governments and would also be discussed along with other pending proposals
on electoral reforms with  political parties.  Further, with a view to finding ways of expediting disposal of election petitions pending
in courts, the Law Commission which was
 
 
requested  in November, 1995 to study the problem of delay in disposal of election petitions and to suggest remedial   measures, has,
in addition, made a number of important recommendations on reform of electoral laws in its 170th report.  The recommendations  of
the Law Commission are also  being examined by the Government.  These may also  be discussed with political parties. The
Committee was also informed that amendment in electoral laws is a serious and contentious
subject and Government does not want to rush  through with the subject and, therefore, considerable   time   and attention are being
given to it.
17.1     The  Committee is of the view that Electoral   Reforms are overdue and  needs utmost attention of the Government
since it has a far   reaching impact on the political system of the country and as such it reiterate its earlier recommendations
made in its 56th Report that the  Government should consider the matter as early as possible.       
Official Languages Wing
18.0     The Official Languages wing came into being as a part of the Legislative Department in the year 1976.  The primary function
of it is to prepare and publish standard  legal terminology  for use in all official languages and to prepare authoritative   texts in Hindi

Committee  in its 56th Report had recommended  to include the officers working in the Official Language Wing  in the Indian Legal

accept the recommendation  due to the separate duties and responsibilities  of the officers  of the Hindi side of the Official Language

18.1     The officers of Indian Legal Service and Official Language Wing are performing separate duties & bearing responsibilities

18.2     The Committee has been informed that during the last three years the Official Languages Wing has prepared and published
authoritative  texts of 308 Central Acts in Hindi and other Regional languages. 
18.3     The Committee is constrained  to note that there has been decreasing  trend in publishing the authoritative  texts of
Central Acts in Hindi and other regional languages.  The Committee also takes notes of the fact that  the Hindi version of the
Acts are too  complex to be understood easily and feels that if simple Hindi words in common use is used, it will be easy to
understand.

DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
Budget of Department of Justice
 
20.0     The Committee, in its 17 th (1995), 31st (1996), 34th (1996), 39th (1997) and 45th (1998) Reports had taken a serious view of
the anomaly to the effect that the Demands for Grants of the Department   of Justice is met from that of the Ministry of Law, Justice
and Company Affairs whereas  the Department is under the administrative control of the Ministry of Home Affairs. In the action
taken reply on the recommendation of the Committee contained in its 45
th Report  (1998-99), the Department of Justice had stated
that the Government had again examined the recommendation   of the Committee   regarding transfer of the Department   from the
administrative  control of the Ministry of Home Affairs to the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs, but had decided to
continue with the existing system in view  of the  reason inter alia that the  administrative  linkage of the Department of Justice  with
the Ministry of Home Affairs ensures better coordination   in the appointment   of Judges and the administration   of Criminal Justice
with the  States.  The Committee was not at all convinced with arguments put forth for  maintaining   the status quo and,  in its 56 th
Report  (1999),  again reiterated  it earlier stand and recommended  that either the Department of Justice may be made a full fledged
Department  under the Ministry of Law, Justice and Company Affairs, headed by a Secretary like other three Departments in the

Judicial Reforms
21.0     The Law Commission in its 114 th Report, had referred to the assigning of work of the judicial reforms to it, by the then
Union Law Minister, wherein the concern about   delays in the disposal of case pending before courts, rigidity   and dilatoriness of
court procedures etc. was expressed.  Since then the situation has further worsened considerably.
21.1     The term Judicial Reforms involves a critical study of the existing system of laws and administration of justice highlighting
the area of deficiencies and improving upon them by plugging the loopholes  so that the disposal of cases is accelerated and the
hurdles coming in the way of providing speedy justice are removed..  Since the courts are functioning according to the procedures
laid down in the Criminal Procedure Code, Civil Procedure Code,  Indian Evidence Act, the High Courts Acts and Rules etc., there is
a need to amend certain provisions thereof.  The
 
Committee is aware that one of the items of the National Agenda for Governance was to set up National Judicial Commission for
recommendations of judicial appointments in High Courts and Supreme Court and draw up a code of ethics for the judiciary.   The
Law Commission in its 121 st Report,  had also recommended on these lines.  The Committee in 1998, had also constituted a sub-
Committee on Judicial Reforms but could not present its report due to early dissolution of
12th Lok Sabha.  The sub-Committee is  again being constituted after constitution of the present Committee.
21.2     The Committee would like to impress upon the Government to act seriously on  Judicial Reforms and take effective
steps in the matter of administration of justice since about 2.5 crores of cases are pending before the courts and the people is
being disillusioned in its disposal.
Judicial Activism
22.0     The Judicial Activism has been going on for a long time but it got prominence in the country with the Vineet Narayan vs.
Union of India case, popularly known as ‘Jain Hawala’ case.  Since then, there has been plethora of public interest litigations (PIL),
some of which were widely welcomed by the public. However, some of them were considered to be an encroachment  on the domain
of the other wings of the Government.   In the recent past it is felt that there is a growing trend of  transgression of  authority by one
wing on the domain of the others resulting in erosion of institutionalised arrangements which was not contemplated by the makers of
the Constitution when they created three separate wings of the Government, namely, the Parliament, Executive and Judiciary.
22.1     The matter was  raised by some of the Members of the Committee and they were of the view that observance of the self-
restraint by the three wings of the Government is the need of the hour so that institutionalised arrangement,   as envisaged in the
Constitution, is followed in letter and spirit.   This will also allow the three wings functioning independently and there is no
overlapping of the jurisdiction.
22.2     In the meeting the Committee took note of the recent incident which occurred at the New Delhi Railway Station, widely
reported in the press, that a sitting Judge got a train stopped, held an open court on the platform and reprimanded the officer of the
Station.
22.3     The Committee is of the opinion that it is high time that the Government, particularly the Prime Minister, the Union
Law Minister and the Judiciary should look into the matter and necessary remedial measures be taken for an
institutionalised and transparent arrangement and code of ethics be formulated for judicial officers.   The Committee is also
of the view that expeditious setting up of the National Judicial Commission would be an important step in the direction
otherwise judicial activism would itself be self-defeating.
  
Centrally Sponsored Scheme Relating to Infrastructural Facilities for the Judiciary
 
23.0     The Centrally Sponsored Schemes approved by the Government from the year 1993-94  relating to infrastructural   facilities
for the judiciary   includes   construction   of court buildings and residential   accommodation for judicial   officers/judges covering
High Court and subordinate   courts.  The expenditure   on the scheme  is to be shared by the Union and the State Governments  on
50:50  basis.  The Central  share is, however, restricted to the amount allocated for this purpose by the Planning Commission, which
has to be  distributed as per the guidelines laid down
 
 
by them.  The expenditure  in respect of the Union Territories is to be met fully by the Government  of India. The Secretary, Ministry
of Home Affairs  (ex-officio Secretary of Department of  Justice) during his presentation before the Committee on 30.3.2000 has
informed
that under the plan   schemes, the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for the  development of infrastructural facilities for the  judiciary was
allotted Rs.55 crore during 1999-2000.  This amount has been fully utilized and includes Rs.78 lakh to the Government  of Orissa for
reconstruction  of  buildings damaged by the super-cyclone   and transfer of Rs.1.97 crore to the Central non-lapsable pool for the
North Eastern States.  The allotment   under the scheme has been enhanced   from Rs.55 crore in 1999-2000 to Rs.74.95 crore in
th th

the Union Government’s share for the centrally sponsored  scheme for development of infrastructural   facilities for judiciary should
be raised to 75% and good performing states may be released additional amount.  The states which have failed to utilize the amount

National Judicial Pay Commission
24.0     The first National Judicial Pay Commission was set up on the 21 st March, 1996 with headquarter at Bangalore, under the
Chairmanship of the retired High Court Judge, Justice Shri K.J. Shetty  in pursuance of the Supreme Court’s direction in 1991 in writ
petition No. 1022/89 (All India Judges Association v/s Union of India and other) for examining the pay structure and other service
conditions of the Judicial Officers in the States and Union Territories.   The Commission submitted its report on 11.11.1999. The
Supreme Court, vide its Order dated 7.1.1998 in the All India Judges Association case, requested the Shetty Commission to examine
and make a report to the Court about the steps, if any, required to be taken in each State/Union Territory for the improvement of
service conditions of the supporting staff attached to the subordinate courts. In view of the strong opposition by the State
Governments, the proposal for the enlargement of the terms of reference of the Shetty Commission was deferred by the Government.
However, the supreme Court, vide its order of 27.7.1999 in the said case, directed the Central Government to continue the
Commission with the existing staff till a report was made to that court regarding the service conditions of the court staff of all the
States/Union Territories and the same was considered by that Court. No time frame has been specified for the Commission to submit
its report. For 2000-2001, a budget provision of Rs. 63 lakhs has been made for the Commission
24.1     The Committee notes the reply of the Government and recommends that a definite time frame should be specified for
the Commission to submit its report.
 
All India Judicial Service
25.0     The Committee in its 56 th Report (1999) had recommended that an early decision be taken to create All India Judicial
Service. The Committee has been informed that the 1 st, 8th  and 11th Law Commissions had, inter alia , recommended for formation
of an All India Judicial Service. The recommendations of the Law Commission were also discussed in a Conference of Chief
Justices held in October, 1988 which passed a resolution opposing the formation of All India Judicial Service. Having regard to the
poor response received from the State Governments and the total opposition exhibited by the Conference of Chief Justice of 1988,
the proposal for setting up the All India Judicial Service was dropped and the matter was treated as closed in December, 1989. Later
on, the Supreme Court recommended vide its judgement dated 13.11.1991 in W.P. No. 1022/89 and judgement dated on 24.8.1993
in review Petition No. 249/92-All India Judges Association Vs. Union of India and others, that an All India Judicial Service should
be set up and the Union of India should take appropriate steps in this regard. The Government has further informed that in view of
the Supreme Court’s recommendation, the matter is being examined further. The All India Judicial Service can be set up through an
appropriate Resolution by the Rajya Sabha followed by an Act of Parliament under Article 312 of the Constitution.
25.1     In view of the position explained by the Government, the Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation and hopes
that the Government would take appropriate steps for formation of All India Judicial Service at the earliest.
Pendency in Courts
26.0     The Committee in its 56 th Report (1999) took strong exception to the huge pendecny of cases in courts which has shaken the
confidence of the people in the administration of Justice. The Department has informed that the pendency  of cases in the Courts is
an area of major concern for Government.   Only the Supreme Court of India has been able to control and reduce its pendency inter
alia through categorization and grouping of cases, non-accumulation of defective matters, earmarking more time for old pending
cases and computerization of records.  As a result, the pendency in the Apex Court has come down from 1,04,936 as on 31 st
December, 1991 to 20,260 as on 1 st February, 2000.  However, the High Courts and Subordinate Courts have not yet been able to
effectively grapple with increasing pendencies.   As on 31 st December, 1999, there are around 32 lakh cases pending in the High
Courts and around 2 crore cases pending in the Subordinate Courts.  The Government has been seized of the grave situation arising
out of such huge pendency and has been taking a series  of steps for amending legal procedures and for providing speedy justice to
