the litigants.  This includes steps for the amendment of the Civil Procedure Code and the Criminal Procedure Code, increase in the
number of posts of Judges in the High Courts and Subordinate Courts, provision of a statutory base to Lok Adalats and vesting it
with the powers of a civil court, appointment of Special Judicial Magistrates/Metropolitan Magistrates and adoption of other
alternative and locally appropriate methods of dispute resolution.   The Supreme Court and various High Courts have been taking a
number of steps for expeditious disposal of cases, viz., grouping and classification of cases involving similar question of law, setting
up of specialized benches, computerization of records, etc.
26.1     The Committee takes very serious view of the pendency in courts and recommends that the Government should take
all possible steps to minimise pendency  and closely monitor  the result of the various  measures taken for expeditious
disposal of pending cases.
 
Vacancies of Judges in Supreme Court and High Courts
27.0          Department has informed that it has always been the endeavour of the Government to fill vacancies of Judges in the
Supreme Court and the High Courts as and when such vacancies arise.  During the year 1999-2000, 5 Judges have been appointed to
the Supreme Court and 67 permanent or additional Judges, to various High Courts.  As on date, against a sanctioned   strength of 26
in the Supreme Court, 25 Judges are in position,  one vacancy arose due to the sad
demise of  a  Judge.  In so far as the High Courts are concerned, against a sanctioned strength of 591 Judges, 457 Judges are in
position leaving 134 places vacant.  Of these 134 vacancies, proposals have so far been received in respect of 77 vacancies only; out
of these 77 proposals, 44 are not complete and the remaining 33 are at various stages of consideration.  Filling up of vacancies in the
district and other subordinate courts is the responsibility of the State Government and High Court concerned.   As on 31
st December,
1997, there are 1323 vacancies at these levels against a sanctioned strength of 11924 Judicial Officers and Judges.  In January, 2000,
the Minister of Law, Justice and Company Affairs requested the Chief Justices of the High Courts to initiate proposals for filling   up
the existing vacancies of Judges in their High Court and also vacancies of Judges that would arise till June 2000, so that   vacancies
of Judges in the High Courts are filled up expeditiously.  A copy of this letter was also sent to the Chief Ministers and the Governors
of the States for their information and necessary action.   The Committee in its 56 th Report (1999), had felt that in the matter
regarding the appointment of Judges in Supreme Court and High Courts and transfer of Judges in High Courts and the delay in filling
up the vacancies of Judges, the time has come when the basic substantial issues should be deliberated at the highest level of the
Government so that there could be an overall improvement in the situation.   The Department in its action taken report, has intimated
that one of the items of the National Agenda for Governance is to set up a National Judicial Commission to recommend for judicial
appointments in the Supreme Court and the High Courts.  To a reply of a query regarding reservation for Schedule Castes/Schedule
Tribes/Other Backward Classes, women and minority in the matter of appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts,
the Committee has been informed that appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts is made under Article 124 and
217 of the Constitution which do not provide for reservation for any caste or class of persons.
27.1     The Committee notes that there has been inordinate delay in filling in vacancies. Therefore an urgent step is necessary
to deal with it  forthwith before long term decision  is taken in the form of setting up a new forum for judicial appointments.
The vacancy occurs on elevation, retirement or death of a judge in position. Death  is such an uncertain event that one cannot
foresee it and rationally deal with it in advance.  But, retirement is known in advance.  In the past the Committee has time
and again   observed that the  process for filling up the vacancy must start considerably in advance before the actual date of
retirement of a Judge which would cause the vacancy.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the process of filling in
the vacancy should be initiated in such a manner that the vacancy is filled on the day it occurs.
Setting up of
  Benches of Supreme Court and High Courts
28.0          The Law Commission in its 125th Report on “The Supreme Court – A fresh look”
observed as follows:-
‘The Supreme Court sits at Delhi alone. Government of India on couple of occasions sought the opinion of the Supreme
Court of India for setting up a Bench in the South. This proposal did not find favour with the Supreme Court. The result is
that those coming
 
from distant places like Tamil Nadu in the South. Gujarat in the West and Assam and other States in the East have to spend
huge amount on travel to reach the Supreme Court. There is a practice of bringing one’s own laywer who has handled the
matter in the High Court to the Supreme Court. That adds to the cost. And an adjournment becomes prohibitive.
Adjournment is a recurrent phenomenon in the Court.’
28.1     During the consideration of the Demands for Grants (1999-2000) the Committee was informed that the Governments of
Tamil  Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka had also suggested that  a bench of Supreme Court may be established in the respective
State Capitals  for South India.
28.2     The Chief Minister  of Tripura, in August 1983,  had requested the then Union Law Minister for acceptance of the resolution

28.3     The Law Ministers of the eastern and the north-eastern states adopted a resolution unanimously in their meeting   held on
4.10.96 in Calcutta that it is essential for the Supreme Court to sit  at a suitable place in their regions to promote   equal opportunity 
to all in operation of their Legal system.
28.4     According to Article 130 of the Constitution, “ The Supreme Court shall sit in Delhi or in such other place or places  as the
Chief Justice of India may, with  the approval of the President from time to time  appoint.”
28.5     The Committee in its 56 th Report (1999), had recommended for setting up benches of Supreme Court in southern, western
and north-eastern  parts  of the country.
28.6     In the action taken reply and subsequent communication, the Government has stated that the Chief Justice of India has
intimated that a full Court meeting of the Judges of the Supreme Court discussed the subject matter on 15 December 1999 and
opposed the setting up of the benches outside Delhi since it would affect the structural and financial integrity of the institution.
28.7     The Committee notes the factual position and the reply of the Government.  The Committee is not convinced with the
reason for opposition for setting up of benches of Supreme Court  in Southern, Western and North-eastern parts of the
country and  reiterates its recommendations made in its 56 th Report for setting up of Benches in the above mentioned places
so that the people of far flung areas get easy access to the Apex Court. The Committee also urges upon the Government to
again take up the matter with the Chief Justice of India.
28.8     The Committee in its 56 th Report had also recommended for setting up of benches of High Courts away from their principal
seats keeping in view the problems of the poor people and asked the Government to sort out the hurdles coming in the way of setting
up of benches speedily.
28.9     In reply the Government has informed that necessary infrastructural   facilities for setting up of benches of High Courts have
to be provided by the concerned State Governments and Judges have to be deputed from the principal seat of the High Court to its
Bench/Benches by the Chief Justice of the High Court.  Entire expenditure of the High Court and its benches is met by the State
Government and day-to-day functioning of the High Court and its bench/benches is looked after by the Chief Justice.  Accordingly,
the recommendation of Committee has been conveyed to the Chief Ministers of States for their considered views, in consultation
with the Chief Justices of the respective High Courts.
 
 
28.10   The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation in the interest of the public and hopes that the Government
would remove all the hurdles at the earliest coming in the way of setting up benches of High Courts.
DEMAND NO.61 – DEPARTMENT OF COMPANY AFFAIRS
Plan Provision for Department of Company Affairs
 
29.0     The total budgetary allocation (Budget Estimates) made for the Department of Company Affairs for 2000-2001 is Rs.42
crores (i.e. Rs.39.10 crores under the Revenue Section and Rs.2.90 crores under the Capital Section).   The Department has no plan
expenditure.  The entire budget of the Department is non-plan and establishment oriented.
29.1     The Committee in its 45 th Report (1998),  had recommended that the efforts should be made to house the Offices of the
Department, most of  which are housed in rental buildings, in their own buildings so that it may not spend substantial amount of
money on the rents.  The Department, in its action taken reply,  had intimated that some of the offices were housed in rented
buildings and the Government was making efforts to either house the offices in the buildings owned by CPWD or in Government
accommodation.  The Committee  has further been informed that over the years inspite of best efforts, the Department has not been
in position to own its own buildings as the entire budget of the Department is Non-Plan.
29.2              The Committee is of the opinion that if the Department of Company Affairs can have plan provision, then it can
modernise their offices and house their offices in their own buildings.  Therefore, it is of utmost importance and necessity
that the Government makes a plan provision to the Department..  The Committee also understands that for purchase of land
for offices of Regional Directors, Kanpur, Registrar of Companies of Kanpur and Delhi etc. and to develop the Training
Institute for training in Corporate  Governance for South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation Nations and also to
modernise the field offices for making people oriented and various other modernisation programmes, the Department would
need Rs.100 crores as a plan provision.  The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Department of Company
Affairs should be provided a plan budget of Rs.100 crores at Revised Estimates stage so that it may undertake major project
components e.g. infrastructural development, human resource development & training, networking, automation, document 
imaging, electronic facilitation counter etc.

(xii)
R E P O R T
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having been
authorised by it, present this Sixty-second Report of the Committee.  The Report pertains to the Salaries, Allowances,
Leave and Pensions of  Officers and Servants of the Supreme Court Bill, 1994 *.  The Bill,  as per its Statement of
Objects and Reasons, seeks to rectify the serious anomalies that had crept into the pay scales of the employees  of  the
Supreme Court on account of various judgements and orders passed by the Courts  in  various Writ  Petitions filed by
the employees.
2.         Pursuant to the provisions of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Home Affairs, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred§
 the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 19 August, 1994 and
pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.
3.0       The Committee (1994-95) considered the Bill in its meeting held on 29 November, 1994 and decided to invite
views/suggestions of Employees’ Welfare Associations of the Supreme Court on the provisions contained in the Bill.
The Supreme Court Employees, Welfare Associations had submitted vide
 communication dated 28 November, 1994
views/suggestions on the various provisions of the Bill for consideration of the Committee and requested for providing
an opportunity to give oral evidence on the provisions of the Bill  before it. It was decided to hear the representatives of
the Associations at an appropriate stage.
3.1       While the Bill was still under consideration of the Committee, the Tenth Lok Sabha got dissolved and so did the
previous Committee.  
3.2       Meanwhile, the matter relating to service conditions of the employees of the Court was referred to the Fifth
Central Pay Commission.   
3.3       The Committee (1996-97), which was constituted on 1 August, 1996,   further  considered  the Bill in its meeting
held on 23 September 1996 and decided to ascertain the views of the Government regarding enactment of the Bill in its
present form in view of the fact that one of the terms of  reference of the Fifth Central  Pay Commission was to examine
and recommend scales of pay in respect of the employees of the Supreme Court.  In response thereto the Committee was
informed by the Department of Justice vide
 its communication dated 23 December, 1996 that since the employees of the
Supreme Court had been included in the terms of reference of the Fifth Central Pay Commission and the report was
expected shortly, the Committee may wait till the presentation of the report by the Commission to the Government, 
before taking further action on the Bill. 

62nd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/62ndreport.htm[30-06-2016 17:34:35]
3.4       In the meantime, the Committee’s tenure came to an abrupt end consequent upon the dissolution of Eleventh
Lok Sabha on 4 December, .1997.
3.5              In 1997, the Fifth Central Pay Commission, in its report  (para 103.32), recommended as
follows :-
(a)        The entire question of conditions of service, including pay scales, allowances, etc. of the officers and
employees of the Supreme Court of India and the High Court of Delhi has to be decided in the manner
laid down in the Constitution of India, as interpreted in the various judgements of the highest court in the
land.
 
(b)     The Fifth  Central Pay Commission finds itself unable to make any  recommendations whatsoever for the
officers and employees of the Supreme Court of India and High Court of Delhi.
(c )    However, we have made our detailed recommendations on pay scales, allowances,
pensions, etc. with regard to different categories of Central Government employees.  We would be happy if
these recommendations are of any assistance to the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India and the Hon’ble Chief
Justice of the Delhi High Court, as background materials for basing their own decisions.
Before we close this discussion, we would like to conclude with one last respectful submission.  In case
the Hon’ble Courts decide to grant pay scales, allowances, etc. to their own employees that are at variance with
the pay scales, allowances, etc. of Central Government employees on the ground that their qualifications, duties
and responsibilities, are different, they may, if they so desire, modify the designations of such posts to make
these different from the designations used in the Central Government so as to avoid any confusion in the future.
3.6       The Committee (1998-99) was reconstituted on 5 June, 1998.  In the light of the recommendations of the Fifth
Central Pay Commission as contained in para 103.32 of their report, and also in view of the passage of a considerable
period of time since the introduction of the Bill, under reference, it was felt that the views of the Government with
regard to the enactment of the legislation may be ascertained so as to enable the Committee to proceed further. 
Accordingly, a reference was made to the Department of Justice on 21 July, 1998 to furnish the views of the
Government on the enactment of the Bill in its present form.  On 11 November, 1998 the Department informed that the
matter was under submission to the Cabinet and as and when a decision of the Cabinet was received, the same would be
conveyed to the Committee.
3.7       Finally, the Department vide
 their O.M. dated 21 December, 1998 informed that the Government had decided to
pursue the Bill further in the Parliament with necessary formal amendments as might be required due to passage of time.
3.8       In response thereto, the Department was requested vide
 O.M. dated 24 December 1998 to furnish a separate note
giving details of the proposed formal amendments to the Bill so that the Committee may be in a position to proceed
further with their examination.  The Department, vide their O.M. dated 4 February 1999, forwarded a note giving details
of the formal amendments (appendix)  to the Bill for consideration by the Committee.
3.9       The Committee’s tenure again came to an end consequent upon the dissolution of the Twelfth Lok Sabha on 26
April 1999 and the present Committee (1999-2000) was re-constituted on 31 December 1999.
3.10          The Department of Justice vide  Secretariat’s communication dated  13 January 2000 was requested to furnish a
detailed Background Note on the Bill, indicating therein inter alia in chronological order the various developments
which had taken place in the matter, including summation of the main contentions in the Writ Petitions filed by the
employees of the Court, judgements thereon, the present structure of salaries and allowances of the employees and
officers of the  Court and the formal amendments which the Government proposed to  make in the Bill, so that a
complete information was before the Committee while considering the Bill.
3.11     In the meantime, the Supreme Court Employees Welfare Associations were requested vide
 communication dated
20 January, 2000 to submit their updated memoranda on the provisions of the Bill for consideration of the Committee. 
 
3.12     The Department of Justice vide communication dated 24 January, 2000 forwarded the detailed Background Note
along with a statement containing inter alia the details of Writ Petitions filed by the Court employees, recommendations
of the Fifth Central  Pay Commission, salary structure of employees proposed to be given through the Bill.

5.         The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill reads as under :-
Serious anomalies have crept into the pay scales of  the employees of Supreme Court of India on account
of  various judgements and orders passed by the Court in Writ Petitions filed by its employees.  These
distortions and anomalies in the pay structures of the staff  of Supreme Court are likely to cause serious
agitation amongst similarly placed Central Government staff. 
This might ultimately lead to large scale distortions in the pay structure of the Central Government
employees with attendant serious consequential financial implications.  The Government examined the
implications of the emerging distortions in the pay structures of Court employees and considered it appropriate
to enact suitable legislation to rectify the situation as that was the only remedy available to the Government.
6.         Article 146(2) of the Constitution provides as under :-
Subject to the provisions of any law made by Parliament
, the conditions of service of officers and
servants of the Supreme Court shall be such as may be prescribed by rules made by the Chief Justice of
India or by some other Judge or officer of the Court authorised by the Chief Justice of India to make
rules for the purpose:
Provided that the rules made under this clause shall, so far as they relate to the salaries,
allowances, leave or pensions, require the approval of the President
.
 
7.         In this connection  the observations  of  Shri T.T. Krishnamachari and Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, made  in  the  course 
of  the   debates   in   the  Constituent  Assembly  on  Articles 146  and  229 of the Constitution, are relevant. Shri T.T.
Krishnamachari  observed as follows :-
“At the same time, Sir, I think it should be made clear that it is not the intention of the House or of the framers of
this Constitution that they want to create specially favoured bodies which in themselves become an Imperium in
Imperio, completely independent of the Executive and Legislature and operate as a sort of superior body to the
general body politic.”   ( C.A. Deb. Vol.VIII, 16 May – 16 June, 1949;p.389)
The submission of Dr. Ambedkar  is also extracted below :-
But it seems to me that there is another consideration which goes to support the proposition that we should retain
the phrase with the approval of the President and it is this.  It  is undoubtedly a desirable thing that salaries,
allowances and pensions payable to the servants of the State should be uniform and there ought not to be
material variations in these matters with regard to the civil service.  It is likely to create a good deal of heart
burning and might impose on the treasury an unnecessary burden.  Now if you leave the matter to the Chief
Justice to decide, it is quite conceivable – I do not say that it will happen – but it is quite conceivable that the
Chief Justice might fix the scales of allowances, pensions and salaries very different from those fixed for civil
servants who are working in other departments besides the Judiciary, and I do not think that such a state of
things is desirable thing.”      (ibid)

8.0       The Department of Justice has stated in their Background Note that the Chief Justice of India framed the
Supreme Court Officers and Servants (Conditions of Service and Conduct) Rules, 1961.  Under these Rules, the officers
and servants of the Supreme Court were placed at par with corresponding employees of the Central Government and the
pay scales were accordingly fixed on the standard Central Government pattern. 
8.1       The Department further stated that under the Delhi High Court Officers and Servants (Salaries, Allowances,
Leave and Pension) Rules, 1970, the employees of the Delhi High Court were getting the pay scales at par with the
corresponding staff of the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi, which was following the standard Central
Government pattern.  However, the employees of the Delhi High Court got higher scales of pay by  taking matters to the
Courts which allowed their petitions.  This resulted in serious anomalies in the pay scales of the employees of the Delhi
High Court, the Department stated. 
8.2       The Department further informed that, in early, 1986, the Supreme Court employees decided to take advantage
of the anomalous higher scales of pay of the employees of the Delhi High Court and filed two Writ Petitions in the
Supreme Court praying that :-
(i)
                  They should be given higher pay scales than admissible to corresponding categories of employees in
Central Government because of special nature of work in the Supreme Court, and
(ii)                As an interim measure, parity should be accorded with Delhi High Court staff wherever the latter was
getting emoluments higher than the Supreme Court employees.
 
8.3       The Supreme Court passed a number of interim orders from 25 July, 1986 onwards and granted parity to
different categories of its employees with employees of the Delhi High Court, wherever the latter was getting higher pay
and allowances, the Committee was informed by the Department of Justice.
 
8.4       The Department then added that in February, 1989, a Group of Ministers was constituted to examine the
implications of the emerging distortions in the pay structures of Court employees due to Court decisions.  The Group of
Ministers recommended  that the only remedy available to the Government was to enact suitable legislation to rectify
the situation.  The Department stated that as per the basic scheme of the Constitution (Article 146),   Parliament is
competent to enact a law regulating the service conditions including those relating to pay, allowances, leave and
pensions of the officers and servants of the Supreme Court, to ensure that no anomalies in respect of these matters are
created vis-à-vis corresponding levels of other Government servants.  Accordingly, the Salaries, Allowances, Leave and
Pensions of Officers and Servants of the Supreme Court Bill, 1994 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 19 August,
1994.                   
8.5       The Government, in the Background Note, further stated that one of the terms of reference of the Fifth Central
Pay Commission was to examine and recommend the scales of pay in respect of officers and servants of the Supreme
Court.  However, the Commission did not give any recommendation in respect of the employees of the Supreme Court,
as the Commission was of the view that the appointments and conditions of  service, including matters relating to
salaries, allowances, leave and pensions of the officers and  servants of the Supreme Court   were to be decided in the
manner laid down  in the Constitution of India.  The Government further stated  that it is proposed that the officers and
servants of the Supreme Court may be given scales   of pay on the analogy of the Fifth Central Pay Commission’s
recommendations and as such the Schedule to the Bill would be modified accordingly. 
8.6       The Bill will have prospective effect and would cover the entire staff of the Supreme Court including those who
are presently enjoying the anomalous pay scales so that from the date of effect of the proposed legislation, the scales of
these persons also would be brought in line with the corresponding Government scales.  A provision has also been made
to protect the existing higher pay drawn by the employees under proviso to Clause 3 of the Bill, the Committee has been
informed.

of the employees of the Supreme Court. 
 
12.2     As already stated, the Government through the Bill proposed that the Officers and Servants of the Supreme
Court be given pay scales on the analogy of the Fourth Pay Commission’s recommendations and the Schedule to the
Bill was  accordingly prepared.
12.3     Thereafter, the recommendations of the Fifth Central Pay Commission became available and the scales of pay of
the Central Government Employees were revised accordingly.  Therefore, the Department of Justice informed the
Committee that the pay scales indicated in the Schedule to the Bill would be replaced by the revised pay scales
approved by the Government in respect of corresponding Central Government employees on the basis of the

12.5     The Schedule, as proposed to be  amended by the Government, was adopted. 
13.       Clause 1, the Enacting Formula and the Title were adopted with some changes which were of consequential or
drafting nature, namely, “1994” and “Forty-fifth” to be substituted by “2000” and “Fifty-first” respectively.
14.0     The Committee while examining the Bill dwelt at length on the constitutional provisions empowering Parliament
to legislate on the service matters of the employees of the Supreme Court.  It also took note of the observations made in
the Constituent Assembly with regard to Articles 146 and   229.  The Committee wishes to reiterate the explicit
constitutional position fully empowering Parliament to legislate on the subject.
14.1     In the light of the discussions held in the meetings of the Committee and the submissions made before it by the
representatives of various Employees Welfare Associations of the Supreme Court, the Committee is of the view that  the
Government, if it deems fit, discuss  the matter with the Chief Justice of India and arrive at a final view thereon after
consulting him.
14.2     The contents of the Statement of Objects and Reasons, appended to the Bill,  also came up for discussion in the
Committee.  Having considered all aspects of the matter, the Committee feels that the contents of the Statement of
Objects and Reasons may be modified in such a way that it indicates the relevant constitutional provisions under which
the enactment is sought to be made and other references connected with the issue be avoided.

5.         The Home Secretary in his presentation, informed that the two Bills sought to rectify the anomalies and
discrepancies that had crept into the pay-scales of the employees of the Supreme Court and the Delhi High Court since
1979 on account of various judgements and orders of these two Courts which had granted higher scales of pay to their
employees compared to the corresponding categories of employees in the Central Government.  He stated that the Chief
Justice of India and Chief Justice of Delhi High Court were empowered to make rules regarding the conditions of
service of their Officers and Servants under Articles 146(2) & 229(2) of the Constitution, respectively, subject to the
provisions of any law made by Parliament.  In pursuance of Article 146(2), the Chief Justice of India had framed rules
with regard to the Officers and Staff of Supreme Court in 1961 and in pursuance of Article 229(2) the Chief Justice of
Delhi High Court had made rules for the Officers and Employees of the Delhi High Court in 1970.  At that time their
pay-scales were at par with corresponding categories of Central Government employees.  However, the rules under the
proviso to Clause (2) of Articles 146 and 229, so far as they related to the salaries, allowances, leave or pensions,
required the approval of the President in case of Supreme Court and the Lt. Governor of Delhi, in case of Delhi High
Court.  Since Parliament had not made any law in that regard, the officers and employees of the Supreme Court & Delhi
High Court were enjoying higher scales of pay due to judgements of the Courts despite the Government’s opposition to
it.  The Home Secretary stated that the Government of India through these Bills would like to clear the existing
distortions in the pay-scales of employees of the two Courts by reverting to the original principle of parity in their pay
scales with those corresponding to the Central Government employees.  However, he submitted that the pay of
employees of the two Courts who were drawing higher scales after the enactment of law, would be protected.  The
Home Secretary then sought the considered recommendations of the Committee so that the law could be enacted.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS
 
 
      Serious  anomalies have crept  into the pay-scales of the employees of the Supreme Court of India on account of
various judgments and orders passed by the Court in Writ Petitions filed by its employees.  These distortions  and
anomalies in the pay-structure  of the staff of Supreme Court are likely to cause serious agitation amongst similarly
placed  Central Government staff.
 
      2.   This might   ultimately lead to large-scale distortions in the pay-structure of the Central Government employees
with attendant serious consequential financial  implications.  The Government  examined the implications of the
emerging distortions in the pay-structures of Court employees and considered  it  appropriate to enact suitable
legislation  to rectify the situation as that was the only remedy available to the Government.
 
      3.   The Bill seeks to achieve the above object.

DEPARTMENT  OF JUSTICE
 
 
      Sub:           The Salaries, Allowances, Leave and Pensions of the Officers and Servants of the Supreme Court and
Delhi High Court  Bills, 1994 – further  pursuing thereof by the Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Home Affairs. – proposed amendments thereof.
 
 
      Under the Supreme Court Officers and Servants (Conditions of Service and Conduct) Rules, 1961, the  officers and
servants of the Supreme Court have been  placed at par with  corresponding  employees of the Central  Government  and
their  pay scales  had accordingly  been  fixed  on the standard  Central Government  pattern.  Similarly, in the Delhi
High Court  officers and Servants  (Salaries, Allowances, Leave and Pension) Rules, 1970,  the employees  of the Delhi
High Court were getting the pay scales  at par with the corresponding staff of Delhi  Administration which is following
the Standard Central  Government pattern.  However, the Court’s  employees  got higher scales of pay by taking
matters  to the Courts  which allowed their petitions.  This resulted in serious anomalies in the pay scales of the
employees of the Delhi High Court as well as those of the Supreme Court of India.
 
2.   With a view to rectify the anomalies which had crept into the pay scales of the Courts employees, the aforesaid 
Bills of 1994 were introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 19.8.1994.  It was proposed through the Bills that the Officers and
Servants of the Delhi High Court and the Supreme Court be given pay scales on the analogy of the IVth Pay
Commission’s recommendations and the Schedule to the Bills were accordingly prepared.
 
3.   The recommendations of the Vth Pay Commission have become available and the scales of pay  of the Central
Government  Employees  have already   been revised  accordingly.  The pay scales  indicated in the Schedules to the
1994  Bills will be replaced  by the revised  pay scales approved by the Government in respect of corresponding  Central
Government employees on the basis of the recommendations of the  Fifth Central Pay Commission.  Accordingly, the
Schedules to the 1994  Bills  indicating  the revised pay scales based on the  recommendations of the Vth Pay
Commission are prepared and annexed to this NOTe at Annexe-I.
 
4.   In the revised Schedule to the Supreme Court Bill, 1994, the posts from Sl.Nos.1 to 14, 20 and 22 to 46 have been
granted normal replacement scales of those proposed in the 1994 Bill.  For the posts  15 to 19  the proposed  scale in the
1994 Bill was Rs.2300-3700/-which is not a standard pay scale, for this scale the replacement of the pre-revised  scales 
of Rs.2375-3500/-  and Rs.2375-3750/-, i.e. Rs.7450-11500/-  has been indicated.  The post of Assistant Accounts
Officer in the  Scales of Rs.6,500-200-10,500/- has been added at Sl.No. 21, this is a standard scale for the AAOs in the
Central Government.
 
5.   In the revised Schedule to the Delhi High Court  Bill,  1994, normal replacement scales have been indicated for all
the posts.

R E P O R T
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having been
authorised by it, present this Sixty-third Report of the Committee.  The Report pertains to the Salaries, Allowances,
Leave and Pensions of  Officers and Servants of the Delhi High Court Bill, 1994 *
.  The Bill, as per its Statement of
Objects and Reasons, seeks to rectify the  serious anomalies that had crept into the pay scales of the employees  of  the
Delhi High Court on account of various judgements and orders passed by the Courts in various Writ Petitions filed by
the  employees.
2.         Pursuant to the provisions of the Rules relating to the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Home Affairs, the Chairman, Rajya Sabha, referred§
 the Bill, as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 19 August, 1994 and
pending therein, to the Committee for examination and report.
3.0       The Committee (1994-95) considered the Bill in its meeting held on 29 November, 1994 and decided to invite
views/suggestions of the Employees’ Welfare Association of the Delhi High Court on the provisions contained in the
Bill. The Delhi High Court Employees Welfare Association had submitted vide communication dated 28 November,
1994 their views/suggestions on the various provisions of the Bill for consideration of the Committee and requested for
providing an opportunity to give oral evidence on the provisions of the Bill before it.  It was decided to hear the
representatives of the Association at an appropriate stage.  
3.1       While the Bill was still under consideration of the Committee, the Tenth Lok Sabha got dissolved and so did the
previous Committee.
3.2       Meanwhile, the matter relating to service conditions of the employees of the Court was referred to the Fifth
Central Pay Commission.

63rd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/63rdreport.htm[30-06-2016 17:34:36]
3.3       The Committee (1996-97), which was constituted on 1August, 1996,   further  considered  the Bill in its meeting
held on 23 September 1996 and decided to ascertain the views of the Government regarding enactment of the Bill in its
present form in view of the fact that one of the terms of  reference of the Fifth Central  Pay Commission was to examine
and recommend scales of pay in respect of the employees of the Delhi High Court.  In response thereto the Committee
was informed by the Department of Justice vide its communication dated 23 December, 1996 that since the employees
of the Delhi High Court had been included in the terms and reference of the Fifth Central Pay Commission and the
report was expected shortly, the Committee may wait till the presentation of the report by the Commission to the
Government,  before taking further action on the Bill.
3.4       In the meantime, the Committee’s tenure came to an abrupt end consequent upon the dissolution of Eleventh
Lok Sabha on 4 December, 1997.
3.5       In 1997, the Fifth Central Pay Commission in its report (para 103.32), recommended as follows :-
(a)         The entire question of conditions of service, including pay scales,     
allowances, etc. of the officers and employees and employees of the     Supreme Court of India and    the
High Court of Delhi has to be decided in the manner laid
down in the Constitution of India, as interpreted in the various judgements of the highest court    in the
land.
(b)
            The Fifth Central Pay Commission finds itself unable to make any recommendations whatsoever for the
officers and employees of the Supreme Court of India and High Court of Delhi.
(c)        However, we have made our detailed recommendations on pay scales, allowances, pensions, etc. with
regard to different categories of Central Government employees.  We would be happy if these
recommendations are of any assistance to the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India and the Hon’ble Chief
Justice of the Delhi High Court, as background materials for basing their own decisions.
Before we close this discussion, we would like to conclude with one last respectful submission. 
In case the Hon’ble Courts decide to grant pay scales, allowances, etc. to their own employees that are at
variance with the pay scales, allowances, etc. of Central Government employees on the ground that their
qualifications, duties and responsibilities, are different, they may, if they so desire, modify the
designations of such posts to make these different from the designations used in the Central Government
so as to avoid any confusion in the future.
3.6
              The Committee (1998-99) was re-constituted on 5 June, 1998.  In the light of the recommendations of the Fifth
Central Pay Commission as contained in para 103.32 of their report and also in view of the passage of a considerable
period of time since the introduction of the Bill, under reference, it was felt that the views of the Government with
regard to the enactment of the  legislation might be ascertained so as to enable the Committee to proceed further. 
Accordingly, a reference was made to the Department of Justice on 21 July, 1998 to furnish the views of the
Government on the enactment of the Bill in its present form.  On 11 November, 1998 the Department  informed that the
matter was under submission to the Cabinet
and as and when a decision of the Cabinet was received, the same would be conveyed to the Committee.  
3.7       Finally, the Department vide
 their O.M. dated 21December, 1998 informed that the Government had decided to
pursue the Bill further in the Parliament with necessary formal amendments as might be required due to passage of time.
3.8       In response thereto, the Department was requested vide
 O.M. dated 24 December, 1998 to furnish a separate note
giving details of the proposed formal amendments to the Bill so that the Committee may be in a position to proceed
further with their examination.  The Department, vide their O.M. dated 4 February, 1999, forwarded a note giving
details of the formal amendments ( see appendix)  to the Bill for consideration by the Committee. 
3.9       The Committee’s tenure again came to an end consequent upon the dissolution of the Twelfth Lok Sabha on 26
April 1999 and the present Committee (1999-2000) was re-constituted on 31 December, 1999.
3.10          The Department of Justice vide Secretariat’s communication dated  13 January 2000 was requested to furnish a
detailed Background Note on the Bill, indicating therein inter alia in chronological order the various developments
which had taken place in the matter, including summation of the main contentions in the Writ Petitions filed by the
employees of the Court, judgements thereon, the present structure of salaries and allowances of the employees and
officers of the  Court and the formal amendments which the Government proposed to  make in the Bill, so that a
complete information was before the Committee while considering the Bill.

63rd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/63rdreport.htm[30-06-2016 17:34:36]
3.11     In the meantime, the Delhi High Court Employees Welfare Association was requested vide communication dated
20 January 2000 to submit their  updated memorandum on the provisions of the Bill for consideration of the
Committee. 
3.12     The Department of Justice vide communication dated 24 January, 2000 forwarded the detailed Background Note
alongwith a statement containing inter alia the details of Writ Petitions filed by the Court employees, recommendations
of the Fifth Central  Pay Commission, salary structure of the employees, proposed to be given through the Bill.
3.13     The Committee heard the presentation of the Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs on the provisions of the Bill in
the meeting held on 27 January, 2000.  The Committee in its meeting held on 8 February, 2000 decided to invite the
representatives of  the Delhi High Court Employees Welfare Association to hear their views in person before making
recommendations on their salaries, allowances, leave, pensions, etc.  
3.14     The Delhi High Court Employees Welfare Association submitted their updated memorandum (see appendix) on
4 February, 2000. 
3.15.    The Department of Justice  was requested vide 
communication 14 February, 2000 to furnish the para-wise
comments of the Government on the memorandum of the Association.   The Department submitted their response vide
communication dated 23 March, 2000 (see appendix). 
3.16
          The representatives of the Delhi High Court Employees’ Welfare Association appeared before the Committee on
29 May, 2000 to tender their oral evidence on the various provisions of the Bill.  The Association furnished  their
written responses (see appendix) to the points raised by the Members of the Committee during the course of their
evidence.
4.         The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill reads as under :-
Serious anomalies have crept into the pay scales of  the employees of the High Court of Delhi on account
of  various judgements and orders passed by the Court in Writ Petitions filed by its employees.  These
distortions and anomalies in the pay structures of the staff  of Delhi High Court are likely to cause serious
agitation amongst similarly placed staff of the Central Government and the Government of the National
Capital Territory of Delhi. 
This might ultimately lead to large scale distortions in the pay structure of the employees of the
Central Government and the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi  with attendant serious
consequential financial implications.  The Government examined the implications of the emerging
distortions in the pay structure of Court employees and considered it appropriate to enact suitable
legislation to rectify the situation as that was the only remedy available to the Government.
5.0       The High Court of Delhi has jurisdiction over the Union Territory of Delhi, now known as the National Capital
Territory of Delhi.  The NCT of Delhi has its own Legislative Assembly  and a Council of Ministers under the
Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991. 
5.1       Article 229(2) of the Constitution provides that –
Subject to the provisions of any law made by the Legislature of the State, the conditions of services of officers and
servants of a High Court shall be such as may be prescribed byrules made by the Chief Justice of the Court or by some
other judge or officer of the    Court authorised by the Chief Justice to make rules for the purpose:
 
Provided that the rules made under this clause shall, so far as they relate to salaries, allowances, leave or pensions,
require the approval of the Governor of the State.
5.2       The Delhi High Court  Act, 1966 constituted the High Court of Delhi.  Section 4(1)(d) (ii) of the Act of 1966
which relates to Article 229 provides as follows:
The references to the State Public Service Commission, the Legislature of the State and the Consolidated
Fund of the State shall be construed, respectively, as references to the Union Public Service Commission,
Parliament and the Consolidated Fund of India.
5.3       The Government of NCT Act, 1991 did not make any modification in the Delhi High Court Act of 1966 and,
therefore, Parliament continues to be the State Legislature for the Delhi High Court under the meaning of Article 229(2)
of the Constitution. 

63rd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/63rdreport.htm[30-06-2016 17:34:36]
5.4       Article 239AA of the Constitution which was inserted by the Constitution (Sixty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1991
relates to special provisions with respect to Delhi.  Although under sub-clause 3(a) of Article 239AA, the Legislative
Assembly of Delhi has power to make laws with respect to officers and servants of the Delhi High Court, but under sub-
clause 3(b) of  Article 239AA,  Parliament has been empowered to make laws with respect to any matter for a Union
Territory or any part thereof.
5.5
              In pursuance of the constitutional provisions the Chief Justice of Delhi High Court framed rules, namely, the
Delhi High Court Officers and Servants (Salaries, Allowances, Leave and Pensions) Rules, 1970.  Under these rules, the
officers and servants of the Delhi High Court were placed at par with corresponding employees of the Government of
NCT, Delhi and the pay scales were accordingly fixed on the standard Central Government pattern which is being
followed in the Government of NCT, Delhi.
6.0       In the Background Note, the Department of Justice has stated that before the setting up of  Delhi High Court in
1966, a Bench of the Punjab High Court was functioning at Delhi.  The salaries, allowances etc. of the employees
working in this Bench were being governed by the rules framed by the Chief Justice of the Punjab High Court.  Even
after the establishment of a separate High Court for Delhi in 1966, the rules relating to salaries etc. continued to apply
till the formulation of Delhi High Court Officers and Servants (Salary, Allowances, Leave and Pensions) Rules, 1970,
with effect from 1 April,1970.  The employees who originally came on deputation from the Punjab High Court were
given the choice of option for the Central scales of pay and being absorbed or reverting to the Punjab High Court within
a period of six months.
6.1       The Department of Justice informed the Committee that the equation of the employees of the Delhi High Court
vis-à-vis the employees of the Delhi Administration was disturbed on account of challenges to the basis of working out
the parities.  In 1980, the Private Secretaries to Judges filed a Writ Petition in the Delhi High Court (C.W.P. No.329/80-
P.N.  Chopra  Vs. Union of India) praying for a revision of pay scales from Rs.550-900/- to Rs.775-1200/- on the
grounds that the Private Secretary  to the Chief Secretary of Delhi Administration was getting the scale of Rs.775-1200/-
and as a Judge of the Delhi High Court was getting pay higher than the Chief Secretary, his PS should also get a salary
atleast equal to the Private Secretary  of the Chief Secretary, Delhi Administration.  This argument rested basically on
the principle of equal pay for equal work and by comparing the responsibility of Private Secretary  to Judge   with the
responsibilities of PS to Chief Secretary, Delhi Administration.  This Writ  was allowed by the Delhi High Court. 
Special Leave Petition against this judgement filed by the Government in the Supreme Court was dismissed .
 
6.2       The Department of Justice also informed the Committee that, thereafter, the Readers of Delhi High Court filed a
Writ stating that they should be given the same scales as Private Secretary to Judges on the basis of  ‘equal status posts’ 
and this Writ was also allowed by the Delhi High Court.  Later on, the Superintendents, Court Masters and Interpreters
in the Delhi High Court also got higher pay than their counterparts in the Delhi Administration as their Writ Petitions
were allowed by the Delhi High Court on the ground of ‘equal status post’.  The scale of  pay of  Private Secretary  to
Judges was further revised to Rs.3000-4500/- to bring them on par with Private Secretary  to Secretary to the
Government of India. 
6.3       The Committee was further informed that another form of challenge to the basis of equation arose in 1994 when
one Shri Kamla Nand, a Restorer in Delhi High Court, who had originally come to Delhi from Punjab & Haryana High
Court and opted for Central scale of pay, filed a Writ Petition seeking parity with the pay scale of Restorer in the Punjab
& Haryana High Court. 
6.4
              As on 1 January, 1978, the Punjab Government had merged dearness allowance with the salary and gave a
revised scale to its employees.  Their basic scale was, therefore, higher but the dearness allowance was lower.  As such,
there was really no basis for drawing comparison between the Delhi scales of pay which was based on Cost Price Index
at 200 and the Punjab scales of pay which was based on that at 320.  However, the Delhi High Court accepted the plea
of Shri Kamla Nand and gave him parity with the Punjab scale.   Accordingly, Shri Kamla Nand was given higher scale
of  pay.
6.5       Subsequently, Shri Kamla Nand filed a Civil Miscellaneous Petition in the Delhi High Court which ruled that he
should also be entitled to Central dearness allowance  on the Punjab pay scale.   This resulted in an anomalous position
viz.  that the total emoluments payable to the Restorers in Delhi High Court, based on Punjab pay scales and Central
dearness allowance,  exceeded the  total emoluments paid to either the Central or Punjab employees, holding
corresponding posts.

the debates in the Constituent Assembly on Articles 146 and 229 of the Constitution are relevant. Shri T.T.
Krishnamachari  observed as follows :-
“At the same time, Sir, I think it should be made clear that it is not the intention of the House or of the framers of
this Constitution that they want to create specially favoured bodies which in themselves become an Imperium in
Imperio, completely independent of
the Executive and Legislature and operate as a sort of superior body to the general body politic.”   (C.A. Deb.
Vol.VIII, 16 May – 16 June, 1949;p.389)
 
The submission of Dr. Ambedkar  is also extracted below :-
“But it seems to me that there is another consideration which goes to support the proposition that we should
retain the phrase with the approval of the President and it is this.  It  is undoubtedly a desirable thing that
salaries, allowances and pensions payable to the servants of the State should be uniform and there ought not to
be materialvariations in these matters with regard to the civil service.  It is likely to create a good deal of heart
burning and might impose on the treasury an unnecessary burden.  Now if you leave the matter to the Chief
Justice to decide, it is quite conceivable – I do not say that it will happen – but it is quite conceivable that the
Chief Justice might fix the scales of allowances, pensions and salaries very different from those fixed for civil
servants who are working in other departments besides the Judiciary, and I do not think that such a state of
things is desirable thing.”  (ibid)

Dissenting Note
 
            At a time when every Central Government employee has been given an abnormal raise in his or her emoluments,
the reduction of pay in certain cases is unfair and uncalled for.  In fact, it is punitive.

63rd Report

            An autonomous institution may have a different Pay structure base on nature of duties and responsibilities of its
employees.  It is for this reason perhaps that the pay structure of the employees of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha is
different from that of Government employees.
            The object of the Bill is meant to remove anomalies.  But no such anomalies exist.  Court judgements did the
job.                         
            There is no departure from the common rule between the scales of two classes of persons if they are not similar
as to their status, nature of work, duties, etc.  Employees of the Government and Courts have no similarity. 
Designations are also not similar.  Therefore, any equation based on mere designations is not fair.
            No evaluation of functions or work of Court employees against government employees has been undertaken.  In
Federation of All India Customs and Central Excise Stenographers (Recognised) and Other vs. Union of India and
Others vs. Union of India and Others (W.P.[Civil] No. 5019/82), a Bench of the Supreme Court questioning the value
judgement without rational basis, held as under :
“Equal pay for equal work is a concomitant of Article 14, but equal pay for unequal work will be a negation of
that right.  Equal pay must depend upon the nature of the work done; it cannot be judged by the mere volume of
work; there may be qualitative difference as regards reliability and responsibility.  Functions may be the same
but the responsibilities make a difference.  The same amount of physical work may entail different quality of
work, some more sensitive, some requiring more tact, some less  -  it varies from nature and culture of
employment.
                                    xx                                 xx                                
There is an element of value judgement by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of
pay and other conditions of service.  Differentiation in implementing the award or the recommendations of Pay
Commission without rational basis may amount to discrimination.  But so long as such value judgement is made
bonafide, reasonably on an intelligible criterion which has a rational nexus with the object of differentiation such
differentiation will not amount to discrimination.”
            The Bill strikes at the very root of the powers enjoyed by the High Courts and Supreme Court under Arts. 226
and 32 of the Constitution.
            Instead of removing anomalies, the bill creates them.  It disturbs the functional hierarchy of the Registry as laid
down in the Delhi High Court (Appointment and Conditions of Service) Rules, 1972.  It makes promotional posts lower
and feeder posts higher.  In an effort to
replace salaries, allowances, leave and pension Rules, the bill, as a matter of fact, touches upon conditions of service, in
respect of which the Chief Justice has already made Rules.
            The protection of pays, as envisaged in the Bill, is fallacious.  Its every application will reduce them in real terms
of allowances, such as DA, HRA etc. which are not payable on Personal Pay.  Similarly, for pension purposes, Personal
Pay would not count as pay, resulting in huge reduction in pay/pension.
            The Vth Pay Commission, an expert body appointed by the Government, went into the conditions of service of
Court employees and came to the conclusion that Court employees deserved higher scales of pay but observed that to
avoid wrong parallels being drawn, nomenclatures of various posts required to be changed/redefined in tune with the
nature of work, etc.  Since this has been done, the very basis of this Bill is knocked out.
            It is submitted that under Article 229(2) of the Constitution, the legislature of the State has power to make law in
respect of the conditions of service of the officers and servants of the High Court and under the proviso to Art. 229(2),
the Chief Justice has power to make rules relating to salaries, allowances, leave or pension in respect of the officers and
servants of the High Court but these would require the approval of the Governor.  Thus, Art. 229(2) is in two parts, first
providing for power of the legislature, besides the Chief Justice, to make laws in respect of conditions of service and
second, providing for framing of rules regarding salary etc. by the Chief Justice with the approval of the Governor.  It
would be seen that the legislature could only legislate in respect of conditions of service and not in respect of salary,
allowances, leave and pension of the High Court employees.
            Thus, the present bill which is in respect of salary, allowances, leave and pension should not be enacted because

of the Supreme Court’s judgement on M. Gurumoorthy vs. Accountant General and Ors (AIR 1971 Vol. 2 SCC 137). 
“Clause (1) read with clause (2) of Article 229 conferred exclusive power not only in the matter of appointments, but
also with regard to prescribing the conditions of service of officers and servants of a High Court by Rules on the Chief
Justice of the Court.  This is subject to any legislation by the state legislature but only in respect of conditions of
service.  In the matter of appointment even the Legislature cannot abridge or modify the powers conferred on the Chief
Justice under clause (1).  The approval of the Governor, as noticed in the matter of rules, is confined only to such rules
as relate to salaries, allowances, leave or pension.”

Committee heard them separately. The representatives pointed out those anomalies in the pay scales occurred due to
granting of separate scales to the officials of same category. This situation was rectified by the different Court orders.
They also questioned the legislative competence of Parliament to legislate on the subject and cited Articles 146 and 229
of the Constitution of India. The representatives also objected to the language of Objects and Reasons appended to the
Bills. They also justified granting of higher scales by the respective Chief Justices of Supreme Court and Delhi High
Court. Thereafter, Members put several queries pertaining to their presentation and the Bills. Some of the queries were
answered by the representatives while for rest of them Chairman directed them to send written responses to the
Secretariat.                                                                                                                    
4.         After presentation some of the Members raised doubt about legislative competence of Parliament. The Chairman
clarified that Articles 146(2) and 229 (2) empowered Parliament to make laws on the subject. Since this has not been
done in the last several years, the Chief Justices of Supreme Court and Delhi High Court had been framing rules
regarding service conditions, pay scales, etc. and getting approval from the President. The Chairman told that
Committee would have to take up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bills and would have to make recommendations
to the Government. Then Chairman ascertained the views of the Members present and it was decided to adopt the Bills
along with some modifications in the Objects of the Reasons of the Bills.

      Serious  anomalies have crept  into the pay-scales of the employees of the High Court  of Delhi on account of

R E P O R T
           I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs, having been
authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this Sixty-fourth Report of the Committee,
relating to the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999¨
.
2.        In pursuance of the Rules relating to Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees, the Chairman,
Rajya Sabha  referred©
 the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999,  as introduced in the Rajya Sabha on  23
December, 1999 and pending therein, to the Committee for examination  and report.
3.0      The Statement of  Objects and Reasons of the Bill states that the Government introduced a comprehensive
Companies Bill, 1997 in Rajya Sabha on 14 August, 1997 and the same was  referred to Standing Committee of
Parliament for examination and report thereon.  As the process of  examination was not yet over and Government
considered it desirable that some more important changes in the Companies  Act, 1956 were brought about in order to
provide immediately certain measures for good corporate governance and for protection of investors,   the present Bill
was introduced.
3.1      This Bill mainly seeks to ensure better corporate governance, transparency in working of companies and also

64th report of committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/64threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:35:37]
ensure more effective enforcement by enhancing the penalty/punishment for contravention so as to ensure better
compliance of the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956.
4.0      The present Committee in its first meeting held on 18 January, 2000, reviewed the status of the Bills/subjects
pending consideration of the Committee and noted that  a new Bill, namely, the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill,
1999, had been referred to it for examination and report.
4.1      The Committee, in its meeting held on 7 February, 2000, decided that it may  take up the Companies (Second
Amendment) Bill, 1999, for examination along with the Companies Bill, 1997, referred to it earlier, after the Budget
Session, as it would take considerable time to dispose them of.
5.        After the Budget Session was over, the Committee again  reviewed the position of the Bills pending before it, at
its meeting held on 17 May, 2000, and decided to give top priority to pending legislation and dispose them of in the
order of priority assigned by it. The Committee decided to take up the two Bills relating to the Company Law first
followed by other Bills, in the four rounds of sittings – 29, 30 & 31 May and 1 & 2 June,  in the first round; 12, 13 & 14
June  in the second round; 26, 27, 28, 29 & 30 June  in the third round;  and 10, 11, 12, 13 & 14 July, 2000 in the fourth
round. 
6.0      In its meeting held on 30May, 2000, the Committee heard the Secretary of the Department of Company Affairs
on the salient features of the two Bills, namely, the Companies Bill, 1997 and the Companies (Second Amendment)
Bill, 1999. 
6.1      The Secretary, Department of Company Affairs made a detailed presentation on the two Bills in the said meeting
of the Committee.  Following are the salient points of his presentation :-
º          As on 1
st January 2000 a total number of 5,32,580 companies were at work and their estimated paid up capital
was Rs. 2,72,865 crores. 
__________________________________________________________________________
2
 
º          India was in the forefront of Company Law.  The first Companies Act was enacted in 1913.  Certain amendments
were passed in 1936 and 1951.  The present Act was enacted  in 1956 as a result of Industrial Policy Resolution and
federalisation of corporate laws in different States, pursuant  to the integration of princely states in the Union of India.
º          The 1956 Act has been amended 17 times, in the years  1960, 1962, 1963, 1964 (twice), 1965, 1966 (twice),
1967, 1969, 1971, 1974, 1977, 1985, 1988, 1996 and 1999. 
º          There is an imperative need to further amend the Companies Act 1956 pursuant to the New Economic Policy
announced in 1991, rapid economic developments taking place globally, liberalisation of economies, access to world
market, WTO etc.
º          Further amendments to the law are necessary to facilitate healthy growth of Indian Corporate Sector under
liberalised and highly competitive environment.  Greater flexibility, transparency, disclosure, efficient enforcement,
tougher penalties, better investors’ protection are the felt needs of the time.
º          The requirements of liberalisation,  deregulation, simplification, changing economic scenario and international
corporate market make it necessary to amend the Company Law, lest our country would be lagging behind in terms of
growth, flexibility and international competitiveness in the globalised world. 
º          U.K., USA, Australia, Canada, EU etc. had already updated their Company Law. 
º          A Working Group was appointed by the Government on 5 August, 1996 which had  members  who were experts
in the fields of  law, economics and company affairs.  The Group  went into the entire gamut of the corporate laws and
submitted a comprehensive report in February 1997.  The said report was placed on the Table of both the Houses of
Parliament.  The comprehensive Companies Bill, 1997 is in essence the reflection of the consensus  in the report of the
Working Group. 
º          While drafting the Bill, the Department of Company Affairs took the help of the Reports  of  various 
Committees  which  went  into  the  concept  of  good   corporate governance, namely, the Cadbury Committee, the
Greenbury Committee, the Blue Ribbon Committee, the Organisation of Economic Cooperation  Development Code on
Corporate Governance (OECD) , besides the report of CII on Desirable Corporate Governance – A Code and Kumar
Mangalam Birla Committee on Corporate Governance.  The underlying themes of all these Reports are  transparency,
openness, disclosure, accountability etc.   The main principle that pervades corporate governance is the control of the
business by shareholders, reliable public reporting, avoidance of exclusive powers at the top, balanced board
composition, strong board of directors, strong audit process, assessment of risk and involvement of all  the shareholders
etc. 

64th report of committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/64threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:35:37]
º          After the introduction of the comprehensive Companies Bill, 1997, certain provisions of the said Bill were
incorporated in the Companies Amendment Act, 1999 which came into force w.e.f. 1.4.1999, first through an ordinance
and thereafter the ordinance was replaced by the Act of Parliament. 
3
º          Following are the salient features of the Companies Amendment Act, 1999 :-
           •          To allow companies to buy-back their shares;
           •          Provide for nomination facility to investors;
           •          Setting up of Investor Education and Protection Fund.
•          To allow companies to issue sweat equity in lieu of intellectual property to employees and directors;
•          Permit inter-corporate investment without prior approval of Central Government;
•          Constitution of National Advisory Committee on Accounting Standards.
º          After having implemented some of the features of the 1997 Bill in the First Amendment Act of 1999, some other
important features of the said Bill  have been included in the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999. 
º          Early passage of the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999 is necessary for the following reasons :-
Provide Investor friendly environment and attract investment in Indian Capital Market.
It will prepare ground for Indian companies to excel in a globally competitive market.
Create wealth for the shareholder and the Nation.
Promote good corporate governance.
7.        The Secretary, Department of Company Affairs then made an audio-visual presentation on the salient features of
the Companies (Second Amendment) Bill, 1999.  The  following are the highlights from his presentation : -
To provide transparency and good corporate governance;
Investors Protection;
Stringent penalties;
Repeal of redundant provisions;
Investors Protection Measures
Dividend including Interim Dividend to be paid within 30 days.
Effective curb on changing registered office frequently.
Offer of securities to more than 50 persons in financial year to be treated as public offer.
Small shareholders right to be represented on the board.
Corporate Governance
Minimum paid-up capital Rs. 1 lac for private companies, Rs. 5 lacs for public limited companies to prevent misuse of
facility of limited liability companies.
Capital market related provisions to be administered by Securities & Exchange Board of India (SEBI).
Director’s report to include a Director’s Responsibility Statement.
4
Public listed companies with paid-up capital of Rs.5 crores to set up Audit Committee.
Companies with paid-up capital of Rs. 10 lakhs or more to obtain a Secretarial Compliance Certificate .
Introduction of Postal Ballot for certain important matters which are crucial to good corporate governance.
 Appointment of Auditors in the Government Companies directly by Comptroller and Auditor General of India and
fixation of their remuneration by the shareholders in the Annual General Meeting.
Directors to be disqualified to be appointed as Directors in other public companies in case of non-filing of Annual
Returns and Annual Accounts for a continuous period of 3 years and non-payment of deposits etc. on maturity.
A person can not be Director in more than 15 companies .
Security holder of a company not to be appointed as Auditor of that company.
Stringent Penalties
Certain offences relating to deposits made cognizable.
Fines and Penalties enhanced by 10 times.
Repeal of Redundant provisions
Managing Agents, Secretaries and Treasures.
Deemed public companies.
Public Trustee.
8.        Having regard to the special importance of the two Bills, the Committee decided to invite views/suggestions in
the form of memoranda from the individuals/organisations /institutions etc. interested in the subject matter of the Bills.
Accordingly, advertisements were published through DAVP in all the major national dailies and vernacular newspapers

64th report of committee on Home Affairs
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Home%20Affairs/64threport.htm[30-06-2016 17:35:37]
all over the country. The Doordarshan’s national network had repeatedly telecast the contents of the press release in
prime time slots inviting suggestions from individuals/institutions/organisations on the provisions of the two Bills. 
9.        The Committee also invited suggestion/views of the major Chambers of Commerce and Industries, professional
bodies, such as, Confederation of Indian Industry (CII); Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India
(ASSOCHAM); Punjab, Haryana and Delhi (PHD) Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Federation of Indian
Chambers of Commerce and Industry (FICCI), Institute of  Company Secretaries of India (ICSI), Institute of Cost and
Works Accountants of India (ICWAI), Institute of  Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), Securities & Exchange
Board of India (SEBI), Industrial Credit & Investment Corporation of India Limited (ICICI), Bombay Chamber of
Commerce & Industry (BCCI), Steel  Authority of India Limited (SAIL), the Council of EU Chamber of  Commerce in
India and the Associated Cement Companies Limited (ACC)  on the amendments sought to be effected in the
Companies Act through these Bill.
10.      In all 56 memoranda containing comments and suggestions on the provisions of these two Bills were received by
the Committee from various organisations, associations and individuals etc. (see list of organisations/individuals etc. at
Appendix – A).
5
11.0     The Committee heard the views of various Chambers of Commerce, professional bodies and other organisations
(vide list at Appendix ‘B’) in its sitting spread over four days i.e. on 1,2,13 & 14 June, 2000 as per schedule given
below :-
Date of  Meeting                            Names of  Organisations heard
1.        1-6-2000                              CII, PHD Chamber of Commerce &                                                                  
Industries and ICSI
2.        2-6-2000                              ICWAI, ASSOCHAM  and  ICAI
3.        13-6-2000                            SEBI and  ICICI
4.        14-6-2000                            FICCI
11.1     A summary of  the suggestions/views received from different organisations and the comments of the Department
of Company Affairs thereon have been placed at Appendix ‘C’.
11.2     In course of evidence of the aforesaid organisations, a large number of suggestions/amendments were placed
before the Committee for its consideration. However, the major thrust of the suggestions/amendments may be
categorised into following five areas:-
Change of Registered Office of a Company – The proposed Section 17A which requires permission from  the
Regional Director even for shifting the Registered Office from one place to another will cause difficulties to the
Companies.It should be clarified that the provision of this clause should apply only in the case of change of Registered
Office of a Company from the jurisdiction of  one ROC to another ROC in the same State.
Postal Ballot -  It was contended that this system would be expensive, time consuming and un-implementable.
Offences  with regard to small depositors proposed to be made cognisable – This provision was rather drastic and
needed deletion.  Only Managing Director, Whole Time Director and promoters should be held responsible.  Only such
offences as are committed knowingly, willfully or with fraudulent intention should be severely punished.
Audit Committee – It was contended that since the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors was a creation thereof,
it would not be proper  to make its recommendations binding on its creator i.e. the Board of Directors.
Representation of small shareholders on the Board of Directors -     The provision for appointment of Directors on
the Board of Directors to represent the small investors may jeopardise  the homogeneity and integrated character of the
Board of Directors.
12.      The Committee would like to place on record its appreciation of the Secretary, Department of Company Affairs
and his team of officers for rendering valuable assistance to it from time to time in the course of consideration of the
Bills. The Committee would also like to thank the officers of the Department of Legal Affairs and the Legislative
Department for the assistance provided to it during the consideration of the Bills. The Committee also wishes to express
its sincere thanks to all the organisations/ persons who either appeared before it and/ or sent their valuable

19.0     The Committee notes that the nomenclature of the Companies Act  was framed almost a century ago.  In
the present day corporate parlance, corporate governance is being talked about.  In this context, the Committee
feels that the Government may deliberate on the need for changing the nomenclature of the Companies Act to
“Corporate Governance Act” because the whole purpose of the amendments sought to be made through the two
Bills  and those already enforced  by the Companies Amendment Act, 1999, is to ensure that there is 
transparency, efficiency, competitiveness  and effectiveness which are the hallmarks of good corporate

up action in the matter.

management, giving them adequate representation on the Board of Directors of Companies should be considered
by the Government.

Clauses” appended to the Bill were  insufficient, incomplete and examples of  paraphrasing without being able to
convey the purport of the amendments and the rationale behind them.  Such deficient notes were of hardly any
help to the Members while considering the Bills either in Parliament or in Committees.  It was further pointed
out that “Notes on Clauses”  were  being prepared almost in a routine and ritualistic  manner.
20.1     After some discussion, the Committee directed the representatives of the Department of Company Affairs
and the Legislative Department to take note of the objections raised and take corrective steps in future.
20.2     The Committee hopes that in future the “Notes on Clauses”    appended to the Bills  would be meaningful
and helpful to the Members.

years .  The liquidator used to inform the High Court  whether he had discharged his duties as a liquidator or not.  In the
meantime, there were problems like recovery of dues, sale of assets , making recovery as fast as possible, in order to

therefore, suggested that it would be better if  a  liquidator  like  a intermediary,  and registered with the SEBI  and 
fulfilled  some prescribed minimum criteria, was allowed to act as an official liquidator, then he would be in a position
to reduce that time lag.

Section 55A needs substantial amendments to clarify the doubts expressed and issues raised by Securities & Exchange

loan/debenture into equity [Section 81(3) & (4) ], depreciation methods (Section 205) and power to make rule and
